entries.original_title: Molecular architecture of the developing mouse brain
entries.original_abstract: The mammalian brain develops through a complex interplay of spatial cues generated by diffusible morphogens, cell–cell interactions and intrinsic genetic programs that result in probably more than a thousand distinct cell types. A complete understanding of this process requires a systematic characterization of cell states over the entire spatiotemporal range of brain development. The ability of single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics to reveal the molecular heterogeneity of complex tissues has therefore been particularly powerful in the nervous system. Previous studies have explored development in specific brain regions1–8, the whole adult brain9 and even entire embryos10. Here we report a comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the embryonic mouse brain between gastrulation and birth. We identified almost eight hundred cellular states that describe a developmental program for the functional elements of the brain and its enclosing membranes, including the early neuroepithelium, region-specific secondary organizers, and both neurogenic and gliogenic progenitors. We also used in situ mRNA sequencing to map the spatial expression patterns of key developmental genes. Integrating the in situ data with our single-cell clusters revealed the precise spatial organization of neural progenitors during the patterning of the nervous system. A comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the mouse brain between gastrulation and birth identifies hundreds of cellular states and reveals the spatiotemporal organization of brain development.
entries.anonymized_problem: A comprehensive characterization of mammalian brain development requires systematic mapping of cell states across the full spatiotemporal range from early embryogenesis to birth. Previous single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies have addressed specific brain regions, the adult whole brain, or entire embryos, but a unified atlas spanning gastrulation through birth has been lacking. This study presents a single-cell RNA sequencing atlas of the embryonic mouse brain covering this entire developmental window, identifying approximately 800 distinct cellular states that collectively describe the developmental program of major brain functional elements and enclosing membranes. Characterized populations include early neuroepithelium, region-specific secondary organizers, and neurogenic and gliogenic progenitor subtypes. In addition, in situ mRNA sequencing was applied to map the spatial expression patterns of key developmental genes across tissue sections. Integration of spatial transcriptomic data with single-cell cluster annotations revealed the precise spatial organization of neural progenitors during nervous system patterning. Together, these resources provide a molecular framework linking cell-type identity to spatial position across embryonic brain development, offering a foundation for understanding how morphogen gradients, cell–cell interactions, and intrinsic genetic programs collectively generate the diversity of cell types in the mammalian brain.

entries.original_title: Key Parameters of Tumor Epitope Immunogenicity Revealed Through a Consortium Approach Improve Neoantigen Prediction.
entries.original_abstract: Many approaches to identify therapeutically relevant neoantigens couple tumor sequencing with bioinformatic algorithms and inferred rules of tumor epitope immunogenicity. However, there are no reference data to compare these approaches, and the parameters governing tumor epitope immunogenicity remain unclear. Here, we assembled a global consortium wherein each participant predicted immunogenic epitopes from shared tumor sequencing data. 608 epitopes were subsequently assessed for T cell binding in patient-matched samples. By integrating peptide features associated with presentation and recognition, we developed a model of tumor epitope immunogenicity that filtered out 98% of non-immunogenic peptides with a precision above 0.70. Pipelines prioritizing model features had superior performance, and pipeline alterations leveraging them improved prediction performance. These findings were validated in an independent cohort of 310 epitopes prioritized from tumor sequencing data and assessed for T cell binding. This data resource enables identification of parameters underlying effective anti-tumor immunity and is available to the research community.
entries.anonymized_problem: Identifying therapeutically relevant neoantigens typically involves coupling tumor sequencing with bioinformatic algorithms and inferred rules governing epitope immunogenicity, yet no standardized reference datasets exist for comparing these approaches, and the parameters determining tumor epitope immunogenicity remain incompletely understood. To address this, a global consortium was assembled in which multiple independent participants each predicted immunogenic epitopes from shared tumor sequencing data. A total of 608 predicted epitopes were subsequently assessed for T cell binding using patient-matched samples. By integrating peptide features associated with MHC presentation and T cell recognition, an immunogenicity model was developed that filtered out 98% of non-immunogenic peptides while achieving a precision above 0.70. Analytical pipelines that prioritized the identified model features demonstrated superior performance, and targeted modifications to existing pipelines incorporating these features yielded measurable improvements in prediction accuracy. Findings were independently validated in a separate cohort of 310 epitopes prioritized from tumor sequencing data and assessed for T cell binding. The resulting dataset provides a benchmark resource for the research community, enabling systematic identification of the parameters underlying effective anti-tumor immune responses and supporting the refinement of neoantigen prediction methodologies.

entries.original_title: Lymph nodes are innervated by a unique population of sensory neurons with immunomodulatory potential.
entries.original_abstract: Barrier tissue immune responses are regulated in part by nociceptors. Nociceptor ablation alters local immune responses at peripheral sites and within draining lymph nodes (LNs). The mechanisms and significance of nociceptor-dependent modulation of LN function are unknown. Using high-resolution imaging, viral tracing, single-cell transcriptomics, and optogenetics, we identified and functionally tested a sensory neuro-immune circuit that is responsive to lymph-borne inflammatory signals. Transcriptomics profiling revealed that multiple sensory neuron subsets, predominantly peptidergic nociceptors, innervate LNs, distinct from those innervating surrounding skin. To uncover LN-resident cells that may interact with LN-innervating sensory neurons, we generated a LN single-cell transcriptomics atlas and nominated nociceptor target populations and interaction modalities. Optogenetic stimulation of LN-innervating sensory fibers triggered rapid transcriptional changes in the predicted interacting cell types, particularly endothelium, stromal cells, and innate leukocytes. Thus, a unique population of sensory neurons monitors peripheral LNs and may locally regulate gene expression.
entries.anonymized_problem: Barrier tissue immune responses are partially regulated by nociceptors, yet the mechanisms by which these sensory neurons modulate lymph node (LN) function remain poorly understood. This study investigated the identity, connectivity, and functional significance of sensory neurons innervating LNs using high-resolution imaging, viral tracing, single-cell transcriptomics, and optogenetics. Transcriptomic profiling revealed that multiple sensory neuron subsets—predominantly peptidergic nociceptors—innervate LNs, and that this population is transcriptionally distinct from sensory neurons innervating the surrounding skin. A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of LN-resident cells was constructed to identify candidate target populations and interaction modalities for these LN-innervating neurons, nominating endothelium, stromal cells, and innate leukocytes as principal interacting cell types. Optogenetic stimulation of LN-innervating sensory fibers produced rapid transcriptional changes in these predicted interacting populations, consistent with local neuroimmune signaling. Together, the findings demonstrate that a transcriptionally distinct sensory neuron population monitors peripheral LNs and responds to lymph-borne inflammatory signals, with the capacity to locally regulate gene expression in immune and stromal compartments. These results establish a sensory neuro-immune circuit within LNs that may contribute to the modulation of adaptive and innate immune responses at these secondary lymphoid organs.

entries.original_title: Entropic evidence for a Pomeranchuk effect in magic-angle graphene
entries.original_abstract: In the 1950s, Pomeranchuk1 predicted that, counterintuitively, liquid 3He may solidify on heating. This effect arises owing to high excess nuclear spin entropy in the solid phase, where the atoms are spatially localized. Here we find that an analogous effect occurs in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene2–6. Using both local and global electronic entropy measurements, we show that near a filling of one electron per moiré unit cell, there is a marked increase in the electronic entropy to about 1kB per unit cell (kB is the Boltzmann constant). This large excess entropy is quenched by an in-plane magnetic field, pointing to its magnetic origin. A sharp drop in the compressibility as a function of the electron density, associated with a reset of the Fermi level back to the vicinity of the Dirac point, marks a clear boundary between two phases. We map this jump as a function of electron density, temperature and magnetic field. This reveals a phase diagram that is consistent with a Pomeranchuk-like temperature- and field-driven transition from a low-entropy electronic liquid to a high-entropy correlated state with nearly free magnetic moments. The correlated state features an unusual combination of seemingly contradictory properties, some associated with itinerant electrons—such as the absence of a thermodynamic gap, metallicity and a Dirac-like compressibility—and others associated with localized moments, such as a large entropy and its disappearance under a magnetic field. Moreover, the energy scales characterizing these two sets of properties are very different: whereas the compressibility jump has an onset at a temperature of about 30 kelvin, the bandwidth of magnetic excitations is about 3 kelvin or smaller. The hybrid nature of the present correlated state and the large separation of energy scales have implications for the thermodynamic and transport properties of the correlated states in twisted bilayer graphene. Magic-angle graphene is found to have an exotic phase transition where, on heating, entropy is transferred from motional to magnetic degrees of freedom, analogously to the Pomeranchuk effect in 3He.
entries.anonymized_problem: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene hosts a rich variety of correlated electron phases, but the thermodynamic character of transitions between them remains incompletely understood. This study investigates whether a Pomeranchuk-like effect—where heating drives a transition from a low-entropy to a high-entropy phase due to excess magnetic moment entropy—can occur in a two-dimensional moiré electron system. Using both local and global electronic entropy measurements near a filling of one electron per moiré unit cell, a marked increase in electronic entropy to approximately 1k_B per unit cell is observed. This excess entropy is quenched by an in-plane magnetic field, identifying its origin as magnetic. A sharp drop in compressibility with increasing electron density, associated with a reset of the Fermi level toward the Dirac point, delineates two distinct phases. Mapping this feature across electron density, temperature, and magnetic field reveals a phase diagram consistent with a temperature- and field-driven transition from a low-entropy electronic liquid to a high-entropy correlated state bearing nearly free magnetic moments. The correlated phase combines properties of both itinerant electrons (no thermodynamic gap, metallicity, Dirac-like compressibility) and localized moments (large entropy suppressed by magnetic field), with a striking separation of energy scales: the compressibility jump onsets near 30 K, while the magnetic excitation bandwidth is approximately 3 K or less.

entries.original_title: Pathogenesis of SARS-CoV-2 in Transgenic Mice Expressing Human Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2
entries.original_abstract: COVID-19 has spread worldwide since 2019 and is now a severe threat to public health. We previously identified the causative agent as a novel SARS-related coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) that uses human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (hACE2) as the entry receptor. Here, we successfully developed a SARS-CoV-2 hACE2 transgenic mouse (HFH4-hACE2 in C3B6 mice) infection model. The infected mice generated typical interstitial pneumonia and pathology that were similar to those of COVID-19 patients. Viral quantification revealed the lungs as the major site of infection, although viral RNA could also be found in the eye, heart, and brain in some mice. Virus identical to SARS-CoV-2 in full-genome sequences was isolated from the infected lung and brain tissues. Last, we showed that pre-exposure to SARS-CoV-2 could protect mice from severe pneumonia. Our results show that the hACE2 mouse would be a valuable tool for testing potential vaccines and therapeutics.
entries.anonymized_problem: A transgenic mouse model was developed to study SARS-CoV-2 infection by expressing human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (hACE2) under the HFH4 promoter in a C3B6 background, given that standard mice are not susceptible to the virus due to receptor incompatibility. The study aimed to establish a reproducible small-animal model that recapitulates the pathology observed in human COVID-19 cases. Following intranasal inoculation with SARS-CoV-2, infected animals developed interstitial pneumonia with histopathological features consistent with those reported in human patients. Viral quantification across tissues identified the lungs as the primary site of replication, with viral RNA also detected in the eye, heart, and brain in a subset of animals. Virus recovered from infected lung and brain tissues was confirmed to be identical to the input strain by full-genome sequencing. Additionally, prior exposure to SARS-CoV-2 conferred protection against severe pneumonia upon re-challenge, suggesting the induction of protective immunity. These findings establish the hACE2 transgenic mouse as a suitable platform for evaluating candidate vaccines and antiviral therapeutics against SARS-CoV-2, and they provide a defined model system for investigating tissue tropism and disease mechanisms underlying COVID-19.

entries.original_title: Memory Sequencing Reveals Heritable Single-Cell Gene Expression Programs Associated with Distinct Cellular Behaviors.
entries.original_abstract: Non-genetic factors can cause individual cells to fluctuate substantially in gene expression levels over time. It remains unclear whether these fluctuations can persist for much longer than the time of one cell division. Current methods for measuring gene expression in single cells mostly rely on single time point measurements, making the duration of gene expression fluctuations or cellular memory difficult to measure. Here, we combined Luria and Delbrück's fluctuation analysis with population-based RNA sequencing (MemorySeq) for identifying genes transcriptome-wide whose fluctuations persist for several divisions. MemorySeq revealed multiple gene modules that expressed together in rare cells within otherwise homogeneous clonal populations. These rare cell subpopulations were associated with biologically distinct behaviors like proliferation in the face of anti-cancer therapeutics. The identification of non-genetic, multigenerational fluctuations can reveal new forms of biological memory in single cells and suggests that non-genetic heritability of cellular state may be a quantitative property.
entries.anonymized_problem: Isogenic cell populations exhibit substantial cell-to-cell variability in gene expression, yet it remains unclear whether non-genetic fluctuations in gene expression can persist across multiple cell divisions. Standard single-cell transcriptomic approaches capture only single time points, making it difficult to assess the duration or heritability of such fluctuations. To address this, a method combining classical fluctuation analysis (originally developed to distinguish random mutation timing from induced variation) with population-level RNA sequencing was applied to identify, transcriptome-wide, genes whose expression fluctuations persist across several cell divisions. Applied to clonal, otherwise homogeneous cell populations, this approach identified multiple co-expressed gene modules that appear transiently in rare cell subpopulations. These rare subpopulations exhibited functionally distinct behaviors, including the capacity to proliferate in the presence of anti-cancer therapeutics, suggesting that transient non-genetic states can have meaningful phenotypic consequences. The findings indicate that multigenerational, non-genetic heritability of gene expression states is a measurable and quantitative property of cell populations, distinct from genetic mutation. This framework offers a means to detect and characterize forms of cellular memory that are invisible to conventional single time point measurements, with implications for understanding drug resistance and phenotypic heterogeneity in cancer.

entries.original_title: PLA2G6 guards placental trophoblasts against ferroptotic injury
entries.original_abstract: Significance Placental dysfunction has been causally linked to major pregnancy complications that are implicated in maternal–fetal morbidity and mortality, but the mechanisms underlying placental dysfunction are largely unknown. The recently identified ferroptotic cell death is characterized by excessive accumulation of hydroperoxide phosphatidylethanolamines. While oxidative damage commonly defines placental dysfunction, the role of ferroptosis in this process is largely unknown. We found that preterm birth is associated with ferroptotic signals, and that inhibition of GPX4, which converts unstable lipid hydroperoxides to nontoxic lipid alcohols, causes ferroptotic injury in primary human trophoblasts and in mouse pregnancy. Importantly, we found that the phospholipase PLA2G6 mitigates trophoblast and placental ferroptosis. Together, we identified placental ferroptosis and established a role for PLA2G6 in attenuating ferroptosis. The recently identified ferroptotic cell death is characterized by excessive accumulation of hydroperoxy-arachidonoyl (C20:4)- or adrenoyl (C22:4)- phosphatidylethanolamine (Hp-PE). The selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) inhibits ferroptosis, converting unstable ferroptotic lipid hydroperoxides to nontoxic lipid alcohols in a tissue-specific manner. While placental oxidative stress and lipotoxicity are hallmarks of placental dysfunction, the possible role of ferroptosis in placental dysfunction is largely unknown. We found that spontaneous preterm birth is associated with ferroptosis and that inhibition of GPX4 causes ferroptotic injury in primary human trophoblasts and during mouse pregnancy. Importantly, we uncovered a role for the phospholipase PLA2G6 (PNPLA9, iPLA2beta), known to metabolize Hp-PE to lyso-PE and oxidized fatty acid, in mitigating ferroptosis induced by GPX4 inhibition in vitro or by hypoxia/reoxygenation injury in vivo. Together, we identified ferroptosis signaling in the human and mouse placenta, established a role for PLA2G6 in attenuating trophoblastic ferroptosis, and provided mechanistic insights into the ill-defined placental lipotoxicity that may inspire PLA2G6-targeted therapeutic strategies.
entries.anonymized_problem: Placental dysfunction underlies major pregnancy complications contributing to maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality, yet the molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined. This study investigates whether ferroptosis — a form of regulated cell death driven by excessive accumulation of hydroperoxy-phosphatidylethanolamine (Hp-PE) species — contributes to placental dysfunction and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Using primary human trophoblasts, mouse pregnancy models, and human placental tissue from spontaneous preterm births, the study combined pharmacological inhibition of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), hypoxia/reoxygenation injury, lipidomic profiling, and genetic approaches to interrogate ferroptotic signaling. Spontaneous preterm birth was found to be associated with ferroptotic lipid peroxidation signatures in placental tissue. Inhibition of GPX4, which normally converts ferroptotic lipid hydroperoxides to nontoxic lipid alcohols, induced ferroptotic injury in both trophoblast cell cultures and in vivo mouse pregnancy. The phospholipase PLA2G6 — which cleaves Hp-PE to generate lyso-PE and oxidized fatty acids — was identified as a protective factor that mitigates ferroptosis under both GPX4 inhibition in vitro and hypoxia/reoxygenation conditions in vivo. These findings establish ferroptosis as a mechanism in placental lipotoxicity and identify PLA2G6 as an endogenous attenuator of trophoblastic ferroptosis, suggesting it as a potential therapeutic target for placental dysfunction-related pregnancy complications.

entries.original_title: A hydrophobic ratchet entrenches molecular complexes
entries.original_abstract: Most proteins assemble into multisubunit complexes 1 . The persistence of these complexes across evolutionary time is usually explained as the result of natural selection for functional properties that depend on multimerization, such as intersubunit allostery or the capacity to do mechanical work 2 . In many complexes, however, multimerization does not enable any known function 3 . An alternative explanation is that multimers could become entrenched if substitutions accumulate that are neutral in multimers but deleterious in monomers; purifying selection would then prevent reversion to the unassembled form, even if assembly per se does not enhance biological function 3 – 7 . Here we show that a hydrophobic mutational ratchet systematically entrenches molecular complexes. By applying ancestral protein reconstruction and biochemical assays to the evolution of steroid hormone receptors, we show that an ancient hydrophobic interface, conserved for hundreds of millions of years, is entrenched because exposure of this interface to solvent reduces protein stability and causes aggregation, even though the interface makes no detectable contribution to function. Using structural bioinformatics, we show that a universal mutational propensity drives sites that are buried in multimeric interfaces to accumulate hydrophobic substitutions to levels that are not tolerated in monomers. In a database of hundreds of families of multimers, most show signatures of long-term hydrophobic entrenchment. It is therefore likely that many protein complexes persist because a simple ratchet-like mechanism entrenches them across evolutionary time, even when they are functionally gratuitous. Accumulation of hydrophobic residues at the interface between monomers may favour the maintenance of multimeric protein states during evolution, even if multimerization confers no functional advantage.
entries.anonymized_problem: Proteins commonly assemble into multisubunit complexes, yet the evolutionary mechanisms maintaining these assemblies remain incompletely understood. Functional explanations invoke selection for properties requiring multimerization—such as allostery or mechanical work—but many complexes lack identifiable multimerization-dependent functions. An alternative hypothesis holds that assemblies become entrenched when neutral substitutions accumulate that are tolerated in multimers but deleterious in monomers, causing purifying selection to prevent reversion to unassembled forms regardless of whether assembly confers functional benefit. This study investigates whether a hydrophobic mutational ratchet systematically drives such entrenchment. Ancestral protein reconstruction combined with biochemical assays was applied to steroid hormone receptor evolution, demonstrating that an ancient hydrophobic interface conserved over hundreds of millions of years is entrenched because solvent exposure of that interface reduces protein stability and induces aggregation, despite making no detectable functional contribution. Structural bioinformatics analysis across a large database of multimer families reveals a universal mutational propensity: sites buried at multimeric interfaces systematically accumulate hydrophobic substitutions at levels incompatible with monomeric stability. Signatures of long-term hydrophobic entrenchment are observed in most surveyed multimer families. These findings indicate that accumulation of hydrophobic residues at subunit interfaces constitutes a broadly operating ratchet-like mechanism that maintains protein complexes across evolutionary time independent of any functional advantage conferred by multimerization.

entries.original_title: Patrolling Alveolar Macrophages Conceal Bacteria from the Immune System to Maintain Homeostasis.
entries.original_abstract: During respiration, humans breathe in more than 10,000 liters of non-sterile air daily, allowing some pathogens access to alveoli. Interestingly, alveoli outnumber alveolar macrophages (AMs), which favors alveoli devoid of AMs. If AMs, like most tissue macrophages, are sessile, then this numerical advantage would be exploited by pathogens unless neutrophils from the blood stream intervened. However, this would translate to omnipresent persistent inflammation. Developing in vivo real-time intravital imaging of alveoli revealed AMs crawling in and between alveoli using the pores of Kohn. Importantly, these macrophages sensed, chemotaxed, and, with high efficiency, phagocytosed inhaled bacterial pathogens such as P. aeruginosa and S. aureus, cloaking the bacteria from neutrophils. Impairing AM chemotaxis toward bacteria induced superfluous neutrophil recruitment, leading to inappropriate inflammation and injury. In a disease context, influenza A virus infection impaired AM crawling via the type II interferon signaling pathway, and this greatly increased secondary bacterial co-infection.
entries.anonymized_problem: Alveolar macrophages (AMs) are the primary immune sentinels of the lung, yet alveoli outnumber AMs, raising the question of how respiratory surfaces are efficiently surveilled without triggering persistent inflammation. To address this, real-time intravital imaging of alveoli was developed to observe AM behavior in living animals. AMs were found to actively patrol alveolar surfaces by crawling within and between alveoli through the pores of Kohn, rather than remaining sessile as many tissue macrophages do. These patrolling cells efficiently sensed and chemotaxed toward inhaled bacterial pathogens, including *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and *Staphylococcus aureus*, phagocytosing them with high efficiency and physically concealing them from circulating neutrophils—a process termed cloaking. When AM chemotaxis was experimentally impaired, excessive neutrophil recruitment occurred, resulting in inappropriate inflammation and tissue injury. In a disease-relevant context, influenza A virus infection disrupted AM crawling behavior through the type II interferon signaling pathway, substantially increasing susceptibility to secondary bacterial co-infection. These findings establish active AM patrolling as a critical homeostatic mechanism that balances effective bacterial clearance against the inflammatory costs of neutrophil mobilization, and identify its disruption as a mechanism underlying post-viral bacterial co-infection.

entries.original_title: Performance vs. competence in human–machine comparisons
entries.original_abstract: Does the human mind resemble the machines that can behave like it? Biologically inspired machine-learning systems approach “human-level” accuracy in an astounding variety of domains, and even predict human brain activity—raising the exciting possibility that such systems represent the world like we do. However, even seemingly intelligent machines fail in strange and “unhumanlike” ways, threatening their status as models of our minds. How can we know when human–machine behavioral differences reflect deep disparities in their underlying capacities, vs. when such failures are only superficial or peripheral? This article draws on a foundational insight from cognitive science—the distinction between performance and competence—to encourage “species-fair” comparisons between humans and machines. The performance/competence distinction urges us to consider whether the failure of a system to behave as ideally hypothesized, or the failure of one creature to behave like another, arises not because the system lacks the relevant knowledge or internal capacities (“competence”), but instead because of superficial constraints on demonstrating that knowledge (“performance”). I argue that this distinction has been neglected by research comparing human and machine behavior, and that it should be essential to any such comparison. Focusing on the domain of image classification, I identify three factors contributing to the species-fairness of human–machine comparisons, extracted from recent work that equates such constraints. Species-fair comparisons level the playing field between natural and artificial intelligence, so that we can separate more superficial differences from those that may be deep and enduring.
entries.anonymized_problem: The question of whether artificial neural systems represent the world similarly to the human mind motivates this theoretical and empirical synthesis. Although machine-learning systems increasingly match human-level accuracy across many domains and can predict neural activity patterns, such systems also fail in qualitatively atypical ways, casting doubt on their value as cognitive models. The core conceptual problem addressed is how to determine whether observed behavioral differences between humans and machines reflect genuine disparities in underlying knowledge and representational capacity (competence) versus superficial constraints on expressing that knowledge (performance). Drawing on the foundational performance/competence distinction from cognitive science, the analysis argues for "species-fair" comparisons that equate task conditions across natural and artificial systems before drawing inferences about internal representations. Focusing on image classification as a test domain, three factors that contribute to the fairness of such comparisons are identified by synthesizing recent empirical work that attempts to equate task constraints across humans and machines. The central finding is that many apparent human–machine differences dissolve or diminish under species-fair conditions, suggesting that conclusions about deep representational disparities drawn from conventional comparisons may be premature. Adopting the performance/competence framework is proposed as a principled requirement for any behavioral comparison between biological and artificial intelligence.

entries.original_title: A Global Map of G Protein Signaling Regulation by RGS Proteins
entries.original_abstract: Summary The control over the extent and timing of G protein signaling is provided by the regulator of G protein signaling (RGS) proteins that deactivate G protein α subunits (Gα). Mammalian genomes encode 20 canonical RGS and 16 Gα genes with key roles in physiology and disease. To understand the principles governing the selectivity of Gα regulation by RGS, we examine the catalytic activity of all canonical human RGS proteins and their selectivity for a complete set of Gα substrates using real-time kinetic measurements in living cells. The data reveal rules governing RGS-Gα recognition, the structural basis of its selectivity, and provide principles for engineering RGS proteins with defined selectivity. The study also explores the evolution of RGS-Gα selectivity through ancestral reconstruction and demonstrates how naturally occurring non-synonymous variants in RGS alter signaling. These results provide a blueprint for decoding signaling selectivity and advance our understanding of molecular recognition principles.
entries.anonymized_problem: A comprehensive examination of the selectivity governing interactions between regulators of G protein signaling (RGS proteins) and G protein α subunits (Gα) is presented. Mammalian genomes encode 20 canonical RGS proteins and 16 Gα genes, yet the principles determining which RGS proteins regulate which Gα substrates remain incompletely understood. To address this gap, the catalytic activity of all 20 canonical human RGS proteins was systematically measured against a complete set of Gα substrates using real-time kinetic assays in living cells, generating a global interaction map. Analysis of this dataset reveals rules governing RGS-Gα molecular recognition and the structural basis of selectivity, providing a framework for engineering RGS proteins with defined substrate preferences. The study further employs ancestral sequence reconstruction to trace the evolutionary origins of RGS-Gα selectivity, and examines how naturally occurring non-synonymous variants in RGS genes alter downstream signaling outcomes. Collectively, these findings establish a systematic blueprint for decoding signaling selectivity across the full RGS-Gα interaction space and advance mechanistic understanding of molecular recognition within G protein signaling networks relevant to both physiology and disease.

entries.original_title: SARS-CoV-2 Disrupts Splicing, Translation, and Protein Trafficking to Suppress Host Defenses
entries.original_abstract: Summary Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is a recently identified coronavirus that causes the respiratory disease known as coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Despite the urgent need, we still do not fully understand the molecular basis of SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis. Here, we comprehensively define the interactions between SARS-CoV-2 proteins and human RNAs. NSP16 binds to the mRNA recognition domains of the U1 and U2 splicing RNAs and acts to suppress global mRNA splicing upon SARS-CoV-2 infection. NSP1 binds to 18S ribosomal RNA in the mRNA entry channel of the ribosome and leads to global inhibition of mRNA translation upon infection. Finally, NSP8 and NSP9 bind to the 7SL RNA in the signal recognition particle and interfere with protein trafficking to the cell membrane upon infection. Disruption of each of these essential cellular functions acts to suppress the interferon response to viral infection. Our results uncover a multipronged strategy utilized by SARS-CoV-2 to antagonize essential cellular processes to suppress host defenses.
entries.anonymized_problem: SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis involves complex virus-host interactions that remain incompletely understood at the molecular level. This study comprehensively maps the interactions between SARS-CoV-2 proteins and human RNAs to elucidate how the virus suppresses cellular antiviral responses. Using systematic protein-RNA interaction profiling, three distinct mechanisms were identified. One viral nonstructural protein binds to the mRNA recognition domains of U1 and U2 splicing RNAs, globally suppressing host mRNA splicing during infection. A second nonstructural protein binds to 18S ribosomal RNA within the mRNA entry channel of the ribosome, causing global inhibition of host mRNA translation. Two additional viral proteins bind to 7SL RNA within the signal recognition particle, disrupting protein trafficking to the cell membrane. Each of these disruptions individually impairs the interferon response to viral infection, and together they constitute a multipronged strategy by which SARS-CoV-2 antagonizes three essential cellular processes—splicing, translation, and protein secretion—to collectively suppress innate immune defenses. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how SARS-CoV-2 co-opts fundamental host RNA-based machinery to evade immune detection and establish infection.

entries.original_title: Stressful Beginnings with Long-Term Consequences.
entries.original_abstract: Early-life stress can have long-term health consequences, but the mechanisms of this are unknown. In this issue of Cell, Hong et al. demonstrate one such mechanism linking perinatal corticosteroid exposure to reduced CD8+ T cell function later in life and impaired anti-cancer and anti-bacterial immune responses.
entries.anonymized_problem: Early-life stress is associated with long-term health consequences, but the underlying biological mechanisms remain poorly understood. This work examines how perinatal exposure to corticosteroids — stress hormones present during early developmental windows — affects immune function in later life. The approach involves analyzing research demonstrating a mechanistic link between corticosteroid exposure during the perinatal period and durable alterations in CD8+ T cell function. The findings indicate that early corticosteroid exposure impairs CD8+ T cell activity in adulthood, with downstream consequences for both anti-tumor and anti-bacterial immune responses. This work identifies a specific immunological pathway through which early-life physiological stress can program long-lasting deficits in adaptive immunity, providing a mechanistic explanation for the well-documented but poorly understood relationship between perinatal stress and increased susceptibility to disease later in life. These findings have implications for understanding how developmental timing of stress hormone exposure shapes immune competence across the lifespan, particularly in the context of cancer surveillance and defense against intracellular bacterial pathogens.

entries.original_title: Real-time optimal quantum control of mechanical motion at room temperature
entries.original_abstract: The ability to accurately control the dynamics of physical systems by measurement and feedback is a pillar of modern engineering1. Today, the increasing demand for applied quantum technologies requires adaptation of this level of control to individual quantum systems2,3. Achieving this in an optimal way is a challenging task that relies on both quantum-limited measurements and specifically tailored algorithms for state estimation and feedback4. Successful implementations thus far include experiments on the level of optical and atomic systems5–7. Here we demonstrate real-time optimal control of the quantum trajectory8 of an optically trapped nanoparticle. We combine confocal position sensing close to the Heisenberg limit with optimal state estimation via Kalman filtering to track the particle motion in phase space in real time with a position uncertainty of 1.3 times the zero-point fluctuation. Optimal feedback allows us to stabilize the quantum harmonic oscillator to a mean occupation of 0.56 ± 0.02 quanta, realizing quantum ground-state cooling from room temperature. Our work establishes quantum Kalman filtering as a method to achieve quantum control of mechanical motion, with potential implications for sensing on all scales. In combination with levitation, this paves the way to full-scale control over the wavepacket dynamics of solid-state macroscopic quantum objects in linear and nonlinear systems. Optimal quantum control of an optically trapped nanoparticle in its ground state is demonstrated at room temperature, using Kalman filtering to track its quantum trajectory in real time.
entries.anonymized_problem: Controlling individual quantum systems through measurement and feedback represents a key challenge for applied quantum technologies, requiring quantum-limited measurements alongside algorithms optimized for state estimation and real-time feedback. This work addresses the problem of achieving such optimal quantum control over a macroscopic mechanical object at room temperature. The experimental approach combines confocal position sensing operating near the Heisenberg limit with Kalman filtering for optimal state estimation, enabling tracking of a levitated nanoparticle's motion in phase space in real time. Position uncertainty is maintained at 1.3 times the zero-point fluctuation. Optimal feedback control is then applied to cool the quantum harmonic oscillator to a mean phonon occupation of 0.56 ± 0.02 quanta, corresponding to quantum ground-state cooling from room temperature. The results establish Kalman filtering as a viable framework for quantum control of mechanical motion, applicable to sensing across multiple scales. The levitated geometry further opens prospects for controlling wavepacket dynamics of macroscopic solid-state objects in both linear and nonlinear regimes, extending prior demonstrations of optimal quantum control—previously limited to optical and atomic systems—to the domain of optomechanical systems at ambient conditions.

entries.original_title: Exposing the distinctive modular behavior of β-strands and α-helices in folded proteins
entries.original_abstract: Significance Despite the vast number of known protein topologies, the actual behavior and selective traits of their constituent α- and β-secondary-structure elements remain elusive. The reason is that the high-energy fluctuations associated with their motions in folded proteins are intrinsically difficult to measure. Here, we circumvent this problem by presenting an alternative, and generally applicable, protein-design strategy that activates dynamic swapping of entire α- and β-elements in the folded ground state. We find that the behavior of the α- and β-elements is, indeed, very distinct where the differences in structural and dynamic properties have relevance not only for the understanding of protein function, but also for the mechanism of structural evolution per se. Although folded proteins are commonly depicted as simplistic combinations of β-strands and α-helices, the actual properties and functions of these secondary-structure elements in their native contexts are just partly understood. The principal reason is that the behavior of individual β- and α-elements is obscured by the global folding cooperativity. In this study, we have circumvented this problem by designing frustrated variants of the mixed α/β-protein S6, which allow the structural behavior of individual β-strands and α-helices to be targeted selectively by stopped-flow kinetics, X-ray crystallography, and solution-state NMR. Essentially, our approach is based on provoking intramolecular "domain swap." The results show that the α- and β-elements have quite different characteristics: The swaps of β-strands proceed via global unfolding, whereas the α-helices are free to swap locally in the native basin. Moreover, the α-helices tend to hybridize and to promote protein association by gliding over to neighboring molecules. This difference in structural behavior follows directly from hydrogen-bonding restrictions and suggests that the protein secondary structure defines not only tertiary geometry, but also maintains control in function and structural evolution. Finally, our alternative approach to protein folding and native-state dynamics presents a generally applicable strategy for in silico design of protein models that are computationally testable in the microsecond–millisecond regime.
entries.anonymized_problem: This study investigates the distinct structural and dynamic behaviors of α-helices and β-strands within folded proteins, a question historically obscured by global folding cooperativity. To isolate the contributions of individual secondary-structure elements, frustrated variants of a mixed α/β-protein were designed to provoke intramolecular domain swapping, enabling selective targeting of β-strands and α-helices using stopped-flow kinetics, X-ray crystallography, and solution-state NMR. The results reveal markedly different characteristics for the two element types: β-strand swaps proceed through global unfolding, while α-helices can swap locally within the native basin without global unfolding. Additionally, α-helices exhibit a tendency to hybridize and promote intermolecular association by gliding onto neighboring molecules. These behavioral differences are traced to fundamental hydrogen-bonding geometry constraints inherent to each secondary-structure type. The findings suggest that secondary structure not only dictates tertiary geometry but also governs functional dynamics and the mechanisms of structural evolution. The design strategy presented is proposed as a generally applicable framework for generating computationally testable protein models amenable to simulation in the microsecond-to-millisecond timescale regime.

entries.original_title: Functional Long Non-coding RNAs Evolve from Junk Transcripts.
entries.original_abstract: Transcriptome studies reveal pervasive transcription of complex genomes, such as those of mammals. Despite popular arguments for functionality of most, if not all, of these transcripts, genome-wide analysis of selective constraints indicates that most of the produced RNA are junk. However, junk is not garbage. On the contrary, junk transcripts provide the raw material for the evolution of diverse long non-coding (lnc) RNAs by non-adaptive mechanisms, such as constructive neutral evolution. The generation of many novel functional entities, such as lncRNAs, that fuels organismal complexity does not seem to be driven by strong positive selection. Rather, the weak selection regime that dominates the evolution of most multicellular eukaryotes provides ample material for functional innovation with relatively little adaptation involved.
entries.anonymized_problem: Pervasive transcription in complex genomes, particularly those of mammals, generates large numbers of RNA transcripts whose functional significance remains debated. This work addresses the tension between evidence for widespread transcription and population-genetic analyses showing that most produced transcripts bear little signature of purifying selection, suggesting they are non-functional "junk." The central question examined is how functional long non-coding RNAs can arise within a genomic landscape dominated by apparently non-functional transcription. The approach integrates transcriptome-scale analyses of selective constraints with evolutionary theory, evaluating the roles of adaptive versus non-adaptive mechanisms in the origin of functional RNAs. The key argument is that junk transcripts, while not immediately functional, serve as raw material for the emergence of long non-coding RNAs through non-adaptive processes such as constructive neutral evolution. Under this framework, the weak selection regimes characteristic of multicellular eukaryotes—rather than strong positive selection—are sufficient to permit functional innovation. The findings suggest that increased organismal complexity driven by the proliferation of long non-coding RNA species does not require pervasive adaptive evolution, but instead emerges from neutral and near-neutral evolutionary dynamics acting on a substrate of otherwise non-functional transcriptional output.

entries.original_title: Insight into the multifunctional RNA synthesis machine of rabies virus
entries.original_abstract:
Rabies virus (RABV) is the causative agent of a fatal neurological disease in humans and animals. It is transmitted to humans from infected animals, mainly domestic dogs, through their saliva by biting or by scratching. Rabies is controlled by vaccination of domestic dogs and cats, but RABV nevertheless kills more than 50,000 people annually, especially in developing countries where vaccination rates in domestic dogs are lower. In humans, rabies is preventable by vaccination prior to or immediately after exposure, but there are no specific antiviral drugs available that target the virus directly (1). In PNAS, Horwitz et al. (2) present a high-resolution electron cryomicroscopy structure of the RNA synthesis machine of RABV, providing valuable mechanistic insight into its activities and opening up the way toward developing antiviral approaches for this fatal virus.

RABV belongs to the group of negative-strand RNA viruses that includes many human pathogens such as the influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), Ebola virus, and measles virus. The genomes of these viruses consist of one or more single-stranded, negative-sense RNA molecules that are always assembled with multiple copies of viral nucleoprotein (N) into megadalton-sized complexes (3). In order to initiate infection, viruses such as RABV must first transcribe their negative-sense RNA into mRNA and therefore must carry an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase within their infectious particle. These viral polymerases are multifunctional machines that not only transcribe the negative-strand RNA into mRNA but also replicate the genome through a complementary replicative intermediate, the antigenome. In addition to catalyzing RNA synthesis, these polymerases also ensure that viral transcripts are protected with a 5′-cap structure. This is achieved either by a cap-snatching mechanism that involves stealing caps from host capped RNAs through cap-binding and endonuclease functions, or de novo synthesis of a 5′-cap structure using capping and methyltransferase enzymes, which are …

entries.anonymized_problem: Rabies virus (RABV) causes a fatal neurological disease responsible for over 50,000 human deaths annually, with no specific antiviral drugs currently available that directly target the virus. RABV belongs to the negative-strand RNA virus group, which includes numerous human pathogens such as influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, Ebola virus, and measles virus. Like other members of this group, RABV encodes a multifunctional RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that must perform several distinct activities: transcribing the negative-sense genomic RNA into mRNA, replicating the genome via an antigenomic intermediate, and protecting viral transcripts through 5′-cap addition via de novo capping and methyltransferase activities. Understanding the structural basis of these coordinated functions has remained an important open question for antiviral development. A high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structure of the RABV RNA synthesis machinery is examined, providing mechanistic insight into how this polymerase complex coordinates its multiple enzymatic activities. The structural analysis clarifies the organization of functional domains within the polymerase and its cofactor, illuminating how transcription, replication, capping, and methylation are integrated within a single molecular machine. These structural findings offer a foundation for rational design of antiviral compounds targeting the RABV polymerase complex.

entries.original_title: Angiosperms versus gymnosperms in the Cretaceous
entries.original_abstract:
In a letter to Sir Joseph Hooker dated July 22, 1879, Charles Darwin described the abrupt origin, highly accelerated rate of diversification, and rise to dominance of flowering plants (angiosperms) in the Mid-Cretaceous (100 to 110 Ma) as an “abominable mystery” (1, 2). Knowledge of the paleobotanical record has greatly increased since Darwin’s day. The currently available fossil record clearly documents a sudden and rapid increase in the diversification and geographical extent of angiosperms since the Mid-Cretaceous, resulting in the ecological dominance of flowering plants in almost all terrestrial biomes on Earth today. It has been widely assumed that this major expansion of angiosperms outcompeted other land plants, most particularly the gymnosperms (mainly conifers). As a botany student in the mid-1960s, I was taught this not as a hypothesis but as an “established fact.” In PNAS, Condamine et al. (3) use all of the available fossil and molecular data for conifers to test the competing hypotheses that competition from angiosperms, climate change, or time alone led to the decline of conifers to the benefit of angiosperms. Results from detailed numerical analyses suggest that the increased extinction rates of conifers in the Mid- and Late Cretaceous are most parsimoniously interpreted as a response to the rise of angiosperms, and the alternative hypotheses of climate change or time alone as drivers of the conifer demise are falsified (3).

Within the gymnosperms today (12 families, 79 genera, 985 species), the Pinidae (conifers) is the major group with 6 families, 65 genera, and 627 species (4), such as pines, spruces, and firs. Conifers often occur in relatively harsh environments today such as in boreal areas, at high elevations, and/or on poor or shallow soils. However, conifers were a dominant and widespread component of the Earth’s flora in the Mesozoic, especially in … 

[↵][1]1Email: john.birks{at}uib.no.

 [1]: #xref-corresp-1-1
entries.anonymized_problem: The long-standing question of why conifers declined during the Cretaceous — commonly attributed to competitive displacement by flowering plants (angiosperms) but never rigorously tested against alternative drivers — is the focus of this work. The central debate concerns whether the rise of angiosperms caused elevated extinction rates in conifers, or whether climate change or time-dependent processes alone can account for the observed decline. To address this, all available fossil and molecular data for conifers were integrated into detailed numerical analyses, allowing simultaneous evaluation of competing macroevolutionary hypotheses. Results indicate that increased conifer extinction rates in the Mid- and Late Cretaceous are most parsimoniously explained by the ecological expansion of angiosperms, effectively falsifying climate change and time-dependent models as primary drivers. This finding lends quantitative support to a hypothesis long treated as established fact in botanical teaching but never formally tested: that the rapid diversification and geographic spread of angiosperms from approximately 100–110 Ma directly suppressed conifer diversity. The work contextualizes the modern conifer flora — roughly 627 species often restricted to climatically harsh or edaphically marginal environments — as a relict of a formerly dominant Mesozoic lineage shaped by competitive exclusion during one of the major ecological transitions in terrestrial plant history.

entries.original_title: The role of saltwater and waves in continental shelf formation with seaward migrating clinoform
entries.original_abstract: Significance Continental shelves have been generally interpreted to be coastal plains that have been drowned by sea-level rise. Here we offer an alternative mechanism. Dissolved salt in seawater generally forces sediment-laden fresh water from rivers into surface water flows, from which sediment (mud) settles out in the near-shore zone. Over time, this platform can build up to wave base, constructing a shelf within a mud belt. Wave-induced sediment resuspension can drive the seaward extension of the shelf. This implies that changing sea level is not the only mechanism for building continental shelves. Continental shelves have generally been interpreted as drowned coastal plains associated with the allogenic effect of sea-level variation. Here, without disputing this mechanism we describe an alternative autogenic mechanism for subaqueous shelf formation, driven by the presence of dissolved salt in seawater and surface waves. We use a numerical model describing flow hydrodynamics, sediment transport, and morphodynamics in order to do this. More specifically, we focus on two major aspects: 1) the role of saltwater in the subaqueous construction of continental shelves and 2) the transformation of these shelves into seaward-migrating clinoforms under the condition of repeated pulses of water and sediment input and steady wave effects, but no allogenic forcing such as sea-level change. In the case for which the receiving basin contains fresh water of the same density as the sediment-laden river water, the hyperpycnal river water plunges to form a turbidity current that can run out to deep water. In the case for which the receiving basin contains sea water but the river contains sediment-laden fresh water, the hypopycnal river water forms a surface plume that deposits sediment proximally. This proximate proto-shelf can then grow to wave base, after which wave-supported turbidity currents can extend it seaward. The feature we refer to is synonymous with near-shore mud belts.
entries.anonymized_problem: Continental shelves are conventionally interpreted as drowned coastal plains shaped by sea-level fluctuation (allogenic forcing). This study examines an alternative autogenic mechanism by which shelves can form and prograde seaward without any change in sea level, driven instead by the density contrast between saltwater and sediment-laden freshwater, combined with surface wave action. A numerical model coupling flow hydrodynamics, sediment transport, and morphodynamics is used to investigate two scenarios: one in which the receiving basin contains freshwater of equal density to river water, causing hyperpycnal plunging and turbidity currents that carry sediment to deep water; and one in which the basin contains seawater, causing hypopycnal surface plumes that deposit sediment proximally in the nearshore zone. In the saltwater case, this proximal sediment accumulation builds a subaqueous platform—analogous to observed nearshore mud belts—upward to wave base. Once the platform reaches wave base, wave-induced resuspension drives wave-supported turbidity currents that extend the shelf seaward, generating a migrating clinoform without any allogenic forcing. These results indicate that dissolved salt in seawater and surface waves together constitute a sufficient physical mechanism for continental shelf construction and progradation, independent of sea-level change.

entries.original_title: A vital gene for modified vaccinia virus Ankara replication in human cells
entries.original_abstract:
Vaccinia virus (VACV), the prototype orthopoxvirus, is the first live viral vaccine used to protect against smallpox, one of the most feared infectious diseases of humans (1). This outstanding achievement was possible because even as the various orthopoxviruses evolved and diversified they often retained major parts of their virion composition in common. In consequence, productive infection with one orthopoxvirus, VACV, effectively immunizes the host against infection by other orthopoxviruses including variola virus, the closely related agent of smallpox. Successful vaccination against smallpox positively correlated with the productive replication of VACV in the skin of vaccinated individuals. However, on occasion the inoculation of live VACV had risk because the vaccine virus could develop generalized infections and cause other severe adverse events following vaccination (2). Ever since, research with VACV seeks to elucidate the many secrets of this unique virus–human host interaction. What makes VACV efficiently grow in human cells? This might sound like a simple question since the growth tropism of many other viruses is largely determined by the binding of a specific viral protein (ligand) to its host cell counterpart (receptor) for successful entry. In contrast, the host tropism of VACV and poxviruses, in general, is far more complex and wonderful with numerous, postentry, intracellular events dictating whether productive virus replication will occur at the level of the host cell, the tissue, or the whole organism (3). VACV can readily bind to and enter many different cells from diverse animal species. After entry, however, successful VACV replication in a specific host cell depends on the functional activity of an appropriate subset of viral genes, the so-called host-range genes, predicted to control the intracellular host defenses at various levels.

In PNAS, Peng and Moss (4) identify and explore a previously unknown viral protein as a major facilitator of VACV growth in …

entries.anonymized_problem: Vaccinia virus (VACV), the prototypic orthopoxvirus and the basis of smallpox vaccination, replicates productively in human cells through mechanisms that extend well beyond initial receptor-mediated entry. Unlike many viruses whose host tropism is governed primarily by ligand–receptor interactions at the cell surface, poxvirus host range is determined largely by post-entry, intracellular events. A specific subset of viral genes—termed host-range genes—is thought to counteract intracellular host defense mechanisms, thereby enabling productive replication in permissive cell types. Despite decades of research, the full complement of viral factors that facilitate VACV replication in human cells remains incompletely characterized. A study recently reported in PNAS investig

entries.original_title: Base rate neglect and neural computations for subjective weight in decision under uncertainty
entries.original_abstract: Significance Estimating probability of potential outcomes is essential to many decisions we make under uncertainty. Yet humans often exhibit systematic biases in probability estimation. We investigated the neural mechanisms for base rate neglect, an important bias that describes people’s tendency to underweight base rate relative to individuating information. We found that activity in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and putamen carry information about the degree to which human participants underweight base rate through representing relative subjective weight assigned to base rate (OFC, mPFC, and putamen) and sensitivity to the variability of prior and individuating information (putamen). Our findings suggest that when combining multiple sources of information, relative sensitivity to information variability and information-weighting computations contribute to judgment bias. Base rate neglect, an important bias in estimating probability of uncertain events, describes humans’ tendency to underweight base rate (prior) relative to individuating information (likelihood). However, the neural mechanisms that give rise to this bias remain elusive. In this study, subjects chose between uncertain prospects where estimating reward probability was essential. We found that when the variability of prior and likelihood information about reward probability were systematically manipulated, prior variability significantly affected the degree to which subjects underweight the base rate of reward probability. Activity in the orbitofrontal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, and putamen represented the relative subjective weight that reflected such bias. Further, sensitivity to likelihood relative to prior variability in the putamen correlated with individuals’ overall tendency to underweight base rate. These findings suggest that in combining prior and likelihood, relative sensitivity to information variability and subjective-weight computations critically contribute to the individual heterogeneity in base rate neglect.
entries.anonymized_problem: Humans systematically underweight prior probability (base rate) relative to case-specific (individuating) information when estimating uncertain outcomes, a phenomenon known as base rate neglect. Despite its behavioral importance, the neural substrates underlying this bias remain poorly understood. This study investigated the neural computations supporting base rate neglect using a decision-making task in which participants chose between uncertain prospects requiring integration of reward probability from both base rate and individuating information. The variability of prior and likelihood information was systematically manipulated across trials, allowing examination of how variability sensitivity influences weighting behavior. Neuroimaging data revealed that activity in the orbitofrontal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, and putamen encoded the relative subjective weight assigned to the base rate, directly reflecting the degree of underweighting bias. Additionally, differential sensitivity to likelihood versus prior variability in the putamen correlated with individual participants' overall tendency to neglect the base rate across the experiment. These findings indicate that base rate neglect arises at least partly from how the brain represents the relative variability of competing information sources and translates that representation into differential weighting during probabilistic inference, with individual differences in these neural computations accounting for heterogeneity in the magnitude of the bias across participants.

entries.original_title: Two classes of active transcription sites and their roles in developmental regulation
entries.original_abstract: Significance Transcription occurs at chromosomal sites known as active transcription sites (ATS). We report that ATS can exist in two classes when assessed at key regulatory genes in their natural context: these “iATS” and “cATS” possess incomplete and complete nascent transcripts, respectively. Frequencies of the two classes are patterned within the developing tissue in a gene-, developmental stage-, and sex-specific manner, revealing ATS class regulation. Moreover, cATS frequency, not iATS frequency, corresponds to mRNA abundance, indicating that regulation of ATS class impacts gene expression. The iATS signature—presence of a long first intron but lacking exons—suggests slowing or pausing of transcriptional progression midway through the gene. We suggest that ATS class regulation can pattern gene expression during development. The expression of genes encoding powerful developmental regulators is exquisitely controlled, often at multiple levels. Here, we investigate developmental expression of three conserved genes, Caenorhabditis elegans mpk-1, lag-1, and lag-3/sel-8, which encode homologs of ERK/MAPK and core components of the Notch-dependent transcription complex, respectively. We use single-molecule FISH (smFISH) and MATLAB to visualize and quantify nuclear nascent transcripts and cytoplasmic mRNAs as a function of position along the germline developmental axis. Using differentially labeled probes, one spanning an exceptionally long first intron and the other spanning exons, we identify two classes of active transcription sites (ATS). The iATS class, for “incomplete” ATS, harbors only partial nascent transcripts; the cATS class, for “complete” ATS, harbors full-length nascent transcripts. Remarkably, the frequencies of iATS and cATS are patterned along the germline axis. For example, most mpk-1 ATS are iATS in hermaphrodite germline stem cells, but most are cATS in differentiating stem cell daughters. Thus, mpk-1 ATS class frequencies switch in a graded manner as stem cell daughters begin differentiation. Importantly, the patterns of ATS class frequency are gene-, stage-, and sex-specific, and cATS frequency strongly correlates with transcriptional output. Although the molecular mechanism underlying ATS classes is not understood, their primary difference is the extent of transcriptional progression. To generate only partial nascent transcripts in iATS, progression must be slowed, paused, or aborted midway through the gene. We propose that regulation of ATS class can be a critical mode of developmental gene regulation.
entries.anonymized_problem: Active transcription sites (ATS) are chromosomal loci where nascent RNA synthesis occurs, but the functional heterogeneity of ATS and its developmental significance remain poorly understood. This study examines ATS diversity at key regulatory loci in a living developmental system, using single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization combined with quantitative image analysis to simultaneously visualize nuclear nascent transcripts and cytoplasmic mRNAs along the germline developmental axis of Caenorhabditis elegans. Differentially labeled probes targeting a long first intron versus exonic sequences were used to distinguish two classes of ATS: one harboring only partial nascent transcripts lacking exonic signal (incomplete ATS), and one harboring full-length nascent transcripts spanning both intronic and exonic regions (complete ATS). These two classes were identified at three conserved developmental regulator loci encoding homologs of ERK/MAPK and components of the Notch-dependent transcription complex. The relative frequencies of the two ATS classes are patterned along the germline axis in a gene-, developmental stage-, and sex-specific manner. Notably, only complete ATS frequency correlates with mRNA abundance, while incomplete ATS frequency does not, indicating that ATS class composition—rather than total ATS number—determines transcriptional output. The incomplete ATS signature is consistent with slowed, paused, or aborted transcriptional progression within the gene body. These findings identify regulation of transcriptional progression as a mechanism for patterning gene expression during development.

entries.original_title: Detecting electronic coherences by time-domain high-harmonic spectroscopy
entries.original_abstract: Significance To generate and monitor the coherent excitation without using X-ray light source, we propose an all-optical method called strong-field Raman scattering which is analogous to the three-step model for the high-order harmonic generation. Once such superposition is prepared, a follow-up probe optical laser can monitor its dynamics by detecting HHG signal which has already been proven to be very sensitive to the small fractions of the excited states. A semiperturbative model combining strong-field and perturbative techniques is developed to describe excitation and measurement of the electronic coherences and populations in multiwave mixing involving strong fields. This opens a route to transfer the powerful techniques of perturbative nonlinear optics to the strong-field regime. Ultrafast spectroscopy is capable of monitoring electronic and vibrational states. For electronic states a few eV apart, an X-ray laser source is required. We propose an alternative method based on the time-domain high-order harmonic spectroscopy where a coherent superposition of the electronic states is first prepared by the strong optical laser pulse. The coherent dynamics can then be probed by the higher-order harmonics generated by the delayed probe pulse. The high nonlinearity typically modeled by the three-step mechanism introduced by Lewenstein and Corkum can serve as a recipe for generation of the coherent excitation with broad bandwidth. The main advantage of the method is that only optical (non–X-ray) lasers are needed. A semiperturbative model based on the Liouville space superoperator approach is developed for the bookkeeping of the different orders of the nonlinear response for the high-order harmonic generation using multiple pulses. Coherence between bound electronic states is monitored in the harmonic spectra from both first- and second-order responses.
entries.anonymized_problem: Ultrafast spectroscopy of electronic states separated by several electron volts typically requires X-ray laser sources, posing significant experimental challenges. This work investigates an all-optical alternative based on time-domain high-harmonic spectroscopy, in which only optical (non-X-ray) laser pulses are used to both prepare and probe coherent superpositions of electronic states. The approach draws on an analogy to the three-step strong-field mechanism: a strong optical pump pulse generates coherent electronic excitations with broad bandwidth through a process analogous to high-harmonic generation, and a delayed probe pulse subsequently interrogates the resulting coherent dynamics via the high-harmonic emission signal, which is sensitive to small excited-state populations. To describe excitation and measurement of electronic coherences and populations in multiwave mixing involving strong fields, a semiperturbative theoretical framework is developed that combines strong-field and perturbative techniques using a Liouville space superoperator formalism. This formalism systematically tracks different orders of the nonlinear response for high-harmonic generation driven by multiple pulses. Coherences between bound electronic states are shown to be detectable in the harmonic spectra through both first- and second-order responses. The approach provides a pathway to extend the toolkit of perturbative nonlinear optical spectroscopy into the strong-field regime without requiring X-ray sources.

entries.original_title: Dicer up-regulation by inhibition of specific proteolysis in differentiating monocytic cells
entries.original_abstract: Significance Dicer is a ribonuclease III enzyme in biosynthesis of miRNAs, regulators of gene expression involved in macrophage differentiation. We found a specific truncation of Dicer in monocytic cells resulting from apparently constitutive cleavage by a serine protease. Inhibition of this proteolytic truncation, which occurred during macrophage differentiation in presence of TLR ligands or prostaglandin E2, up-regulates full-length Dicer and promotes miR biosynthesis. Regulation of transcription of pri-miRNA is one mode to regulate biosynthesis of mature miRNA. Inhibition of constitutive proteolysis of Dicer, as described here, provides a second layer of regulation, at the level of miRNA processing. Our data provide insights to Dicer and miRNAs in macrophage polarization/differentiation, a key process in the innate immune response. Dicer is a ribonuclease III enzyme in biosynthesis of micro-RNAs (miRNAs). Here we describe a regulation of Dicer expression in monocytic cells, based on proteolysis. In undifferentiated Mono Mac 6 (MM6) cells, full-length Dicer was undetectable; only an ∼50-kDa fragment appeared in Western blots. However, when MM6 cells were treated with zymosan or LPS during differentiation with TGF-β and 1,25diOHvitD3, full-length Dicer became abundant together with varying amounts of ∼170- and ∼50-kDa Dicer fragments. Mass spectrometry identified the Dicer fragments and showed cleavage about 450 residues upstream from the C terminus. Also, PGE2 (prostaglandin E2) added to differentiating MM6 cells up-regulated full-length Dicer, through EP2/EP4 and cAMP. The TLR stimuli strongly induced miR-146a-5p, while PGE2 increased miR-99a-5p and miR-125a-5p, both implicated in down-regulation of TNFα. The Ser protease inhibitor AEBSF (4-[2-aminoethyl] benzene sulfonyl fluoride) up-regulated full-length Dicer, both in MM6 cells and in primary human blood monocytes, indicating a specific proteolytic degradation. However, AEBSF alone did not lead to a general increase in miR expression, indicating that additional mechanisms are required to increase miRNA biosynthesis. Finally, differentiation of monocytes to macrophages with M-CSF or GM-CSF strongly up-regulated full-length Dicer. Our results suggest that differentiation regimens, both in the MM6 cell line and of peripheral blood monocytes, inhibit an apparently constitutive Dicer proteolysis, allowing for increased formation of miRNAs.
entries.anonymized_problem: This study investigates how expression of Dicer, the ribonuclease III enzyme responsible for microRNA (miRNA) processing, is regulated in monocytic cells during macrophage differentiation. In undifferentiated monocytic cell line cultures, full-length Dicer protein was undetectable by Western blot, with only an approximately 50-kDa fragment present. Mass spectrometry analysis identified that constitutive cleavage by a serine protease occurs approximately 450 residues upstream from the C terminus, generating approximately 170-kDa and 50-kDa fragments. Treatment with Toll-like receptor ligands (zymosan or LPS) during differentiation induced by TGF-β and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 restored full-length Dicer abundance. Prostaglandin E2 similarly up-regulated full-length Dicer through EP2/EP4 receptor signaling and cAMP. A serine protease inhibitor (AEBSF) up-regulated full-length Dicer in both the cell line and primary human blood monocytes, confirming proteolytic degradation as a regulatory mechanism. However, protease inhibition alone did not broadly increase miRNA levels, indicating that additional mechanisms are required for full miRNA biosynthetic activity. Differentiation toward macrophages using M-CSF or GM-CSF also strongly up-regulated full-length Dicer. TLR stimuli induced miR-146a-5p, while prostaglandin E2 increased miR-99a-5p and miR-125a-5p, both associated with TNFα suppression. These findings identify post-translational proteolytic regulation of Dicer as a distinct layer of miRNA biosynthesis control during innate immune cell differentiation.

entries.original_title: Genetic and structural studies of RABL3 reveal an essential role in lymphoid development and function
entries.original_abstract: Significance Using forward genetic analysis, we identified a previously unknown regulator of mouse lymphopoiesis, RABL3. The small GTPase RABL3 is also necessary for embryonic development. We found that GPR89, a putative GPCR or ion channel, interacts with, and is stabilized by, RABL3, and mice with hypomorphic mutations in either protein displayed B cell and T cell deficiencies. We crystallized RABL3 and showed it forms a homodimer with subunits similar to other small G proteins. However, the conformation of mutated RABL3 is abnormal and may disrupt effector binding. Critical proteins that control hematopoiesis remain to be discovered, and RABL3 is one such example. The small GTPase RABL3 is an oncogene of unknown physiological function. Homozygous knockout alleles of mouse Rabl3 were embryonic lethal, but a viable hypomorphic allele (xiamen [xm]) causing in-frame deletion of four amino acids from the interswitch region resulted in profound defects in lymphopoiesis. Impaired lymphoid progenitor development led to deficiencies of B cells, T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells in Rabl3xm/xm mice. T cells and NK cells exhibited impaired cytolytic activity, and mice infected with mouse cytomegalovirus (MCMV) displayed elevated titers in the spleen. Myeloid cells were normal in number and function. Biophysical and crystallographic studies demonstrated that RABL3 formed a homodimer in solution via interactions between the effector binding surfaces on each subunit; monomers adopted a typical small G protein fold. RABL3xm displayed a large compensatory alteration in switch I, which adopted a β-strand configuration normally provided by the deleted interswitch residues, thereby permitting homodimer formation. Dysregulated effector binding due to conformational changes in the switch I–interswitch–switch II module likely underlies the xm phenotype. One such effector may be GPR89, putatively an ion channel or G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR). RABL3, but not RABL3xm, strongly associated with and stabilized GPR89, and an N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea (ENU)-induced mutation (explorer) in Gpr89 phenocopied Rabl3xm.
