entries.anonymized_problem: Forward genetic screening was used to investigate regulators of mouse lymphopoiesis, identifying a small GTPase as an essential component of lymphoid development. Homozygous knockout of the corresponding gene caused embryonic lethality, but a viable hypomorphic allele carrying an in-frame four-amino-acid deletion in the interswitch region produced profound defects in lymphopoiesis, with marked reductions in B cells, T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells. T cells and NK cells exhibited impaired cytolytic activity, and mice infected with mouse cytomegalovirus showed elevated splenic viral titers, while myeloid lineages remained numerically and functionally normal. Crystallographic and biophysical analyses revealed that the wild-type protein forms a homodimer in solution through interactions between the effector-binding surfaces of each subunit, with monomers adopting a canonical small G protein fold. The hypomorphic variant displayed a compensatory structural rearrangement in switch I, which adopted a β-strand configuration to substitute for the deleted interswitch residues, preserving homodimer formation but likely disrupting effector binding through conformational changes in the switch I–interswitch–switch II module. A putative ion channel or G protein-coupled receptor was identified as one candidate effector: the wild-type protein strongly associated with and stabilized this interactor, whereas the hypomorphic variant did not, and an independently induced point mutation in the gene encoding this interactor produced an equivalent lymphoid deficiency phenotype.

entries.original_title: Alternative splicing of DSP1 enhances snRNA accumulation by promoting transcription termination and recycle of the processing complex
entries.original_abstract: Significance snRNAs are conserved noncoding RNAs in eukaryotes. Their biogenesis is spatiotemporally regulated in various biological processes. However, related mechanisms regulating snRNA accumulation are less known. DSP1 is an essential component of the DSP1 complex that catalyzes snRNA maturation. Here, we show that DSP1 is subjected to alternative splicing in the pollens, resulting in two splicing variants, DSP1α and DSP1β. DSP1β does not participate in the 3′ maturation of snRNAs but interacts with CPSF73-I and promotes efficient release of CPSF73-I and Poll II from the 3′ end of the snRNA loci and thereby facilitates snRNA transcription termination, resulting in increased snRNA levels in pollens. Our results uncover a mechanism spatiotemporally regulating snRNA biogenesis in plants. Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are the basal components of the spliceosome and play crucial roles in splicing. Their biogenesis is spatiotemporally regulated. However, related mechanisms are still poorly understood. Defective in snRNA processing (DSP1) is an essential component of the DSP1 complex that catalyzes plant snRNA 3′-end maturation by cotranscriptional endonucleolytic cleavage of the primary snRNA transcripts (presnRNAs). Here, we show that DSP1 is subjected to alternative splicing in pollens and embryos, resulting in two splicing variants, DSP1α and DSP1β. Unlike DSP1α, DSP1β is not required for presnRNA 3′-end cleavage. Rather, it competes with DSP1α for the interaction with CPSF73-I, the catalytic subunit of the DSP1 complex, which promotes efficient release of CPSF73-I and the DNA-dependent RNA polymerease II (Pol II) from the 3′ end of snRNA loci thereby facilitates snRNA transcription termination, resulting in increased snRNA levels in pollens. Taken together, this study uncovers a mechanism that spatially regulates snRNA accumulation.
entries.anonymized_problem: Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are essential spliceosomal components whose biogenesis is spatiotemporally regulated, yet the underlying mechanisms controlling tissue-specific snRNA accumulation remain poorly understood. This study investigates how alternative splicing of a gene encoding a core subunit of the snRNA 3′-end processing complex regulates snRNA levels in specific plant cell types, particularly pollen and embryos. The gene in question undergoes alternative splicing to produce two distinct isoforms: one that participates in cotranscriptional endonucleolytic cleavage of precursor snRNA transcripts, and a shorter isoform that lacks this processing activity. The shorter isoform competes with the functional isoform for binding to the catalytic endonuclease subunit of the processing complex. This competitive interaction promotes efficient dissociation of the endonuclease and RNA polymerase II from the 3′ ends of snRNA loci, thereby facilitating transcription termination and enabling recycling of the processing machinery. The net result is elevated snRNA accumulation in pollen. Genetic and biochemical analyses, including interaction assays and quantification of snRNA levels in isoform-specific mutants, support this model. These findings reveal a regulatory mechanism in which alternative splicing of a processing complex component fine-tunes snRNA biogenesis in a spatially restricted manner during plant development.

entries.original_title: How canyons evolve by incision into bedrock: Rainbow Canyon, Death Valley National Park, United States
entries.original_abstract: Significance The motion of tectonic plates gives rise to striking landforms. Canyons such as Rainbow Canyon near Death Valley are the products of tectonics operating over several million years. Tectonics has driven bedrock incision, canyon widening, and knickpoint migration. Here we capture these processes in a moving boundary model of canyon evolution. We treat bedrock incision in terms of abrasion caused by stones colliding with the bed. We estimate that based on present-day conditions, the knickpoint would have required 120,000 y to migrate to its current position. Rainbow Canyon offers a template for the understanding of canyons in general and how they deliver water and sediment to lowlands. Incising rivers may be confined by low-slope, erodible hillslopes or steep, resistant sidewalls. In the latter case, the system forms a canyon. We present a morphodynamic model that includes the essential elements of a canyon incising into a plateau, including 1) abrasion-driven channel incision, 2) migration of a canyon-head knickpoint, 3) sediment feed from an alluvial channel upstream of the knickpoint, and 4) production of sediment by sidewall collapse. We calculate incision in terms of collision of clasts with the bed. We calculate knickpoint migration using a moving-boundary formulation that allows a slope discontinuity where the channel head meets an alluvial plateau feeder channel. Rather than modeling sidewall collapse events, we model long-term behavior using a constant sidewall slope as the channel incises. Our morphodynamic model specifically applies to canyon, rather than river–hillslope evolution. We implement it for Rainbow Canyon, CA. Salient results are as follows: 1) Sediment supply from collapsing canyon sidewalls can be substantially larger than that supplied from the feeder channel on the plateau. 2) For any given quasi-equilibrium canyon bedrock slope, two conjugate slopes are possible for the alluvial channel upstream, with the lower of the two corresponding to a substantially lower knickpoint migration rate and higher preservation potential. 3) Knickpoint migration occurs at a substantially faster time scale than regrading of the bedrock channel itself, underlying the significance of disequilibrium processes. Although implemented for constant climactic conditions, the model warrants extension to long-term climate variation.
entries.anonymized_problem: Canyon incision into bedrock involves the interplay of tectonic forcing, fluvial erosion, knickpoint migration, and sediment supply from collapsing sidewalls, yet quantitative morphodynamic models capturing these coupled processes remain limited. This study develops a moving-boundary morphodynamic model for canyon evolution in which a bedrock channel incises into a plateau, incorporating four key elements: abrasion-driven incision modeled as clast–bed collisions, upstream knickpoint migration using a moving-boundary formulation that permits a slope discontinuity at the junction between the bedrock canyon head and an alluvial feeder channel, sediment supply from the upstream plateau channel, and long-term sidewall retreat represented by a constant sidewall slope during incision. The model is applied to a canyon in Death Valley National Park as a case study. Key findings include: (1) sediment delivered by collapsing canyon sidewalls can substantially exceed sediment input from the upstream feeder channel; (2) for a given quasi-equilibrium bedrock canyon slope, two conjugate alluvial feeder slopes are possible, with the lower slope associated with markedly slower knickpoint migration and higher stratigraphic preservation potential; and (3) knickpoint migration operates at a faster timescale than channel-wide regrading, highlighting the importance of disequilibrium dynamics. Based on present-day conditions, knickpoint migration to its observed position is estimated to require approximately 120,000 years. The framework provides a generalizable template for understanding bedrock canyon systems and their role in routing water and sediment to lowlands.

entries.original_title: Protecting Copper Oxidation State via Intermediate Confinement for Selective CO2 Electroreduction to C2+ Fuels.
entries.original_abstract: Selective and efficient catalytic conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) into value-added fuels and feedstocks provides an ideal avenue to high-density renewable energy storage. An impediment to enabling deep CO2 reduction to oxygenates and hydrocarbons (e.g., C2+ compounds) is the difficulty of coupling carbon-carbon bonds efficiently. Copper in the +1 oxidation state has been thought to be active for catalyzing C2+ formation, whereas it is prone to being reduced to Cu0 at cathodic potentials. Here we report that catalysts with nanocavities can confine carbon intermediates formed in situ, which in turn covers the local catalyst surface and thereby stabilizes Cu+ species. Experimental measurements on multi-hollow cuprous oxide catalyst exhibit a C2+ Faradaic efficiency of 75.2 ±2.7% at a C2+ partial current density of 267± 13 mA cm-2 and a large C2+-to-C1 ratio of ~7.2. Operando Raman spectra, in conjunction with X-ray absorption studies, confirm that Cu+ species in the as-designed catalyst are well retained during CO2 reduction, which leads to the marked C2+ selectivity at large conversion rate.
entries.anonymized_problem: Selective electrochemical reduction of CO₂ to multi-carbon (C2+) products such as oxygenates and hydrocarbons requires efficient carbon–carbon coupling, which is facilitated by copper in the +1 oxidation state (Cu⁺). A central challenge is that Cu⁺ is thermodynamically unstable under the cathodic potentials required for deep CO₂ reduction, readily converting to metallic Cu⁰ and diminishing C2+ selectivity. This work investigates whether confining reaction intermediates within catalyst nanocavities can kinetically stabilize Cu⁺ during operation. A cuprous oxide catalyst with a multi-hollow nanostructure was synthesized to provide internal cavities where carbon intermediates generated in situ accumulate, covering the local surface and suppressing further reduction of Cu⁺ to Cu⁰. Electrochemical testing demonstrates a C2+ Faradaic efficiency of 75.2 ± 2.7% at a C2+ partial current density of 267 ± 13 mA cm⁻² and a C2+-to-C1 product ratio of approximately 7.2. Operando Raman spectroscopy and X-ray absorption spectroscopy confirm that Cu⁺ species are retained throughout CO₂ reduction under operating conditions. These results establish intermediate confinement within nanocavities as a mechanism for preserving active oxidation states in copper-based electrocatalysts and achieving high selectivity toward C2+ products at practically relevant current densities.

entries.original_title: Synthesis of Co‐Doped MoS2 Monolayers with Enhanced Valley Splitting
entries.original_abstract: Internal magnetic moments induced by magnetic dopants in MoS2 monolayers are shown to serve as a new means to engineer valley Zeeman splitting (VZS). Specifically, successful synthesis of monolayer MoS2 doped with the magnetic element Co is reported, and the magnitude of the valley splitting is engineered by manipulating the dopant concentration. Valley splittings of 3.9, 5.2, and 6.15 meV at 7 T in Co‐doped MoS2 with Co concentrations of 0.8%, 1.7%, and 2.5%, respectively, are achieved as revealed by polarization‐resolved photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. Atomic‐resolution electron microscopy studies clearly identify the magnetic sites of Co substitution in the MoS2 lattice, forming two distinct types of configurations, namely isolated single dopants and tridopant clusters. Density functional theory (DFT) and model calculations reveal that the observed enhanced VZS arises from an internal magnetic field induced by the tridopant clusters, which couples to the spin, atomic orbital, and valley magnetic moment of carriers from the conduction and valence bands. The present study demonstrates a new method to control the valley pseudospin via magnetic dopants in layered semiconducting materials, paving the way toward magneto‐optical and spintronic devices.
entries.anonymized_problem: Controlling valley pseudospin in two-dimensional semiconductors is a key challenge for valleytronic and spintronic applications. This study investigates whether magnetic dopants in monolayer MoS₂ can serve as an internal mechanism to engineer valley Zeeman splitting (VZS), complementing external magnetic field approaches. Monolayer MoS₂ samples doped with cobalt at concentrations of 0.8%, 1.7%, and 2.5% were synthesized, and their optical properties were characterized using polarization-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy. Valley splittings of 3.9, 5.2, and 6.15 meV at 7 T were measured for the respective Co concentrations, demonstrating a systematic dependence on dopant concentration. Atomic-resolution electron microscopy identified two structural configurations of Co substitution within the MoS₂ lattice: isolated single dopants and tridopant clusters. Density functional theory and model calculations attribute the enhanced VZS primarily to an internal magnetic field generated by the tridopant clusters, which couples to the spin, atomic orbital, and valley magnetic moments of carriers in both the conduction and valence bands. These findings establish dopant concentration as a tunable parameter for controlling valley splitting in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers and suggest a pathway toward magneto-optical and spintronic device architectures based on magnetically doped layered semiconductors.

entries.original_title: Sodium/Potassium‐Ion Batteries: Boosting the Rate Capability and Cycle Life by Combining Morphology, Defect and Structure Engineering
entries.original_abstract: Carbon‐based materials have been considered as the most promising anode materials for both sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) and potassium‐ion batteries (PIBs), owing to their good chemical stability, high electrical conductivity, and environmental benignity. However, due to the large sizes of sodium and potassium ions, it is a great challenge to realize a carbon anode with high reversible capacity, long cycle life, and high rate capability. Herein, by rational design, N‐doped 3D mesoporous carbon nanosheets (N‐CNS) are successfully synthesized, which can realize unprecedented electrochemical performance for both SIBs and PIBs. The N‐CNS possess an ultrathin nanosheet structure with hierarchical pores, ultrahigh level of pyridinic N/pyrrolic N, and an expanded interlayer distance. The beneficial features that can enhance the Na‐/K‐ion intercalation/deintercalation kinetic process, shorten the diffusion length for both ions and electrons, and accommodate the volume change are demonstrated. Hence, the N‐CNS‐based electrode delivers a high capacity of 239 mAh g−1 at 5 A g−1 after 10 000 cycles for SIBs and 321 mAh g−1 at 5 A g−1 after 5000 cycles for PIBs. First‐principles calculation shows that the ultrahigh doping level of pyridinic N/pyrrolic N contributes to the enhanced sodium and potassium storage performance by modulating the charge density distribution on the carbon surface.
entries.anonymized_problem: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) and potassium-ion batteries (PIBs) face a fundamental challenge in developing carbon-based anodes that simultaneously achieve high reversible capacity, long cycle life, and high rate capability, largely because the large ionic radii of Na⁺ and K⁺ impede intercalation kinetics and induce significant volume changes. This work addresses these limitations through combined morphology, defect, and structure engineering of nitrogen-doped three-dimensional mesoporous carbon nanosheets. The material is synthesized to feature an ultrathin nanosheet architecture with hierarchical porosity, an expanded interlayer spacing, and an exceptionally high concentration of pyridinic and pyrrolic nitrogen dopants. These structural attributes are shown to enhance ion intercalation/deintercalation kinetics, shorten diffusion pathways for both ions and electrons, and buffer volumetric strain during cycling. Electrochemical testing demonstrates a capacity of 239 mAh g⁻¹ at 5 A g⁻¹ after 10,000 cycles for SIBs and 321 mAh g⁻¹ at 5 A g⁻¹ after 5,000 cycles for PIBs. First-principles calculations reveal that the elevated pyridinic/pyrrolic nitrogen doping level improves sodium and potassium storage by modulating the charge density distribution on the carbon surface, providing a mechanistic basis for the observed electrochemical enhancements.

entries.original_title: Recent Progress in High‐Strength and Robust Regenerated Cellulose Materials
entries.original_abstract: High‐strength petroleum‐based materials like plastics have been widely used in various fields, but their nonbiodegradability has caused serious pollution problems. Cellulose, as the most abundant sustainable polymer, has a great chance to act as the ideal substitute for plastics due to its low cost, wide availability, biodegradability, etc. Herein, the recent achievements for developing cellulose “green” solvents and regenerated cellulose materials with high strength via the “bottom‐up” route are presented. Cellulose can be regenerated to produce films/membranes, hydrogels/aerogels, filaments/fibers, microspheres/beads, bioplastics, etc., which show potential applications in textiles, biomedicine, energy storage, packaging, etc. Importantly, these cellulose‐based materials can be biodegraded in soil and oceans, reducing environmental pollution. The cellulose solvents, dissolving mechanism, and strategies for constructing the regenerated cellulose functional materials with high strength and performances, together with the current achievements and urgent challenges are summarized, and some perspectives are also proposed. The near future will be an exciting era for high‐strength biodegradable and renewable materials. The hope is that many environmentally friendly materials with good properties and low cost will be produced for commercial use, which will be beneficial for sustainable development in the world.
entries.anonymized_problem: Petroleum-based plastics offer high mechanical performance but pose severe environmental challenges due to their non-biodegradability. Cellulose, the most abundant renewable polymer, presents a viable sustainable alternative owing to its low cost, broad availability, and biodegradability. This review examines recent advances in the dissolution and regeneration of cellulose using "green" solvent systems, surveying the mechanistic basis by which various solvent classes disrupt and reassemble cellulose's hydrogen-bonding network. A "bottom-up" fabrication framework is discussed, encompassing the preparation of diverse regenerated cellulose material forms—including films and membranes, hydrogels and aerogels, filaments and fibers, microspheres and beads, and bioplastic composites—with emphasis on strategies for achieving high mechanical strength and multifunctional performance. Application domains surveyed include textiles, biomedical devices, energy storage, and sustainable packaging. The environmental fate of these materials is also addressed, highlighting their capacity for biodegradation in soil and marine environments. Key challenges remaining in solvent recyclability, scalable processing, and achieving commercially competitive mechanical properties are identified, alongside perspectives on future directions for producing low-cost, high-performance biodegradable materials suitable for broad commercial deployment in support of sustainable development goals.

entries.original_title: A new class of ionically conducting fluorinated ether electrolytes with high electrochemical stability.
entries.original_abstract: Increasing battery energy density is greatly desired for applications such as portable electronics and transportation. However, many next generation batteries are limited by electrolyte selection because high ionic conductivity and poor electrochemical stability are typically observed in most electrolytes. For example, ether-based electrolytes have high ionic conductivity, but are oxidatively unstable above 4 V, which prevents the use of high voltage cathodes that promise higher energy densities. In contrast, hydrofluoroethers (HFEs) have high oxidative stability, but do not dissolve lithium salt. In this work, we synthesize a new class of fluorinated ether electrolytes that combine the oxidative stability of HFEs with the ionic conductivity of ethers in a single compound. We show that conductivities of up to 2.7×10⁻4 S/cm (at 30°C) can be obtained with oxidative stability up to 5.6 V. The compounds also show higher lithium transference numbers compared to typical ethers. Furthermore, we use nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and molecular dynamics (MD) to study their ionic transport behavior and ion solvation environment, respectively. Finally, we demonstrate that these new class of electrolytes can be used with a Ni-rich layered cathode (NMC 811) to obtain over 100 cycles at a C/5 rate. The design of new molecules with high ionic conductivity and high electrochemical stability is a novel approach for the rational design of next generation batteries.
entries.anonymized_problem: Electrolyte design for next-generation lithium batteries faces a fundamental trade-off: ether-based solvents offer high ionic conductivity but suffer from oxidative decomposition above approximately 4 V, while hydrofluoroethers (HFEs) exhibit excellent oxidative stability yet cannot dissolve lithium salts. This work addresses that trade-off by synthesizing a class of fluorinated ether compounds that incorporate both properties within a single molecular framework. The approach involves rational molecular design to combine the salt-solvating capability of conventional ethers with the electrochemical robustness of HFEs. The resulting electrolytes achieve ionic conductivities up to 2.7×10⁻⁴ S/cm at 30°C and oxidative stability up to 5.6 V. Lithium transference numbers are higher than those typically observed in conventional ether electrolytes. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are employed to characterize ionic transport mechanisms and ion solvation environments, respectively. Electrochemical performance is validated using a nickel-rich layered oxide cathode (NMC 811), demonstrating stable cycling over more than 100 cycles at a C/5 rate. These findings demonstrate that simultaneous high ionic conductivity and wide electrochemical stability window can be achieved through targeted molecular design, offering a pathway toward electrolytes compatible with high-voltage cathode materials.

entries.original_title: Solid‐State Electrolyte Design for Lithium Dendrite Suppression
entries.original_abstract: All‐solid‐state Li metal batteries have attracted extensive attention due to their high safety and high energy density. However, Li dendrite growth in solid‐state electrolytes (SSEs) still hinders their application. Current efforts mainly aim to reduce the interfacial resistance, neglecting the intrinsic dendrite‐suppression capability of SSEs. Herein, the mechanism for the formation of Li dendrites is investigated, and Li‐dendrite‐free SSE criteria are reported. To achieve a high dendrite‐suppression capability, SSEs should be thermodynamically stable with a high interface energy against Li, and they should have a low electronic conductivity and a high ionic conductivity. A cold‐pressed Li3N–LiF composite is used to validate the Li‐dendrite‐free design criteria, where the highly ionic conductive Li3N reduces the Li plating/stripping overpotential, and LiF with high interface energy suppresses dendrites by enhancing the nucleation energy and suppressing the Li penetration into the SSEs. The Li3N–LiF layer coating on Li3PS4 SSE achieves a record‐high critical current of >6 mA cm−2 even at a high capacity of 6.0 mAh cm−2. The Coulombic efficiency also reaches a record 99% in 150 cycles. The Li3N–LiF/Li3PS4 SSE enables LiCoO2 cathodes to achieve 101.6 mAh g−1 for 50 cycles. The design principle opens a new opportunity to develop high‐energy all‐solid‐state Li metal batteries.
entries.anonymized_problem: Lithium dendrite growth in solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) remains a critical barrier to practical all-solid-state lithium metal batteries, yet most research has focused on reducing interfacial resistance rather than enhancing the intrinsic dendrite-suppression capability of the electrolyte itself. This work investigates the mechanistic origins of lithium dendrite formation and derives design criteria for dendrite-free SSEs. The analysis indicates that effective dendrite suppression requires SSEs to be thermodynamically stable against lithium with high interface energy, combined with low electronic conductivity and high ionic conductivity. These criteria are validated using a cold-pressed Li₃N–LiF composite, where Li₃N provides high ionic conductivity to reduce lithium plating and stripping overpotential, while LiF contributes high interface energy that raises nucleation barriers and suppresses lithium penetration. Coating this composite onto Li₃PS₄ electrolyte yields a critical current density exceeding 6 mA cm⁻² at a high areal capacity of 6.0 mAh cm⁻², along with a Coulombic efficiency of 99% sustained over 150 cycles. Full cells incorporating LiCoO₂ cathodes deliver 101.6 mAh g⁻¹ over 50 cycles. These results establish a thermodynamics- and kinetics-based framework for designing SSEs with inherent dendrite suppression capability in high-energy all-solid-state lithium metal batteries.

entries.original_title: An Atomically Thin Optoelectronic Machine Vision Processor
entries.original_abstract: 2D semiconductors, especially transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers, are extensively studied for electronic and optoelectronic applications. Beyond intensive studies on single transistors and photodetectors, the recent advent of large‐area synthesis of these atomically thin layers has paved the way for 2D integrated circuits, such as digital logic circuits and image sensors, achieving an integration level of ≈100 devices thus far. Here, a decisive advance in 2D integrated circuits is reported, where the device integration scale is increased by tenfold and the functional complexity of 2D electronics is propelled to an unprecedented level. Concretely, an analog optoelectronic processor inspired by biological vision is developed, where 32 × 32 = 1024 MoS2 photosensitive field‐effect transistors manifesting persistent photoconductivity (PPC) effects are arranged in a crossbar array. This optoelectronic processor with PPC memory mimics two core functions of human vision: it captures and stores an optical image into electrical data, like the eye and optic nerve chain, and then recognizes this electrical form of the captured image, like the brain, by executing analog in‐memory neural net computing. In the highlight demonstration, the MoS2 FET crossbar array optically images 1000 handwritten digits and electrically recognizes these imaged data with 94% accuracy.
entries.anonymized_problem: Two-dimensional semiconductors, particularly transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers such as molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂), have been investigated extensively for electronic and optoelectronic device applications. While prior work has demonstrated individual transistors, photodetectors, and small-scale integrated circuits at integration levels around 100 devices, scaling these platforms to higher device counts and greater functional complexity remains an open challenge. This work addresses that gap by fabricating a 32×32 crossbar array of 1024 MoS₂ photosensitive field-effect transistors that exploit persistent photoconductivity (PPC) as an in-situ memory mechanism. The resulting optoelectronic processor is designed to emulate two core functions of biological vision: optical image capture and retention (analogous to the eye and optic nerve), followed by in-memory analog neural network computation for image recognition (analogous to cortical processing). The device integration scale represents a tenfold increase over previously reported 2D integrated circuits. As a benchmark task, the array optically images 1000 handwritten digits and performs electrical recognition of the stored data, achieving 94% classification accuracy. These results demonstrate that atomically thin semiconductor crossbar arrays can support both sensing and analog computing within a single integrated platform, advancing the functional scope of 2D electronics toward machine vision applications.

entries.original_title: Luminescence "Turn-On" Detection of Gossypol using Ln3+-Based Metal-Organic Frameworks and Ln Salts.
entries.original_abstract: Gossypol (Gsp), a natural toxin concentrated in cottonseeds, poses great risks to the safe consumption of cottonseed products which are used extensively throughout the food industry. In this work, we report the first luminescence "turn-on" sensors for Gsp using near infrared emitting lanthanide (Ln3+) materials, including Ln3+ MOFs and Ln3+ salts. We first demonstrate that the Yb3+ photoluminescence of a Yb3+ MOF, Yb-NH2-TPDC, can be employed to selectively detect Gsp with a limit of detection of 25 μg/mL via a "turn-on" response from a completely non-emissive state in the absence of Gsp. The recyclability and stability of Yb-NH2-TPDC in the presence of Gsp was demonstrated by fluorescence spectroscopy and PXRD analysis, respectively. A variety of background substances present in practical samples that would require Gsp sensing, such as refined cottonseed oil, palmitic acid, linoleic acid, and α-tocopherol, did not interfere with the Yb3+ photoluminescence signal. We further identified that the "turn-on" of Yb-NH2-TPDC photoluminescence was due to the "antenna effect" of Gsp, as evidenced by spectroscopic studies and supported by computational analysis. This is the first report that Gsp can effectively sensitize Yb3+ photoluminescence. Leveraging this sensing mechanism, we demonstrate facile, highly sensitive, fast-response detection of Gsp using YbCl3 •6H2O and NdCl3•6H2O solutions. Overall, we show for the first time that Ln3+-based materials are promising luminescent sensors for Gsp detection. We envision that the reported sensing approach will be applicable to the detection of a wide variety of aromatic molecules using Ln3+ compounds including MOFs, complexes, and salts.
entries.anonymized_problem: Gossypol is a natural toxin found in cottonseed products widely used in the food industry, yet reliable, selective detection methods remain limited. This work investigates luminescence-based "turn-on" sensing of gossypol using near-infrared-emitting lanthanide (Ln³⁺) materials, specifically a Yb³⁺ metal-organic framework incorporating an aminoterphenyl dicarboxylate linker and simple lanthanide salt solutions. The Yb³⁺ metal-organic framework, initially non-emissive, produces a selective photoluminescence turn-on response upon gossypol addition, achieving a detection limit of 25 μg/mL. Recyclability and structural stability were confirmed by fluorescence spectroscopy and powder X-ray diffraction. Potential matrix interferents relevant to cottonseed-derived samples—including refined cottonseed oil, palmitic acid, linoleic acid, and α-tocopherol—did not compromise sensor selectivity. Spectroscopic studies and computational analysis indicate the mechanism involves gossypol acting as an antenna chromophore that sensitizes Yb³⁺ emission through energy transfer. Extending this principle, facile and rapid gossypol detection was demonstrated using aqueous YbCl₃·6H₂O and NdCl₃·6H₂O solutions, broadening applicability beyond framework-based sensors. The findings establish that lanthanide-based materials are effective luminescent sensors for gossypol and suggest the antenna-effect mechanism may generalize to detection of diverse aromatic analytes using various lanthanide compounds including metal-organic frameworks, complexes, and salts.

entries.original_title: Enantioselective Three-Component Fluoroalkylarylation of Unactivated Olefins Through Nickel-Catalyzed Cross-Electrophile Coupling.
entries.original_abstract: A nickel-catalyzed, enantioselective, three-component fluoroalkylarylation of unactivated alkenes with aryl halides and perfluoroalkyl iodides has been described. This cross-electrophile coupling protocol utilizes a chiral nickel/BiOx system as well as a pendant chelating group to facilitate the challenging three-component, asymmetric difunctionalization of unactivated alkenes, providing direct access to valuable chiral β-fluoroalkyl arylalkanes with high efficiency and excellent enantioselectivity. The mild conditions allow for a broad substrate scope as well as good functional group toleration.
entries.anonymized_problem: A nickel-catalyzed enantioselective three-component fluoroalkylarylation of unactivated alkenes is described, addressing the challenge of asymmetric 1,2-difunctionalization using two distinct electrophilic coupling partners. The approach employs a chiral nickel/bisoxazoline (BiOx) ligand system in combination with a pendant chelating group on the alkene substrate to control stereochemistry during cross-electrophile coupling between aryl halides and perfluoroalkyl iodides. This strategy enables simultaneous C–C bond formation at both termini of the unactivated olefin under mild reaction conditions. The method provides direct access to chiral β-fluoroalkyl arylalkane scaffolds—a structural motif of pharmaceutical relevance—with high efficiency and excellent enantioselectivity. A broad substrate scope is demonstrated, encompassing diverse aryl halides and perfluoroalkyl iodide partners, along with good tolerance for a range of functional groups. The use of a chelation-assisted approach is key to overcoming the inherent difficulty of achieving enantiocontrol in multicomponent radical-mediated difunctionalization reactions of simple, unactivated alkene substrates.

entries.original_title: A Highly Efficient Metal‐Free Electrocatalyst of F‐Doped Porous Carbon toward N2 Electroreduction
entries.original_abstract: N2 electroreduction into NH3 represents an attractive prospect for N2 utilization. Nevertheless, this process suffers from low Faraday efficiency (FE) and yield rate for NH3. In this work, a highly efficient metal‐free catalyst is developed by introducing F atoms into a 3D porous carbon framework (F‐doped carbon) toward N2 electroreduction. At −0.2 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), the F‐doped carbon achieves the highest FE of 54.8% for NH3, which is 3.0 times as high as that (18.3%) of pristine carbon frameworks. Notably, at −0.3 V versus RHE, the yield rate of F‐doped carbon for NH3 reaches 197.7 µgNH3 mg−1cat. h−1. Such a value is more than one order of magnitude higher than those of other metal‐free electrocatalysts under the near‐ambient conditions for NH3 product to date. Mechanistic studies reveal that the improved performance in N2 electroreduction for F‐doped carbon originates from the enhanced binding strength of N2 and the facilitated dissociation of N2 into *N2H. F bonding to C atom creates a Lewis acid site due to the different electronegativity between the F and C atoms. As such, the repulsive interaction between the Lewis acid site and proton H suppresses the activity of H2 evolution reaction, thus enhancing the selectivity of N2 electroreduction into NH3.
entries.anonymized_problem: Electrochemical reduction of N₂ to NH₃ offers a sustainable alternative to thermochemical ammonia synthesis, but is hindered by low Faradaic efficiency (FE) and slow yield rates under ambient conditions. This study investigates a metal-free electrocatalyst based on fluorine-doped three-dimensional porous carbon frameworks for the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR). The material is synthesized by incorporating F atoms into a porous carbon scaffold, and its electrochemical performance is evaluated in aqueous electrolyte across a range of applied potentials versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). At −0.2 V vs. RHE, the F-doped material achieves an FE of 54.8% for NH₃, compared to 18.3% for undoped carbon. At −0.3 V vs. RHE, the NH₃ yield rate reaches 197.7 µg_NH₃ mg⁻¹_cat h⁻¹. Mechanistic analysis attributes the performance improvement to stronger N₂ adsorption and facilitated dissociation of N₂ to *N₂H intermediates. The C–F bond generates a Lewis acid site due to the electronegativity difference between F and C, which repels protons and thereby suppresses the competing hydrogen evolution reaction, enhancing NRR selectivity. These results demonstrate that heteroatom doping of porous carbon is an effective strategy for improving both activity and selectivity in electrochemical nitrogen fixation.

entries.original_title: Gram‐Scale Synthesis of High‐Loading Single‐Atomic‐Site Fe Catalysts for Effective Epoxidation of Styrene
entries.original_abstract: Single‐atomic‐site (SAS) catalysts, a new frontier of catalysts, always show extremely high atom efficiency and unexpected catalytic properties. Herein, a pyrolyzing coordinated polymer (PCP) strategy is developed, which is facile and widely applicable in the synthesis of a series of SAS catalysts including SAS‐Fe, SAS‐Ni, SAS‐Cu, SAS‐Zn, SAS‐Ru, SAS‐Rh, SAS‐Pd, SAS‐Pt, and SAS‐Ir. The as‐obtained SAS catalysts can be easily synthesized at gram scale and the metal loading of SAS‐Fe catalysts achieves a record value of 30 wt%, which meets the requirement of practical applications. Moreover, it is discovered that SAS‐Fe catalysts show unprecedented catalytic performance for epoxidation of styrene using O2 as the only oxidant (yield: 64%; selectivity: 89%), while Fe nanoparticles and ironporphyrin are inactive. This discovery is believed to pave the way for exploiting the unparalleled properties of SAS catalysts and promoting their industrial applications.
entries.anonymized_problem: Single-atomic-site (SAS) catalysts offer high atom efficiency and distinctive catalytic behavior, but scalable synthesis routes that achieve high metal loadings remain a challenge. This work describes a pyrolysis-based strategy using coordinated polymer precursors to produce a broad series of carbon-supported SAS catalysts bearing Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Ru, Rh, Pd, Pt, and Ir centers. The approach is operationally straightforward and scalable to gram quantities. The iron-based variant achieves a metal loading of 30 wt%, among the highest reported for single-atomic-site systems. Structural characterization confirms atomic dispersion of metal centers without nanoparticle formation. The iron catalyst is evaluated for styrene epoxidation using molecular oxygen as the sole oxidant, yielding 64% product with 89% selectivity toward the epoxide. In contrast, iron nanoparticle and iron-porphyrin controls show negligible activity under identical conditions, indicating that the atomically dispersed coordination environment is essential for catalytic function. These results suggest that the defined coordination geometry around isolated Fe sites activates O₂ for selective epoxidation in a manner inaccessible to bulk iron phases, and that the scalable synthesis strategy may facilitate broader investigation and practical deployment of single-atomic-site catalysts across oxidation and other reactions.

entries.original_title: Water-Soluble BODIPY Photocages with Tunable Cellular Localization
entries.original_abstract: Photoactivation of bioactive molecules allows manipulation of cellular processes with high spatiotemporal precision. The recent emergence of visible-light excitable photoprotecting groups has the potential to further expand the established utility of the photoactivation strategy in biological applications by offering higher tissue penetration, diminished phototoxicity, and compatibility with other light-dependent techniques. Nevertheless, a critical barrier to such applications remains the significant hydrophobicity of most visible-light excitable photocaging groups. Here, we find that applying the conventional 2,6-sulfonation to meso-methyl BODIPY photocages is incompatible with their photoreaction due to an increase in the excited state barrier for photorelease. We present a simple, remote sulfonation solution to BODIPY photocages that imparts water solubility and provides control over cellular permeability while retaining their favorable spectroscopic and photoreaction properties. Peripherally disulfonated BODIPY photocages are cell impermeable, making them useful for modulation of cell-surface receptors, while monosulfonated BODIPY retains the ability to cross the cellular membrane and can modulate intracellular targets. This new approach is generalizable for controlling BODIPY localization and was validated by sensitization of mammalian cells and neurons by visible-light photoactivation of signaling molecules.
entries.anonymized_problem: Photoactivatable protecting groups that respond to visible light offer advantages over ultraviolet-responsive alternatives in biological settings, including greater tissue penetration, reduced phototoxicity, and compatibility with other light-based techniques. However, the inherent hydrophobicity of most visible-light-responsive photocaging scaffolds limits their utility in aqueous and cellular environments. This study investigates the water-solubility problem in BODIPY-based photocages, finding that conventional 2,6-sulfonation of meso-methyl BODIPY is incompatible with the photochemical release mechanism due to an elevated excited-state barrier introduced by that substitution pattern. A remote sulfonation strategy is described in which sulfonate groups are placed at peripheral positions on the BODIPY core, conferring water solubility without disrupting the spectroscopic properties or photorelease efficiency. The number and placement of sulfonate groups tune cellular permeability in a predictable manner: peripherally disulfonated variants are cell-impermeable and thus suitable for targeting cell-surface receptors, whereas monosulfonated variants retain membrane permeability and can reach intracellular targets. The approach is validated through visible-light photoactivation of signaling molecules in mammalian cells and neurons, demonstrating spatiotemporally controlled modulation of both surface and intracellular biological targets. The sulfonation strategy is shown to be generalizable for controlling the subcellular localization of BODIPY-based photocaging platforms.

entries.original_title: Stimuli‐Responsive Dynamic Metaholographic Displays with Designer Liquid Crystal Modulators
entries.original_abstract: Flat optics, realized by the artificially created 2D material platform called optical metasurfaces, is currently undergoing a science‐to‐technology transition. However, “real‐time” active operations of such flat optical devices remain yet unresolved. Here, liquid crystals (LCs)‐integrated metaholograms for ultracompact dynamic holographic displays are proposed. The anisotropic nature of the LCs allows facile and repeatable manipulation of the polarization of light. Specifically designed (“designer”) LCs and efficient helicity‐encoded metaholograms are combined to realize stimuli‐responsive dynamic displays. The designer LC modulators are used as switches that enable a variety of external stimuli (e.g., electric field, heat, surface pressure) to operate holographic images in real‐time. Such a dynamic metaholographic platform will provide a path to external stimuli‐driven “smart” sensing and display applications such as hologram labels for temperature/pressure/touch monitoring and interactive holographic displays with haptic motion recognition.
entries.anonymized_problem: Optical metasurfaces enable flat, ultrathin optical elements, but achieving real-time active control of such devices remains a significant challenge. This work addresses that limitation by integrating liquid crystal (LC) modulators with helicity-encoded metaholograms to create dynamically switchable holographic displays. The anisotropic optical properties of liquid crystals allow polarization-state manipulation in response to external stimuli, and purpose-engineered LC layers are paired with metasurface holograms designed to encode distinct holographic images in different helicity channels. The LC modulators function as switchable polarization controllers, enabling holographic image selection through the application of electric fields, thermal changes, or mechanical surface pressure. This multi-stimulus responsiveness is demonstrated across several application scenarios, including holographic labels capable of monitoring temperature, pressure, and touch events, as well as interactive displays with haptic motion recognition. The platform combines the compactness of metasurface flat optics with the tunability of stimuli-responsive LC materials, providing a route toward smart sensing and display systems that can operate in real time under diverse physical triggers without requiring bulky conventional optical components.

entries.original_title: Measuring aptamer folding energy using a molecular clamp.
entries.original_abstract: Folding energy offers a useful metric for characterizing the stability and function of aptamers. However, experimentally measuring the folding energy is challenging and there is currently no general technique to measure this parameter directly. In this work, we present a simple approach for measuring aptamer folding energy. First, the aptamer is stretched under equilibrium conditions with a double-stranded DNA "molecular clamp" that is coupled to the aptamer ends. We then measure the total internal energy of stressed DNA molecules using time-lapse gel electrophoresis and compare the folding and unfolding behavior of molecular clamp-stressed molecules that incorporate either the aptamer or unstructured random single-stranded DNA in order to derive the aptamer folding energy. Using this approach, we measured a folding energy of 10.40 kJ/mol for the HD22 thrombin aptamer, which is consistent with other predictions and estimates. We also analyzed a simple hairpin structure, generating a folding energy result of 9.05 kJ/mol, consistent with the value predicted by computational models (9.24 kJ/mol). We believe our strategy offers an accessible and generalizable approach for obtaining such measurements with virtually any aptamer.
entries.anonymized_problem: Aptamer folding energy is a useful metric for characterizing structural stability and functional behavior, yet no general experimental method exists for measuring this parameter directly. This work addresses that gap by introducing a double-stranded DNA "molecular clamp" approach that stretches an aptamer under equilibrium conditions by coupling the clamp to the aptamer's ends. The total internal energy of the stressed DNA constructs is measured via time-lapse gel electrophoresis, and folding/unfolding behavior is compared between constructs incorporating either the aptamer or an unstructured random single-stranded DNA sequence of equivalent length, allowing the aptamer folding energy to be isolated and quantified. Applying this method to the HD22 thrombin aptamer yielded a folding energy of 10.40 kJ/mol, consistent with existing predictions and estimates from complementary approaches. Validation using a simple hairpin structure produced a folding energy of 9.05 kJ/mol, in close agreement with a computationally predicted value of 9.24 kJ/mol. The approach requires only standard gel electrophoresis equipment and straightforward DNA constructs, suggesting it is broadly accessible and applicable to a wide range of aptamer sequences without specialized instrumentation.

entries.original_title: Synthesis of azetidines via visible-light-mediated intermolecular [2+2] photocycloadditions
entries.original_abstract: Intermolecular [2+2] photocycloadditions represent a powerful method for the synthesis of highly strained, four-membered rings. Although this approach is commonly employed for the synthesis of oxetanes and cyclobutanes, the synthesis of azetidines via intermolecular aza Paternò–Büchi reactions remains highly underdeveloped. Here we report a visible-light-mediated intermolecular aza Paternò–Büchi reaction that utilizes the unique triplet state reactivity of oximes, specifically 2-isoxazoline-3-carboxylates. The reactivity of this class of oximes can be harnessed via the triplet energy transfer from a commercially available iridium photocatalyst and allows for [2+2] cycloaddition with a wide range of alkenes. This approach is characterized by its operational simplicity, mild conditions and broad scope, and allows for the synthesis of highly functionalized azetidines from readily available precursors. Importantly, the accessible azetidine products can be readily converted into free, unprotected azetidines, which represents a new approach to access these highly desirable synthetic targets. Although azetidines represent highly desirable building blocks in drug discovery, methods for their efficient and straightforward synthesis remain underdeveloped. Now, it has been shown that highly functionalized azetidines can be prepared via an intermolecular [2+2] photocycloaddition reaction between cyclic oximes and alkenes, in a process enabled by a visible-light-mediated triplet energy transfer.
entries.anonymized_problem: Azetidines are valuable four-membered nitrogen-containing ring systems in medicinal chemistry, yet efficient methods for their synthesis—particularly via intermolecular routes—remain limited. This work addresses the synthesis of azetidines through an intermolecular aza Paternò–Büchi reaction employing visible-light photocatalysis. The approach exploits the triplet-state reactivity of cyclic oximes (specifically 2-isoxazoline-3-carboxylates), accessed via triplet energy transfer from a commercially available iridium photocatalyst. Upon sensitization, these oximes undergo [2+2] cycloaddition with a broad range of alkenes under mild conditions, enabling the construction of highly functionalized azetidine scaffolds from readily available starting materials. The reaction proceeds with operational simplicity and tolerates diverse alkene substrates, demonstrating wide synthetic scope. Critically, the cycloadduct products can be converted into free, unprotected azetidines, expanding access to this class of building blocks without requiring protective-group manipulations. The findings establish triplet energy transfer-mediated activation of cyclic oximes as a practical strategy for intermolecular C–N bond-forming photocycloadditions, complementing existing photochemical methods that focus primarily on oxetane and cyclobutane synthesis, and providing a streamlined route to azetidine-containing scaffolds relevant to drug discovery applications.

entries.original_title: Total Synthesis of (-)-Curvulamine.
entries.original_abstract: Curvulamine and related polypyrrole alkaloids represent a fascinating new class of natural products with unprecedented chemical structures, intriguing biological activities, and mysterious biosynthetic origins. Herein we report the first studies towards these molecules, resulting in a 10-step total synthesis of (-)-curvulamine, a dimeric member with promising Gram-positive and -negative antibiotic activity. A number of interesting chemical findings, including exploitation of the heteroaromatic pyrrolo[1,2-a]azepinone nucleus and an efficient stereodivergent reduction, are reported.
entries.anonymized_problem: The total synthesis of (−)-curvulamine, a dimeric polypyrrole alkaloid natural product exhibiting antibiotic activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, is described. Polypyrrole alkaloids of this class possess structurally complex and poorly understood chemical architectures with unclear biosynthetic origins, presenting significant synthetic challenges. A 10-step total synthesis was accomplished, with key strategic elements including exploitation of a pyrrolo[1,2-a]azepinone heteroaromatic nucleus as a core structural scaffold and a stereodivergent reduction step that enables efficient stereocontrol. The synthetic route demonstrates how the bicyclic heteroaromatic framework can be leveraged to address the structural complexity inherent in this natural product class. The completed synthesis provides access to (−)-curvulamine in enantioselective fashion and establishes a foundation for further investigation of related polypyrrole alkaloid family members, whose biological activities and biosynthetic pathways remain subjects of ongoing interest.

entries.original_title: Origin of Metallic Nature of Na3N.
entries.original_abstract: Among inorganic clathrates, the inner cavity space rarely affects the electronic structure of the framework. We report that the anti-ReO3-type compound Na3N has a metallic nature irrespective of the stoichiometric chemical composition of simple representative elements and that this unusual nature originates from the collapse of the bandgap owing to the presence of a crystallographic cavity. We synthesized Na3N by the plasma-assisted nitridation of alkali metals, and diffuse reflectance measurements indicated a metallic nature. The introduction of nitrogen into the Na metal induced the formation of both the Na+ ion and the crystallographic cavity. The former increased the density of the lattice of Na+ ions to form a wide Na 3s conduction band. The latter interacted with the Na 3s band to enhance the bandwidth, resulting in the collapse of the bandgap. Na3N is a unique nitride, which possesses an electronically active cavity space.
entries.anonymized_problem: The electronic structure of anti-ReO₃-type Na₃N is investigated, focusing on the unexpected metallic behavior of a stoichiometrically simple binary nitride. Typically, inorganic clathrate frameworks are electronically insensitive to inner cavity space; this work examines whether crystallographic cavities can directly influence bandgap formation. Na₃N was synthesized via plasma-assisted nitridation of alkali metal precursors, and diffuse reflectance spectroscopy was used to characterize its optical and electronic properties. Analysis of the electronic structure reveals that incorporation of nitrogen into sodium metal simultaneously generates Na⁺ ions and a crystallographic cavity. The increased density of Na⁺ ions broadens the Na 3s conduction band, while the cavity interacts with this band to further enhance bandwidth, ultimately causing bandgap collapse and giving rise to metallic character. This mechanism distinguishes Na₃N from conventional nitrides, which are typically wide-bandgap insulators or semiconductors. The findings demonstrate that crystallographic cavity space can be electronically active, representing a structural origin of metallicity in a compositionally simple binary compound and suggesting that cavity engineering may be a viable strategy for tuning electronic properties in related framework materials.

entries.original_title: A Neutral Silicon(II) Half-Sandwich Compound.
entries.original_abstract: Metathesis reaction of a dilithio borole dianion, a cyclic π-ligand isoelectronic to ubiquitous cyclopentadienyls, with two equivalents of "silicocenium" cation [Cp*Si]+ as a source of low-valent Si(II), cleanly gives a borole half-sandwich π-complex of Si(II) and silicocene. The resulting half-sandwich complex is a neutral isoelectronic analogue to the iconic silicocenium cation and features the rare structural motif of an apical silicon(II) atom with an energetically high lying lone pair of electrons that is shown to be accessible for coordination chemistry toward tungsten carbonyl. Protonation at the Si(II) atom with [H(OEt2)2][Al{OC(CF3)3}4] induces formal oxidation, and the compound rearranges to incorporate the Si atom into the carbocyclic base to give an unprecedented cationic 5-sila-6-borabicyclo[2.1.1]hex-2-ene. This rearrangement is accompanied by drastic changes in the 11B and 29Si NMR chemical shifts.
entries.anonymized_problem: A metathesis reaction between a dilithio borole dianion — a cyclic π-ligand isoelectronic to cyclopentadienyl — and two equivalents of a silicocenium cation serving as a low-valent Si(II) source was investigated to access neutral half-sandwich complexes of silicon. The reaction cleanly affords a borole half-sandwich π-complex of Si(II) alongside silicocene. The resulting neutral complex is isoelectronic to the silicocenium cation and features an apical Si(II) center bearing an energetically high-lying lone pair. Coordination chemistry of this lone pair toward tungsten carbonyl was demonstrated, confirming its accessibility as a donor. Protonation of the Si(II) atom with a strong proton source triggers formal oxidation and skeletal rearrangement, incorporating the silicon atom into the carbocyclic framework to produce a cationic 5-sila-6-borabicyclo[2.1.1]hex-2-ene. This rearrangement is accompanied by pronounced changes in ¹¹B and ²⁹Si NMR chemical shifts, providing spectroscopic evidence for the structural transformation. The work expands the known structural motifs accessible to low-valent silicon compounds and illustrates the reactivity of a borole-based π-ligand system in supporting unusual Si(II) bonding environments.

entries.original_title: Immobilization of Phosphatidylinositides Revealed by Bilayer Leaflet Decoupling.
entries.original_abstract: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) has a significantly lower mobile fraction than most other lipids in supported lipid bilayers (SLBs). Moreover, the fraction of mobile PIP2 continuously decreases with time. To explore this, a bilayer unzipping technique was designed to uncouple the two leaflets of the SLB. The results demonstrate that PIP2 molecules in the top leaflet are fully mobile, while the PIP2 molecules in the lower leaflet are immobilized on the oxide support. Over time, mobile PIP2 species flip from the top leaflet to the bottom leaflet and become trapped. It was found that PIP2 flipped between the leaflets through a defect-mediated process. The flipping could be completely inhibited when holes in the bilayer were backfilled with bovine serum albumin (BSA). Moreover, by switching from H2O to D2O, it was shown that the primary interaction between PIP2 and the underlying substrate was due to hydrogen bond formation, which outcompeted electrostatic repulsion. Using substrates with fewer surface silanol groups, like oxidized polydimethylsiloxane, led to a large increase in the mobile fraction of PIP2. Moreover, PIP2 immobilization also occurred when the bilayer was supported on a protein surface rather than glass. These results may help to explain the behavior of PIP2 on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, where it is involved in attaching the membrane to the underlying cytoskeleton.
entries.anonymized_problem: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) exhibits a substantially lower mobile fraction compared to most lipids in supported lipid bilayers (SLBs), and this mobile fraction decreases progressively over time. To investigate this anomalous behavior, a bilayer unzipping technique was employed to physically decouple the two leaflets of the SLB. This approach revealed that PIP2 in the top leaflet remains fully mobile, whereas PIP2 in the bottom leaflet is immobilized by interactions with the oxide substrate. Over time, mobile PIP2 molecules undergo leaflet-to-leaflet translocation (flip-flop) via a defect-mediated mechanism, becoming trapped upon reaching the lower leaflet. Backfilling bilayer defects with bovine serum albumin completely suppressed this flipping. Isotopic substitution experiments (H2O vs. D2O) indicated that hydrogen bond formation between PIP2 and surface silanol groups is the dominant immobilization mechanism, overcoming electrostatic repulsion. Replacing glass with substrates bearing fewer silanol groups, such as oxidized polydimethylsiloxane, substantially increased PIP2 mobility. Immobilization was also observed when bilayers were supported on protein surfaces rather than glass. These findings provide mechanistic insight relevant to the behavior of PIP2 on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, where it participates in anchoring the membrane to the cytoskeleton.

entries.original_title: Isotope Effect in the Activation of a Mechanophore.
entries.original_abstract: In mechanochemistry, molecules under tension can react in unexpected ways. The reactivity of mechanophores (mechanosensitive molecules) can be controlled using various geometric or electronic factors. Often these factors affect the rate of mechanical activation but sometimes give rise to alternative reaction pathways. Here we show that a simple isotope substitution (H to D) leads to a reversal of selectivity in the activation of a mechanophore. Remarkably this isotope effect is not kinetic in nature but emerges from dynamic effects in which deuteration reduces the ability of the reactant to follow a post-transition-state concerted trajectory on the bifurcated force-modified potential energy surface. These results give a new insight into the reactivity of molecules under tension.
entries.anonymized_problem: Mechanochemistry enables molecules under mechanical tension to undergo reactions that diverge from thermally or photochemically driven pathways, yet the factors governing selectivity among competing reaction channels remain incompletely understood. This study investigates how isotopic substitution influences the selectivity of mechanophore activation. Specifically, hydrogen-to-deuterium substitution in a mechanosensitive molecule is found to reverse product selectivity upon mechanical activation. The effect is not attributable to a conventional kinetic isotope effect operating at the transition state; instead, it arises from post-transition-state dynamics on a bifurcated force-modified potential energy surface. Deuteration reduces the capacity of the reacting system to follow a concerted trajectory after the transition state, thereby redirecting flux toward an alternative product channel. This interpretation is supported by analysis of the reaction dynamics on the force-modified surface, distinguishing the observed selectivity reversal from classical rate-based isotope effects. The findings demonstrate that dynamic trajectory effects, rather than transition-state energetics alone, can govern product outcomes in mechanochemical reactions, and they highlight isotopic substitution as a mechanistic probe for interrogating post-transition-state bifurcations in molecules subjected to mechanical force.

entries.original_title: Position‐ and Orientation‐Controlled Growth of Wulff‐Shaped Colloidal Crystals Engineered with DNA
entries.original_abstract: Colloidal crystals have emerged as promising candidates for building optical microdevices. Techniques now exist for synthesizing them with control over their nanoscale features (e.g., particle compositions, sizes, shapes, and lattice parameters and symmetry); however, the ability to tune macroscale structural features, such as the relative positions of crystals to one another and lattice orientations, has yet to be realized. Here, inspiration is drawn from epitaxial growth strategies in atomic crystallization, and patterned substrates are prepared that, when used in conjunction with DNA‐mediated nanoparticle crystallization, allow for control over individual Wulff‐shaped crystal growth, location, and orientation. In addition, the approach allows exquisite control over the patterned substrate/crystal lattice mismatch, something not yet realized for any epitaxy process. This level of structural control is a significant step toward realizing complex, integrated devices with colloidal crystal components, and this approach provides a model system for further exploration in epitaxy systems.
entries.anonymized_problem: Colloidal crystals are attractive materials for optical microdevices, and established synthesis methods provide control over nanoscale features such as particle composition, size, shape, and lattice parameters. However, controlling macroscale structural attributes—specifically the spatial positions of individual crystals relative to one another and their lattice orientations—has remained an unresolved challenge. This work addresses that gap by adapting epitaxial growth strategies from atomic crystallization to the colloidal domain. Patterned substrates are fabricated and used in combination with DNA-mediated nanoparticle assembly to direct the growth of Wulff-shaped colloidal crystals at defined locations with controlled lattice orientations. The approach also enables precise tuning of the lattice mismatch between the patterned substrate and the growing crystal, a degree of control not previously demonstrated in any epitaxy process. The method is shown to yield individual crystals whose position, orientation, and substrate registry are each independently addressable. These results represent a meaningful advance toward integrating colloidal crystal components into functional, spatially organized optical devices and establish a well-defined model system for investigating epitaxial phenomena in programmable, soft-matter crystallization contexts.

entries.original_title: Sierpiński Pyramids by Molecular Entanglement.
entries.original_abstract: Planar, terpyridine-based metal-complexes with the Sierpiński triangular motif and alkylated corners undergo a second self-assembly event to give megastructural Sierpiński pyramids; assembly is driven by the facile lipophilic-lipophilic association of the alkyl moieties and complementary perfect-fit of the triangular building blocks. Confirmation of the 3D, pyramidal structures was verified and supported by a combination of TEM, AFM, and multiscale simulation techniques.
entries.anonymized_problem: Fractal molecular architectures present an ongoing challenge in supramolecular chemistry: extending planar, two-dimensional fractal motifs into three-dimensional hierarchical structures through controlled self-assembly. This work investigates how planar metal-organic triangular building blocks bearing the Sierpiński triangular motif can be induced to undergo a secondary self-assembly event to form three-dimensional pyramidal megastructures. The building blocks are terpyridine-based metal complexes with alkyl chains installed at their corners; the driving forces for the second-level assembly are lipophilic–lipophilic interactions among the alkyl substituents combined with geometric complementarity between the triangular faces. The resulting pyramidal assemblies represent a Sierpiński fractal extended into three dimensions. Structural characterization was performed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and multiscale computational simulation, collectively confirming the anticipated three-dimensional pyramidal architecture. The findings demonstrate that judicious placement of lipophilic groups on the periphery of planar fractal complexes provides a viable strategy for directing hierarchical self-assembly into higher-dimensional fractal superstructures, with molecular geometry and non-covalent interactions jointly governing the overall assembly outcome.

entries.original_title: Two-Dimensional Coordination Networks from Cyclic Dipeptides.
entries.original_abstract: Peptide-based biomimetic nanostructures and metal-organic coordination networks on surfaces are two promising classes of hybrid materials which have been explored recently. However, despite the great versatility and structural variability of natural and synthetic peptides, the two directions have so far not been merged in fabrication of metal-organic coordination networks using peptides as building blocks. Here we demonstrate that cyclic peptides can be used as ligands to form highly ordered, two-dimensional, peptide-based metal-organic coordination networks. The networks are formed on a Au(111) surface through coadsorption of cyclic dialanine with Cu-adatoms under Ultra-High Vacuum (UHV) conditions. Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) in combination with X-ray Photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) has been utilized to characterize the network structures at submolecular resolution and expound the chemical changes involved in network coordination. The networks involve a motif of three cyclic dialanine molecules coordinating to a central Cu-adatom. Interestingly the networks expose pores functionalized by the side chain of the cyclic peptide, suggesting a general method to form functionalized porous metal-organic networks on surfaces.
entries.anonymized_problem: Peptide-based biomimetic nanostructures and metal-organic coordination networks represent two distinct classes of surface-assembled hybrid materials, yet their combination using peptides directly as coordination ligands has remained largely unexplored. This study investigates whether cyclic dipeptides can serve as building blocks for forming ordered two-dimensional metal-organic coordination networks on surfaces. Cyclic dialanine was co-deposited with copper adatoms on a Au(111) surface under ultra-high vacuum conditions, and the resulting assemblies were characterized using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) at submolecular resolution alongside X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to resolve both structural geometry and coordination chemistry. The networks adopt a recurring motif in which three cyclic dialanine molecules coordinate to a single central copper adatom, producing highly ordered, extended two-dimensional frameworks. The assembled networks contain well-defined pores whose interior surfaces are functionalized by the amino acid side chains of the cyclic peptide ligands. These findings demonstrate that cyclic peptides are viable ligands for surface metal-organic coordination chemistry and suggest a general strategy for constructing porous two-dimensional networks with chemically tunable pore environments, with the peptide side chain offering a straightforward handle for systematic functionalization.

entries.original_title: Addressing Ligand-Based Redox in Molybdenum-Dependent Methionine Sulfoxide Reductase.
entries.original_abstract: A combination of pulsed EPR, CW EPR, and X-ray absorption spectroscopies has been employed to probe the geometric and electronic structure of the E. coli periplasmic molybdenum-dependent methionine sulfoxide reductase (MsrP). 17O and 1H pulsed EPR spectra show that the as-isolated Mo(V) enzyme form does not possess an exchangeable H2O/OH- ligand bound to Mo as found in the sulfite oxidizing enzymes of the same family. The nature of the unusual CW EPR spectrum has been re-evaluated in light of new data on the MsrP-N45R variant and related small-molecule analogues of the active site. These data point to a novel "thiol-blocked" [(PDT)MoVO(SCys)(thiolate)]- structure, which is supported by new EXAFS data. We discuss these new results in the context of ligand-based and metal-based redox chemistry in the enzymatic oxygen atom transfer reaction.
entries.anonymized_problem: The geometric and electronic structure of the periplasmic molybdenum-dependent methionine sulfoxide reductase from *E. coli* (MsrP) was investigated using a combination of pulsed EPR (¹⁷O and ¹H), continuous-wave EPR, and X-ray absorption spectroscopies. A central question concerns the nature of the Mo(V) intermediate and whether it follows the same coordination chemistry as related sulfite-oxidizing molybdoenzymes. Pulsed EPR data demonstrate that the as-isolated Mo(V) form of MsrP lacks an exchangeable H₂O/OH⁻ ligand bound to molybdenum, distinguishing it from other members of the same enzyme family. Reinterpretation of the unusual CW EPR spectrum, informed by data from a site-directed variant (N45R) and small-molecule active-site analogues, points to a "thiol-blocked" coordination structure of the form [(PDT)Mo^V O(SCys)(thiolate)]⁻. This structural assignment is supported by extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) analysis. The results are discussed in the context of distinguishing ligand-based from metal-based redox pathways during the enzymatic oxygen atom transfer reaction, with implications for understanding the mechanistic divergence of MsrP from other molybdenum-containing oxidoreductases.

entries.original_title: Crystal Structure and C-H Bond Cleaving Reactivity of a Mononuclear CoIV-dinitrate Complex.
entries.original_abstract: High-valent FeIV=O intermediates with a terminal metal-oxo moiety are key oxidants in many enzymatic and synthetic C-H bond oxidation reactions. While generating stable metal-oxo species for late transition metals remains synthetically challenging, notably, a number of high-valent non-oxo-metal species of late transition metals have been recently described as strong oxidants that activate C-H bonds. In this work, we obtained an unprecedented mononuclear CoIV-dinitrate complex (2) upon one-electron oxidation of its Co(III) precursor supported by a tridentate di-anionic N3 ligand. 2 was structurally characterized by X-ray crystallography, showing a square pyramidal geometry with two coordinated nitrate anions. Furthermore, characterization of 2 us-ing combined spectroscopic and computational methods revealed that 2 is a low-spin (S = 1/2) Co(IV) species with the unpaired electron located on the cobalt dz2 orbital, which is well positioned for substrate oxidations. Indeed, while having a high thermal stability, 2 is able to cleave sp3 C-H bonds up to 87 kcal/mol to afford rate constants and kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) of 2-6 that are comparable to other high-valent metal oxidants. The ability to oxidize strong C-H bonds has yet to be observed for CoIV-O and CoIII=O species previously reported. Therefore, 2 represents the first high-valent Co(IV) species that is both structurally character-ized by X-ray crystallography and is capable of activating strong C-H bonds.
entries.anonymized_problem: A mononuclear cobalt(IV) dinitrate complex was synthesized and characterized to investigate C–H bond oxidation reactivity by a high-valent, non-oxo late transition metal species. High-valent iron(IV)-oxo intermediates are well-established oxidants in enzymatic and synthetic contexts, but analogous stable metal-oxo species for late transition metals are difficult to access. A Co(IV) complex was obtained via one-electron oxidation of a cobalt(III) precursor supported by a tridentate dianionic N3 ligand. The resulting complex was structurally characterized by X-ray crystallography, revealing a square-pyramidal geometry with two coordinated nitrate anions. Combined spectroscopic and computational methods established a low-spin (S = 1/2) Co(IV) electronic configuration with the unpaired electron residing in the cobalt d_z² orbital, a geometry favorable for substrate oxidation. Despite high thermal stability, the complex cleaves sp³ C–H bonds with bond dissociation energies up to 87 kcal/mol, exhibiting rate constants and kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) of 2–6 comparable to other high-valent metal oxidants. This C–H bond activation capability has not been observed for previously reported Co(IV)-oxo or Co(III)-oxo species. The complex thus represents a structurally authenticated Co(IV) species capable of activating strong C–H bonds without a terminal metal-oxo moiety.

entries.original_title: Design and Synthesis of Megamolecule Mimics of a Therapeutic Antibody.
entries.original_abstract: This communication describes the design, synthesis and biological activity of a megamolecule mimic of an anti-HER2 antibody. The antibody mimic was prepared by linking two Fabs from the therapeutic antibody trastuzumab, which are fused through the heavy chain variable domain to either cutinase or SnapTag, with a linker terminated in an irreversible inhibitor for each enzyme. This mimic binds HER2 with comparable avidity to trastuzumab, has similar activity in a cell-based assay, and can arrest tumor growth in a mouse xenograft BT474 tumor model. A panel of 16 bivalent anti-HER2 antibodies were prepared wherein each varied in the orientation of the fusion domain on the Fabs. The analogs displayed a range of cytotoxic activity and surprisingly, the most active mimic binds to cells with a ten-fold lower avidity than the least active variant suggesting that structure plays a large role in their efficacy. This work suggests that the megamolecule approach can be used to prepare antibody mimics having a broad structural diversity.
entries.anonymized_problem: Therapeutic antibodies such as anti-HER2 agents are highly effective but structurally constrained, limiting the ability to systematically vary their geometry and valency. This study addresses whether synthetic bivalent antibody mimics constructed through site-specific covalent assembly can recapitulate or surpass the biological activity of a clinical monoclonal antibody while enabling broader structural diversity. The approach involved fusing antigen-binding fragments (Fabs) derived from an approved anti-HER2 antibody to one of two self-labeling enzyme tags (cutinase or a related alkyl-transferase tag) via the heavy chain variable domain, then crosslinking pairs of these fusion proteins using bifunctional linkers bearing covalent inhibitors for each enzyme. A panel of 16 bivalent constructs was prepared by varying the orientation of the fusion domain on each Fab. The resulting mimics bind HER2 with avidity comparable to the parent antibody, exhibit similar activity in cell-based assays, and arrest tumor growth in a mouse xenograft model using BT474 cells. Notably, the most cytotoxically active variant displayed ten-fold lower cellular avidity than the least active construct, indicating that three-dimensional geometry rather than binding strength alone governs efficacy. These findings demonstrate that covalent megamolecule assembly offers a versatile platform for generating structurally diverse antibody mimics with tunable biological function.

entries.original_title: Hydrogen Migration-Triggered Diradicaloid Singlet-Fission Switch.
entries.original_abstract: We present a theoretical design of the singlet-fission (SF) interconversion between two hydrogen tautomers to attract attention to electronic devices such as switches in the SF field.
