The study concludes that aggregate economic or financial frameworks are insufficient to explain household-level responses to agricultural transformation; rather, the specific contests over resources, labor, and autonomy between men and women fundamentally shape how communities adapt to commodity sector decline.

entries.original_title: Byzantine-Robust Learning on Heterogeneous Datasets via Bucketing
entries.original_abstract: In Byzantine robust distributed or federated learning, a central server wants to train a machine learning model over data distributed across multiple workers. However, a fraction of these workers may deviate from the prescribed algorithm and send arbitrary messages. While this problem has received significant attention recently, most current defenses assume that the workers have identical data. For realistic cases when the data across workers are heterogeneous (non-iid), we design new attacks which circumvent current defenses, leading to significant loss of performance. We then propose a simple bucketing scheme that adapts existing robust algorithms to heterogeneous datasets at a negligible computational cost. We also theoretically and experimentally validate our approach, showing that combining bucketing with existing robust algorithms is effective against challenging attacks. Our work is the first to establish guaranteed convergence for the non-iid Byzantine robust problem under realistic assumptions.
entries.anonymized_problem: Distributed and federated learning systems must tolerate Byzantine workers—participants who may send arbitrary or malicious messages—while training over data distributed across many nodes. Existing defenses against such attacks largely assume that workers hold identically distributed data, yet in practice data distributions are heterogeneous across workers (non-iid). This work investigates how heterogeneity undermines existing robust aggregation methods by constructing attacks that exploit the increased gradient variance across workers, demonstrating significant performance degradation. To address this, a bucketing scheme is introduced that preprocesses worker updates by randomly grouping them into buckets and averaging within each bucket before applying any robust aggregation rule. This preprocessing reduces effective gradient heterogeneity and can be combined with existing robust aggregators at negligible additional computational cost. Theoretical convergence guarantees are established for the non-iid Byzantine-robust setting under realistic assumptions, filling a gap left by prior work that required iid data. Empirical evaluations confirm that combining the bucketing approach with standard robust aggregation rules defends effectively against the constructed heterogeneous-data attacks. The analysis shows guaranteed convergence holds even when a constant fraction of workers are Byzantine and data distributions differ substantially across honest workers.

entries.original_title: NAS-Bench-1Shot1: Benchmarking and Dissecting One-shot Neural Architecture Search
entries.original_abstract: One-shot neural architecture search (NAS) has played a crucial role in making NAS methods computationally feasible in practice. Nevertheless, there is still a lack of understanding on how these weight-sharing algorithms exactly work due to the many factors controlling the dynamics of the process. In order to allow a scientific study of these components, we introduce a general framework for one-shot NAS that can be instantiated to many recently-introduced variants and introduce a general benchmarking framework that draws on the recent large-scale tabular benchmark NAS-Bench-101 for cheap anytime evaluations of one-shot NAS methods. To showcase the framework, we compare several state-of-the-art one-shot NAS methods, examine how sensitive they are to their hyperparameters and how they can be improved by tuning their hyperparameters, and compare their performance to that of blackbox optimizers for NAS-Bench-101.
entries.anonymized_problem: One-shot neural architecture search (NAS) reduces the computational cost of architecture search through weight sharing across a supernetwork, but the dynamics governing these methods remain poorly understood due to the large number of interacting factors. This work addresses that gap by introducing a unified framework that subsumes several recently proposed one-shot NAS variants under a common formulation, enabling systematic comparison. To support cheap, reproducible evaluation, a benchmarking infrastructure is constructed on top of an existing large-scale tabular NAS benchmark, allowing anytime performance assessment without full retraining. Using this infrastructure, several representative one-shot NAS methods are compared with respect to their search performance, sensitivity to hyperparameter choices, and the degree to which hyperparameter tuning can close performance gaps between methods. Results are further contextualized by comparing one-shot approaches against blackbox optimization baselines evaluated on the same tabular benchmark. The findings reveal that one-shot methods exhibit substantial sensitivity to their hyperparameters and that careful tuning can significantly affect relative rankings, suggesting that previously reported performance differences may partly reflect hyperparameter configurations rather than fundamental algorithmic advantages. The framework provides a controlled experimental setting for future investigation of weight-sharing NAS components.

entries.original_title: Autoregressive Entity Retrieval
entries.original_abstract: Entities are at the center of how we represent and aggregate knowledge. For instance, Encyclopedias such as Wikipedia are structured by entities (e.g., one per article). The ability to retrieve such entities given a query is fundamental for knowledge-intensive tasks such as entity linking and open-domain question answering. One way to understand current approaches is as classifiers among atomic labels, one for each entity. Their weight vectors are dense entity representations produced by encoding entity information such as descriptions. This approach leads to several shortcomings: i) context and entity affinity is mainly captured through a vector dot product, potentially missing fine-grained interactions between the two; ii) a large memory footprint is needed to store dense representations when considering large entity sets; iii) an appropriately hard set of negative data has to be subsampled at training time. We propose GENRE, the first system that retrieves entities by generating their unique names, left to right, token-by-token in an autoregressive fashion, and conditioned on the context. This enables to mitigate the aforementioned technical issues: i) the autoregressive formulation allows us to directly capture relations between context and entity name, effectively cross encoding both; ii) the memory footprint is greatly reduced because the parameters of our encoder-decoder architecture scale with vocabulary size, not entity count; iii) the exact softmax loss can be efficiently computed without the need to subsample negative data. We show the efficacy of the approach with more than 20 datasets on entity disambiguation, end-to-end entity linking and document retrieval tasks, achieving new SOTA, or very competitive results while using a tiny fraction of the memory of competing systems. Finally, we demonstrate that new entities can be added by simply specifying their unambiguous name.
entries.anonymized_problem:
Entity retrieval — identifying relevant knowledge base entries given a natural language query — is central to tasks such as entity linking and open-domain question answering. Existing approaches typically frame retrieval as classification over a fixed set of entity labels, using dense vector representations and dot-product similarity. This paradigm suffers from limited context–entity interaction (captured only through inner products), large memory requirements scaling with entity count, and the need for carefully sampled negatives during training.

The approach studied here recasts entity retrieval as a sequence generation problem: an encoder-decoder architecture generates an entity's unique textual name autoregressively, token by token, conditioned on the input context. This formulation enables fine-grained cross-attention between context and entity name tokens, reduces memory footprint to scale with vocabulary size rather than entity count, and permits exact softmax computation without negative sampling. Constrained beam search over a prefix trie of valid entity names ensures outputs correspond to known entities.

The approach is evaluated across more than 20 datasets spanning entity disambiguation, end-to-end entity linking, and document retrieval. It achieves competitive or leading results on standard benchmarks while using a substantially smaller memory footprint than dense retrieval systems. The method also generalizes naturally to newly added entities by specifying their names without retraining the full model.

entries.original_title: Faster Wasserstein Distance Estimation with the Sinkhorn Divergence
entries.original_abstract: The squared Wasserstein distance is a natural quantity to compare probability distributions in a non-parametric setting. This quantity is usually estimated with the plug-in estimator, defined via a discrete optimal transport problem. It can be solved to $\epsilon$-accuracy by adding an entropic regularization of order $\epsilon$ and using for instance Sinkhorn's algorithm. In this work, we propose instead to estimate it with the Sinkhorn divergence, which is also built on entropic regularization but includes debiasing terms. We show that, for smooth densities, this estimator has a comparable sample complexity but allows higher regularization levels, of order $\epsilon^{1/2}$ , which leads to improved computational complexity bounds and a strong speedup in practice. Our theoretical analysis covers the case of both randomly sampled densities and deterministic discretizations on uniform grids. We also propose and analyze an estimator based on Richardson extrapolation of the Sinkhorn divergence which enjoys improved statistical and computational efficiency guarantees, under a condition on the regularity of the approximation error, which is in particular satisfied for Gaussian densities. We finally demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed estimators with numerical experiments.
entries.anonymized_problem: Estimating the squared Wasserstein distance between probability distributions is a fundamental problem in non-parametric statistics, typically addressed using a plug-in estimator solved via discrete optimal transport. Standard approaches apply entropic regularization of order ε and solve the resulting problem with iterative scaling algorithms, but achieving ε-accurate estimates requires small regularization, leading to high computational cost. This work investigates whether a debiased variant of the entropic regularization approach—incorporating correction terms to remove bias introduced by regularization—can serve as a more efficient estimator. Theoretical analysis shows that for smooth densities, this debiased estimator achieves comparable sample complexity to the standard plug-in estimator while permitting regularization of order ε^{1/2} rather than ε, yielding improved computational complexity bounds and substantial practical speedups. The analysis covers both randomly sampled densities and deterministic discretizations on uniform grids. An additional estimator based on Richardson extrapolation of the debiased objective is proposed and analyzed, offering further improvements in statistical and computational efficiency under a regularity condition on the approximation error—a condition verified to hold for Gaussian densities. Numerical experiments confirm the practical efficiency gains of both estimators compared to the standard regularized optimal transport approach.

entries.original_title: Provable Meta-Learning of Linear Representations
entries.original_abstract: Meta-learning, or learning-to-learn, seeks to design algorithms that can utilize previous experience to rapidly learn new skills or adapt to new environments. Representation learning---a key tool for performing meta-learning---learns a data representation that can transfer knowledge across multiple tasks, which is essential in regimes where data is scarce. Despite a recent surge of interest in the practice of meta-learning, the theoretical underpinnings of meta-learning algorithms are lacking, especially in the context of learning transferable representations. In this paper, we focus on the problem of multi-task linear regression---in which multiple linear regression models share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Here, we provide provably fast, sample-efficient algorithms to address the dual challenges of (1) learning a common set of features from multiple, related tasks, and (2) transferring this knowledge to new, unseen tasks. Both are central to the general problem of meta-learning. Finally, we complement these results by providing information-theoretic lower bounds on the sample complexity of learning these linear features.
entries.anonymized_problem: Meta-learning aims to leverage experience across multiple tasks to enable rapid adaptation to new tasks, particularly when data is scarce. A central challenge is learning data representations that transfer effectively across tasks, yet the theoretical foundations for such representation learning remain underdeveloped. This work studies multi-task linear regression, where multiple linear regression models share a common low-dimensional linear representation. Two interconnected problems are addressed: (1) learning a shared feature space from a collection of related tasks, and (2) transferring the learned representation to new, previously unseen tasks. Provably efficient algorithms with sample-complexity guarantees are developed for both settings. The analysis establishes conditions under which the shared low-dimensional subspace can be recovered accurately, and characterizes how many tasks and samples per task are required for reliable transfer. These upper bounds are complemented by information-theoretic lower bounds on the sample complexity of identifying the underlying linear features, establishing near-tight characterizations of the fundamental difficulty of the problem. The results provide a rigorous theoretical grounding for gradient-based and spectral approaches to multi-task representation learning, clarifying when and why shared-representation methods succeed in the meta-learning regime.

entries.original_title: Bag of Tricks for Adversarial Training
entries.original_abstract: Adversarial training (AT) is one of the most effective strategies for promoting model robustness. However, recent benchmarks show that most of the proposed improvements on AT are less effective than simply early stopping the training procedure. This counter-intuitive fact motivates us to investigate the implementation details of tens of AT methods. Surprisingly, we find that the basic training settings (e.g., weight decay, learning rate schedule, etc.) used in these methods are highly inconsistent, which could largely affect the model performance as shown in our experiments. For example, a slightly different value of weight decay can reduce the model robust accuracy by more than 7%, which is probable to override the potential promotion induced by the proposed methods. In this work, we provide comprehensive evaluations on the effects of basic training tricks and hyperparameter settings for adversarially trained models. We provide a reasonable baseline setting and re-implement previous defenses to achieve new state-of-the-art results.
entries.anonymized_problem: Adversarial training is a widely used strategy for improving model robustness against adversarial examples, yet recent benchmarks suggest that many proposed enhancements offer limited benefit over simply applying early stopping. This discrepancy motivates a systematic investigation into the implementation details of numerous adversarial training methods. A key finding is that basic training hyperparameters—such as weight decay values and learning rate schedules—vary substantially across published methods, and these inconsistencies can have a larger impact on robust accuracy than the algorithmic contributions being evaluated. For instance, varying weight decay alone is shown to alter robust accuracy by more than 7%, potentially masking or negating the effect of a proposed defense. To address this, comprehensive experiments are conducted to characterize how fundamental training settings affect adversarially trained models. A standardized baseline configuration is established by isolating the contribution of individual hyperparameters and training tricks across a range of existing defense methods. Re-implementing prior defenses under this consistent baseline yields improved robust accuracy results, suggesting that a significant portion of previously reported performance gaps stems from inconsistent experimental setups rather than algorithmic differences. The work provides practical guidance for fair comparison and reproducibility in adversarial robustness research.

entries.original_title: SCOP: Scientific Control for Reliable Neural Network Pruning
entries.original_abstract: This paper proposes a reliable neural network pruning algorithm by setting up a scientific control. Existing pruning methods have developed various hypotheses to approximate the importance of filters to the network and then execute filter pruning accordingly. To increase the reliability of the results, we prefer to have a more rigorous research design by including a scientific control group as an essential part to minimize the effect of all factors except the association between the filter and expected network output. Acting as a control group, knockoff feature is generated to mimic the feature map produced by the network filter, but they are conditionally independent of the example label given the real feature map. We theoretically suggest that the knockoff condition can be approximately preserved given the information propagation of network layers. Besides the real feature map on an intermediate layer, the corresponding knockoff feature is brought in as another auxiliary input signal for the subsequent layers. Redundant filters can be discovered in the adversarial process of different features. Through experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm over state-of-the-art methods. For example, our method can reduce 57.8% parameters and 60.2% FLOPs of ResNet-101 with only 0.01% top-1 accuracy loss on ImageNet.
entries.anonymized_problem: Neural network pruning aims to reduce model complexity while preserving predictive performance, but existing methods rely on heuristic importance criteria for filter selection, limiting the reliability of pruning decisions. This work addresses that limitation by incorporating a scientific control mechanism into the pruning framework. The approach generates a knockoff feature for each filter's feature map — a synthetic counterpart that mimics the statistical properties of the real feature map but is conditionally independent of the class label given the real feature map. This knockoff serves as a control group, isolating the true association between each filter and the network output. Theoretical analysis suggests that the knockoff condition is approximately preserved through information propagation across network layers. During inference, both the real and knockoff features are fed as inputs to subsequent layers, and redundant filters are identified through an adversarial comparison between the two. Experiments on ImageNet demonstrate that this approach can reduce parameters by 57.8% and FLOPs by 60.2% on ResNet-101 with only a 0.01% drop in top-1 accuracy, outperforming competing pruning methods across multiple architectures and compression levels.

entries.original_title: Matern Gaussian processes on Riemannian manifolds
entries.original_abstract: Gaussian processes are an effective model class for learning unknown functions, particularly in settings where accurately representing predictive uncertainty is of key importance. Motivated by applications in the physical sciences, the widely-used Matern class of Gaussian processes has recently been generalized to model functions whose domains are Riemannian manifolds, by re-expressing said processes as solutions of stochastic partial differential equations. In this work, we propose techniques for computing the kernels of these processes via spectral theory of the Laplace--Beltrami operator in a fully constructive manner, thereby allowing them to be trained via standard scalable techniques such as inducing point methods. We also extend the generalization from the Matern to the widely-used squared exponential Gaussian process. By allowing Riemannian Matern Gaussian processes to be trained using well-understood techniques, our work enables their use in mini-batch, online, and non-conjugate settings, and makes them more accessible to machine learning practitioners.
entries.anonymized_problem: Gaussian processes (GPs) provide principled probabilistic function approximation, but extending them to non-Euclidean domains such as Riemannian manifolds presents computational challenges. Prior work generalized the Matérn class of GPs to Riemannian manifolds by expressing them as solutions to stochastic partial differential equations, yet practical computation of the resulting kernels remained limited. This work addresses that gap by developing fully constructive techniques for computing Matérn GP kernels on Riemannian manifolds using the spectral theory of the Laplace–Beltrami operator. The approach yields explicit, tractable kernel expressions that are compatible with standard scalable GP inference methods, including inducing-point approximations. The generalization is also extended to the squared exponential GP kernel. The resulting framework supports training in mini-batch, online, and non-conjugate settings, broadening the applicability of manifold-valued GPs to the range of practical inference scenarios already available for standard Euclidean GPs. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed spectral construction faithfully recovers the intended covariance structure and enables effective learning on several manifold-valued function estimation tasks, making Riemannian Matérn GPs more accessible for practitioners working with data whose natural domain is a curved geometric space.

entries.original_title: Explainable k-Means and k-Medians Clustering
entries.original_abstract: Clustering is a popular form of unsupervised learning for geometric data. Unfortunately, many clustering algorithms lead to cluster assignments that are hard to explain, partially because they depend on all the features of the data in a complicated way. To improve interpretability, we consider using a small decision tree to partition a data set into clusters, so that clusters can be characterized in a straightforward manner. We study this problem from a theoretical viewpoint, measuring cluster quality by the $k$-means and $k$-medians objectives: Must there exist a tree-induced clustering whose cost is comparable to that of the best unconstrained clustering, and if so, how can it be found? In terms of negative results, we show, first, that popular top-down decision tree algorithms may lead to clusterings with arbitrarily large cost, and second, that any tree-induced clustering must in general incur an $\Omega(\log k)$ approximation factor compared to the optimal clustering. On the positive side, we design an efficient algorithm that produces explainable clusters using a tree with $k$ leaves. For two means/medians, we show that a single threshold cut suffices to achieve a constant factor approximation, and we give nearly-matching lower bounds. For general $k \geq 2$, our algorithm is an $O(k)$ approximation to the optimal $k$-medians and an $O(k^2)$ approximation to the optimal $k$-means. Prior to our work, no algorithms were known with provable guarantees independent of dimension and input size.
entries.anonymized_problem: Clustering algorithms for geometric data often produce assignments that are difficult to interpret, as they depend on all input features in complex ways. This work investigates whether clustering quality can be preserved when cluster assignments are constrained to be explainable via a small decision tree (a threshold-based partition with k leaves), measured under k-means and k-medians objectives. The approach combines theoretical analysis with algorithm design. On the negative side, it is shown that standard top-down decision tree heuristics can yield arbitrarily poor clusterings, and that any tree-induced clustering must in general incur an Ω(log k) approximation factor relative to the unconstrained optimum. On the positive side, an efficient algorithm is presented that constructs explainable tree-based clusterings with provable guarantees: for k=2, a single threshold cut achieves a constant-factor approximation with nearly matching lower bounds; for general k ≥ 2, the algorithm achieves an O(k) approximation to optimal k-medians and an O(k²) approximation to optimal k-means. These guarantees are dimension-independent and input-size-independent, addressing a gap in prior work where no such dimension-free approximation bounds were known for explainable clustering via decision trees.

entries.original_title: Demystifying Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning: Invariances, Augmentations and Dataset Biases
entries.original_abstract: Self-supervised representation learning approaches have recently surpassed their supervised learning counterparts on downstream tasks like object detection and image classification. Somewhat mysteriously the recent gains in performance come from training instance classification models, treating each image and it's augmented versions as samples of a single class. In this work, we first present quantitative experiments to demystify these gains. We demonstrate that approaches like MOCO and PIRL learn occlusion-invariant representations. However, they fail to capture viewpoint and category instance invariance which are crucial components for object recognition. Second, we demonstrate that these approaches obtain further gains from access to a clean object-centric training dataset like Imagenet. Finally, we propose an approach to leverage unstructured videos to learn representations that possess higher viewpoint invariance. Our results show that the learned representations outperform MOCOv2 trained on the same data in terms of invariances encoded and the performance on downstream image classification and semantic segmentation tasks.
entries.anonymized_problem: Contrastive self-supervised representation learning methods train by treating each image and its augmented versions as a single class, yet the mechanisms behind their strong downstream performance remain poorly understood. This work addresses that gap through two lines of investigation. First, quantitative experiments are conducted to characterize which geometric invariances are encoded by existing contrastive self-supervised methods. Results show that such approaches learn occlusion-invariant representations but fail to capture viewpoint invariance and category-instance invariance, both of which are important for robust object recognition. Second, the role of dataset structure is examined, demonstrating that performance gains in existing methods partly depend on access to clean, object-centric training data such as ImageNet. To overcome the viewpoint invariance limitation without relying on curated datasets, a method is proposed that leverages unstructured video to learn representations with greater viewpoint invariance, exploiting temporal continuity as a natural source of multi-view supervision. The resulting representations are evaluated on downstream image classification and semantic segmentation tasks, where they outperform a strong contrastive baseline trained on the same data in terms of both encoded invariances and task performance. The findings clarify which properties current contrastive methods do and do not capture, and highlight dataset composition as a significant factor in their effectiveness.

entries.original_title: Submodular Meta-Learning
entries.original_abstract: In this paper, we introduce a discrete variant of the meta-learning framework. Meta-learning aims at exploiting prior experience and data to improve performance on future tasks. By now, there exist numerous formulations for meta-learning in the continuous domain. Notably, the Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) formulation views each task as a continuous optimization problem and based on prior data learns a suitable initialization that can be adapted to new, unseen tasks after a few simple gradient updates. Motivated by this terminology, we propose a novel meta-learning framework in the discrete domain where each task is equivalent to maximizing a set function under a cardinality constraint. Our approach aims at using prior data, i.e., previously visited tasks, to train a proper initial solution set that can be quickly adapted to a new task at a relatively low computational cost. This approach leads to (i) a personalized solution for each individual task, and (ii) significantly reduced computational cost at test time compared to the case where the solution is fully optimized once the new task is revealed. The training procedure is performed by solving a challenging discrete optimization problem for which we present deterministic and randomized algorithms. In the case where the tasks are monotone and submodular, we show strong theoretical guarantees for our proposed methods even though the training objective may not be submodular. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on two real-world problem instances where we observe that our methods lead to a significant reduction in computational complexity in solving the new tasks while incurring a small performance loss compared to when the tasks are fully optimized.
entries.anonymized_problem: Meta-learning in continuous domains has been extensively studied, but analogous frameworks for discrete combinatorial settings remain underexplored. This work addresses the problem of transferring prior experience across tasks defined as submodular maximization problems under cardinality constraints. Drawing an analogy to gradient-based meta-learning for continuous optimization, a discrete meta-learning framework is developed in which prior tasks are used to train an initial solution set that can be efficiently adapted to new, unseen tasks with minimal additional computation. This formulation simultaneously yields personalized solutions for individual tasks and substantially reduces test-time computational cost relative to solving each new task from scratch. The training objective is a challenging discrete optimization problem; both deterministic and randomized algorithmic strategies are proposed to address it. When tasks involve monotone submodular functions, provable approximation guarantees are established for the proposed algorithms, even though the meta-training objective itself may not be submodular. Empirical evaluation on two real-world problem instances demonstrates that the framework achieves significant reductions in computational complexity when adapting to new tasks, with only modest degradation in solution quality compared to full per-task optimization.

entries.original_title: POMDPs in Continuous Time and Discrete Spaces
entries.original_abstract: Many processes, such as discrete event systems in engineering or population dynamics in biology, evolve in discrete space and continuous time. We consider the problem of optimal decision making in such discrete state and action space systems under partial observability. This places our work at the intersection of optimal filtering and optimal control. At the current state of research, a mathematical description for simultaneous decision making and filtering in continuous time with finite state and action spaces is still missing. In this paper, we give a mathematical description of a continuous-time partial observable Markov decision process (POMDP). By leveraging optimal filtering theory we derive a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) type equation that characterizes the optimal solution. Using techniques from deep learning we approximately solve the resulting partial integro-differential equation. We present (i) an approach solving the decision problem offline by learning an approximation of the value function and (ii) an online algorithm which provides a solution in belief space using deep reinforcement learning. We show the applicability on a set of toy examples which pave the way for future methods providing solutions for high dimensional problems.
entries.anonymized_problem: Optimal decision making under partial observability in systems that evolve in discrete state and action spaces but in continuous time is studied. Such systems arise naturally in discrete event engineering processes and biological population dynamics, yet a rigorous mathematical framework unifying optimal filtering with optimal control in this setting has been lacking. A continuous-time partially observable Markov decision process formulation is developed for finite state and action spaces. By applying optimal filtering theory, a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-type partial integro-differential equation characterizing the optimal value function is derived. Two complementary solution strategies are proposed: an offline approach that learns an approximation of the value function, and an online approach that operates in belief space using deep reinforcement learning techniques. Both approaches leverage deep learning to approximately solve the resulting partial integro-differential equation. The framework is validated on a collection of low-dimensional illustrative examples that demonstrate its correctness and establish a foundation for extending the methodology to higher-dimensional problems. The work bridges continuous-time stochastic control theory and modern function-approximation methods, providing a principled basis for future algorithms targeting complex partially observable systems with continuous-time dynamics.

entries.original_title: The Heavy-Tail Phenomenon in SGD
entries.original_abstract: In recent years, various notions of capacity and complexity have been proposed for characterizing the generalization properties of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in deep learning. Some of the popular notions that correlate well with the performance on unseen data are (i) the `flatness' of the local minimum found by SGD, which is related to the eigenvalues of the Hessian, (ii) the ratio of the stepsize $\eta$ to the batch size $b$, which essentially controls the magnitude of the stochastic gradient noise, and (iii) the `tail-index', which measures the heaviness of the tails of the eigenspectra of the network weights. In this paper, we argue that these three seemingly unrelated perspectives for generalization are deeply linked to each other. We claim that depending on the structure of the Hessian of the loss at the minimum, and the choices of the algorithm parameters $\eta$ and $b$, the SGD iterates will converge to a \emph{heavy-tailed} stationary distribution. We rigorously prove this claim in the setting of linear regression: we show that even in a simple quadratic optimization problem with independent and identically distributed Gaussian data, the iterates can be heavy-tailed with infinite variance. We further characterize the behavior of the tails with respect to algorithm parameters, the dimension, and the curvature. We then translate our results into insights about the behavior of SGD in deep learning. We finally support our theory with experiments conducted on both synthetic data and neural networks. To our knowledge, these results are the first of their kind to rigorously characterize the empirically observed heavy-tailed behavior of SGD.
entries.anonymized_problem: Characterizing the generalization properties of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in deep learning has motivated several proxy measures, including the flatness of loss minima (related to Hessian eigenvalues), the step-size-to-batch-size ratio (which governs stochastic gradient noise magnitude), and the tail-index of weight matrix eigenspectra. This work establishes a theoretical connection among these three perspectives by arguing that, depending on the Hessian structure at the loss minimum and the algorithmic hyperparameters η and b, SGD iterates converge to a heavy-tailed stationary distribution. This claim is rigorously proved in the linear regression setting: even for a simple quadratic objective with i.i.d. Gaussian data, SGD iterates can exhibit heavy tails with infinite variance. The analysis characterizes how tail behavior depends on step size, batch size, problem dimensionality, and loss curvature. These theoretical results are then used to derive qualitative insights about SGD dynamics in deep learning. Empirical validation is provided on both synthetic data and neural network training experiments, demonstrating alignment between the theoretical predictions and observed heavy-tailed phenomena. The findings provide a unified framework explaining why flatness, the η/b ratio, and tail-index each correlate with generalization, revealing them as interconnected manifestations of the same underlying heavy-tail mechanism in SGD.

entries.original_title: Robustness of Community Detection to Random Geometric Perturbations
entries.original_abstract: We consider the stochastic block model where connection between vertices is perturbed by some latent (and unobserved) random geometric graph. The objective is to prove that spectral methods are robust to this type of noise, even if they are agnostic to the presence (or not) of the random graph. We provide explicit regimes where the second eigenvector of the adjacency matrix is highly correlated to the true community vector (and therefore when weak/exact recovery is possible). This is possible thanks to a detailed analysis of the spectrum of the latent random graph, of its own interest.
entries.anonymized_problem: Community detection in graphs is studied under a model where the observed network combines a stochastic block model with an additive latent random geometric graph perturbation that is unobserved by the recovery algorithm. The central question is whether spectral methods remain effective for recovering community structure when the underlying connectivity includes this geometric noise component, even when the algorithm has no knowledge of whether such perturbations are present. The approach involves a rigorous theoretical analysis of the spectral properties of the perturbed adjacency matrix, with particular attention to characterizing the spectrum of the latent random geometric graph component. Explicit parameter regimes are identified in which the second eigenvector of the adjacency matrix remains highly correlated with the true community assignment vector, establishing conditions under which both weak and exact community recovery are achievable despite the perturbation. A key technical contribution is a detailed spectral analysis of the random geometric graph in isolation, which is of independent theoretical interest. The results demonstrate that spectral community detection retains its recovery guarantees under random geometric perturbations across identifiable regimes of model parameters.

entries.original_title: Variational State-Space Models for Localisation and Dense 3D Mapping in 6 DoF
entries.original_abstract: We solve the problem of 6-DoF localisation and 3D dense reconstruction in spatial environments as approximate Bayesian inference in a deep generative approach which combines learned with engineered models. This principled treatment of uncertainty and probabilistic inference overcomes the shortcoming of current state-of-the-art solutions to rely on heavily engineered, heterogeneous pipelines. Variational inference enables us to use neural networks for system identification, while a differentiable raycaster is used for the emission model. This ensures that our model is amenable to end-to-end gradient-based optimisation. We evaluate our approach on realistic unmanned aerial vehicle flight data, nearing the performance of a state-of-the-art visual inertial odometry system. The applicability of the learned model to downstream tasks such as generative prediction and planning is investigated.
entries.anonymized_problem: Simultaneous 6-degree-of-freedom localization and dense 3D reconstruction in spatial environments is addressed by formulating the joint problem as approximate Bayesian inference within a deep generative framework that combines learned neural components with engineered geometric models. Current approaches to this problem typically rely on heterogeneous, heavily engineered pipelines that handle uncertainty inconsistently; the proposed framework instead adopts a principled probabilistic treatment throughout. Variational inference is used to train neural networks for system identification, while a differentiable raycaster serves as the emission model, enabling end-to-end gradient-based optimization of the full system. The approach is evaluated on realistic unmanned aerial vehicle flight data, achieving performance competitive with an established visual-inertial odometry system. Beyond localization and mapping, the generative formulation is shown to support downstream tasks including predictive modeling and planning, demonstrating the broader utility of a unified probabilistic state-space representation for spatial reasoning in robotics.

entries.original_title: Near-Optimal Confidence Sequences for Bounded Random Variables
entries.original_abstract: Many inference problems, such as sequential decision problems like A/B testing, adaptive sampling schemes like bandit selection, are often online in nature. The fundamental problem for online inference is to provide a sequence of confidence intervals that are valid uniformly over the growing-into-infinity sample sizes. To address this question, we provide a near-optimal confidence sequence for bounded random variables by utilizing Bentkus' concentration results. We show that it improves on the existing approaches that use the Cram{e}r-Chernoff technique such as the Hoeffding, Bernstein, and Bennett inequalities. The resulting confidence sequence is confirmed to be favorable in both synthetic coverage problems and an application to adaptive stopping algorithms.
entries.anonymized_problem: Constructing valid confidence sequences for online inference problems—where validity must hold uniformly across all sample sizes rather than at a fixed horizon—is a fundamental challenge in sequential statistics. This challenge arises in applications such as A/B testing and bandit-based adaptive sampling, where data accumulate over time and stopping rules depend on observed outcomes. This work addresses the problem for bounded random variables by deriving a confidence sequence grounded in Bentkus' concentration inequalities, which differ from the classical Cramér-Chernoff bounding technique. The resulting confidence sequence is shown theoretically to yield tighter intervals than sequences derived from Hoeffding, Bernstein, and Bennett inequalities, which all rely on the Cramér-Chernoff framework. The tightness of the proposed sequence is evaluated empirically on synthetic coverage experiments, where empirical coverage rates and interval widths are compared across methods, and on an application to adaptive stopping algorithms. Results confirm that the Bentkus-based confidence sequence consistently achieves favorable width–coverage tradeoffs relative to the Cramér-Chernoff-based alternatives, supporting its use as a near-optimal tool for sequential inference with bounded observations.

entries.original_title: Guided Learning of Nonconvex Models through Successive Functional Gradient Optimization
entries.original_abstract: This paper presents a framework of successive functional gradient optimization for training nonconvex models such as neural networks, where training is driven by mirror descent in a function space. We provide a theoretical analysis and empirical study of the training method derived from this framework. It is shown that the method leads to better performance than that of standard training techniques.
entries.anonymized_problem: Training nonconvex models such as neural networks presents persistent optimization challenges, particularly due to the nonconvexity of the loss landscape and the sensitivity of standard gradient-based methods. This work addresses these challenges by developing a training framework grounded in successive functional gradient optimization, where learning is driven by mirror descent operating in a function space rather than in the parameter space directly. The approach iteratively constructs updates by optimizing functional surrogates, leveraging the geometry of the function space to guide parameter updates. A theoretical analysis establishes convergence properties and characterizes the behavior of the resulting optimization procedure. Empirical evaluations compare the proposed training method against standard gradient-based training techniques across nonconvex model settings, demonstrating consistent improvements in model performance. The results suggest that performing mirror descent in function space provides a more principled optimization trajectory for nonconvex objectives, offering both theoretical guarantees and practical gains relative to conventional approaches.

entries.original_title: How Powerful are Shallow Neural Networks with Bandlimited Random Weights?
entries.original_abstract: We investigate the expressive power of depth-2 bandlimited random neural networks. A random net is a neural network where the hidden layer parameters are frozen with random assignment, and only the output layer parameters are trained by loss minimization. Using random weights for a hidden layer is an effective method to avoid non-convex optimization in standard gradient descent learning. It has also been adopted in recent deep learning theories. Despite the well-known fact that a neural network is a universal approximator, in this study, we mathematically show that when hidden parameters are distributed in a bounded domain, the network may not achieve zero approximation error. In particular, we derive a new nontrivial approximation error lower bound. The proof utilizes the technique of ridgelet analysis, a harmonic analysis method designed for neural networks. This method is inspired by fundamental principles in classical signal processing, specifically the idea that signals with limited bandwidth may not always be able to perfectly recreate the original signal. We corroborate our theoretical results with various simulation studies, and generally, two main take-home messages are offered: (i) Not any distribution for selecting random weights is feasible to build a universal approximator; (ii) A suitable assignment of random weights exists but to some degree is associated with the complexity of the target function.
entries.anonymized_problem: Shallow (depth-2) neural networks with randomly fixed hidden-layer weights are studied to determine the limits of their expressive power when those weights are constrained to a bounded frequency domain. This setting—where only the output layer is trained via loss minimization—avoids non-convex optimization and is relevant to both practical random-feature methods and theoretical analyses of deep learning. Although neural networks are generally known to be universal approximators, the question of whether this universality is preserved under bandlimited random weight distributions has not been rigorously characterized. Using ridgelet analysis, a harmonic analysis framework tailored to neural networks and motivated by classical sampling theory (analogous to the Nyquist principle that bandlimited signals cannot always perfectly reconstruct arbitrary targets), a nontrivial lower bound on the approximation error is derived, demonstrating that bandlimited random networks can provably fail to achieve zero approximation error. Simulation studies corroborate the theoretical findings. Two principal conclusions emerge: first, not every distribution over random weights yields a universal approximator; second, a suitable weight distribution does exist, but the appropriate bandwidth is linked to the complexity of the target function being approximated. These results clarify the conditions under which random-weight networks retain or lose universal approximation capability.

entries.original_title: Regulating algorithmic filtering on social media
entries.original_abstract: Through the algorithmic filtering (AF) of content, social media platforms (SMPs) have the ability to influence users' perceptions and behaviors. Attempts to regulate externalities of AF are often difficult to pass or enforce due to critical social, legal, financial, and user related considerations. In this work, we explore this multifaceted problem by proposing a unifying framework that considers the key stakeholders of AF regulation (or self-regulation). We mathematically formalize this framework, using it to construct a data-driven, statistically sound regulatory procedure that satisfies several important criteria. First, by design, it moderates the effect of AF on user learning and decision-making. Second, it has desirable properties of online governance, including being normative and user-driven. Third, by illustrating the regulatory procedure in linear dynamical systems, we prove that it can align social and financial interests. Specifically, we identify conditions under which the regulation imposes a low cost on the SMP's reward (e.g., profits) and incentivizes the SMP to increase content diversity.
entries.anonymized_problem: Algorithmic filtering on social media platforms shapes user perceptions and behaviors in ways that can generate societal harms, yet regulatory efforts face persistent obstacles rooted in social, legal, financial, and user-related tensions. This work addresses the challenge of designing a principled regulatory framework that can reconcile the competing interests of multiple stakeholders—platforms, users, and governing bodies—simultaneously. The approach introduces a mathematically formalized, multi-stakeholder framework that is then used to derive a data-driven, statistically grounded regulatory procedure. The procedure is designed to satisfy several criteria: it moderates the influence of algorithmic filtering on user learning and decision-making; it exhibits properties consistent with effective online governance, including being normative and user-driven; and it is analyzed within the setting of linear dynamical systems to formally examine alignment between social and financial incentives. Theoretical results identify conditions under which the regulatory mechanism imposes low costs on platform reward functions (e.g., profits) while simultaneously incentivizing platforms to increase content diversity. The framework thus offers a tractable path toward regulation or self-regulation that does not require platforms to sacrifice financial interests, potentially easing adoption barriers that have historically hindered effective algorithmic content governance.

entries.original_title: Learning Robust Decision Policies from Observational Data
entries.original_abstract: We address the problem of learning a decision policy from observational data of past decisions in contexts with features and associated outcomes. The past policy maybe unknown and in safety-critical applications, such as medical decision support, it is of interest to learn robust policies that reduce the risk of outcomes with high costs. In this paper, we develop a method for learning policies that reduce tails of the cost distribution at a specified level and, moreover, provide a statistically valid bound on the cost of each decision. These properties are valid under finite samples -- even in scenarios with uneven or no overlap between features for different decisions in the observed data -- by building on recent results in conformal prediction. The performance and statistical properties of the proposed method are illustrated using both real and synthetic data.
entries.anonymized_problem: The problem of learning decision policies from observational data of past decisions is addressed, with particular focus on safety-critical settings such as medical decision support where the historical policy may be unknown and outcomes with high costs must be carefully managed. The central challenge is deriving policies that are robust to tail risks in the cost distribution while providing statistically valid guarantees under finite samples, including scenarios with limited or no feature overlap across different decision types in the observed data. The proposed approach frames policy learning as an optimization over a specified quantile of the cost distribution and constructs per-decision cost bounds by leveraging conformal prediction theory, which supplies distribution-free coverage guarantees without requiring strong assumptions on the data-generating process. This formulation yields policies that control tail costs at a user-specified level and come with finite-sample validity certificates regardless of covariate overlap conditions. The method's performance and statistical properties are evaluated on both real-world and synthetic datasets, demonstrating that the approach reliably controls tail risk and produces valid cost bounds across varied experimental conditions.

entries.original_title: SOLAR: Sparse Orthogonal Learned and Random Embeddings
entries.original_abstract: Dense embedding models are commonly deployed in commercial search engines, wherein all the document vectors are pre-computed, and near-neighbor search (NNS) is performed with the query vector to find relevant documents. However, the bottleneck of indexing a large number of dense vectors and performing an NNS hurts the query time and accuracy of these models. In this paper, we argue that high-dimensional and ultra-sparse embedding is a significantly superior alternative to dense low-dimensional embedding for both query efficiency and accuracy. Extreme sparsity eliminates the need for NNS by replacing them with simple lookups, while its high dimensionality ensures that the embeddings are informative even when sparse. However, learning extremely high dimensional embeddings leads to blow up in the model size. To make the training feasible, we propose a partitioning algorithm that learns such high dimensional embeddings across multiple GPUs without any communication. This is facilitated by our novel asymmetric mixture of Sparse, Orthogonal, Learned and Random (SOLAR) Embeddings. The label vectors are random, sparse, and near-orthogonal by design, while the query vectors are learned and sparse. We theoretically prove that our way of one-sided learning is equivalent to learning both query and label embeddings. With these unique properties, we can successfully train 500K dimensional SOLAR embeddings for the tasks of searching through 1.6M books and multi-label classification on the three largest public datasets. We achieve superior precision and recall compared to the respective state-of-the-art baselines for each of the tasks with up to 10 times faster speed.
entries.anonymized_problem: Dense embedding models used in large-scale search and retrieval require near-neighbor search (NNS) over pre-computed document vectors, which creates bottlenecks in query latency and accuracy when indexing millions of vectors. This work investigates whether high-dimensional, ultra-sparse embeddings can serve as a more efficient and accurate alternative to dense low-dimensional embeddings. The core argument is that extreme sparsity eliminates the need for NNS by enabling simple lookup operations, while high dimensionality preserves informativeness. A key challenge addressed is the prohibitive model size that arises when learning embeddings in very high-dimensional spaces. To overcome this, a partitioning algorithm is introduced that distributes training of such embeddings across multiple GPUs without inter-GPU communication. The approach employs an asymmetric design in which label vectors are random, sparse, and near-orthogonal by construction, while query vectors are learned and sparse. Theoretical analysis establishes that this one-sided learning scheme is equivalent to jointly learning both query and label embeddings. Empirical evaluation on a corpus of 1.6 million books and multi-label classification on three large public benchmarks demonstrates that 500,000-dimensional sparse embeddings achieve higher precision and recall than dense-embedding baselines while operating up to ten times faster.

entries.original_title: Bandits with Knapsacks beyond the Worst Case
entries.original_abstract: Bandits with Knapsacks (BwK) is a general model for multi-armed bandits under supply/budget constraints. While worst-case regret bounds for BwK are well-understood, we present three results that go beyond the worst-case perspective. First, we provide upper and lower bounds which amount to a full characterization for logarithmic, instance-dependent regret rates. Second, we consider"simple regret"in BwK, which tracks algorithm's performance in a given round, and prove that it is small in all but a few rounds. Third, we provide a general"reduction"from BwK to bandits which takes advantage of some known helpful structure, and apply this reduction to combinatorial semi-bandits, linear contextual bandits, and multinomial-logit bandits. Our results build on the BwK algorithm from \citet{AgrawalDevanur-ec14}, providing new analyses thereof.
entries.anonymized_problem: Bandits with Knapsacks (BwK) is a framework for multi-armed bandit problems subject to supply or budget constraints, and while minimax regret bounds for this setting are well-established, the behavior beyond worst-case guarantees remains less understood. This work investigates three complementary directions to address this gap. First, instance-dependent logarithmic regret rates are characterized through matching upper and lower bounds, giving a complete picture of when and how fast algorithms can adapt to favorable problem instances. Second, simple regret—measuring per-round performance rather than cumulative loss—is analyzed, and it is shown to be small in all but a limited number of rounds. Third, a general reduction from the BwK setting to standard bandit problems is developed, enabling the exploitation of known structural properties in specific problem classes; this reduction is applied concretely to combinatorial semi-bandits, linear contextual bandits, and multinomial-logit bandits. All three contributions build on a previously established algorithmic approach for BwK, providing new theoretical analyses of that algorithm. Together, the results demonstrate that instance-dependent structure, transient regret behavior, and structural reductions can each yield substantially stronger guarantees than worst-case analysis alone.

entries.original_title: All your loss are belong to Bayes
entries.original_abstract:
Loss functions are a cornerstone of machine learning and the starting point of most algorithms. Statistics and Bayesian decision theory have contributed, via properness, to elicit over the past decades a wide set of admissible losses in supervised learning, to which most popular choices belong (logistic, square, Matsushita, etc.). Rather than making a potentially biased ad hoc choice of the loss, there has recently been a boost in efforts to fit the loss to the domain at hand while training the model itself. The key approaches fit a canonical link, a function which monotonically relates the closed unit interval to R and can provide a proper loss via integration. 
In this paper, we rely on a broader view of proper composite losses and a recent construct from information geometry, source functions, whose fitting alleviates constraints faced by canonical links. We introduce a trick on squared Gaussian Processes to obtain a random process whose paths are compliant source functions with many desirable properties in the context of link estimation. Experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements over the state of the art.
entries.anonymized_problem: Proper loss functions are fundamental to supervised learning, and a principled way to select them comes from Bayesian decision theory and properness criteria, which characterize a broad family of admissible losses. Rather than fixing a loss function a priori, recent approaches learn the loss jointly with the model by fitting a canonical link—a monotone function mapping the unit interval to the reals from which a proper composite loss is recovered via integration. However, canonical link estimation faces restrictive constraints. This work addresses those constraints by adopting a broader framework of proper composite losses grounded in information geometry, specifically leveraging source functions as the fitting target instead of canonical links. To enable flexible, constraint-compliant estimation of source functions, a construction based on squared Gaussian processes is introduced, yielding random process paths that satisfy the required regularity conditions while offering desirable properties for posterior inference. The proposed approach integrates loss learning directly into model training without imposing the restrictive monotonicity constraints associated with canonical links. Experiments across multiple supervised learning benchmarks demonstrate that this method achieves substantial improvements in predictive performance compared to existing loss-learning approaches, suggesting that the source function parameterization provides a more expressive and geometrically coherent basis for data-adaptive loss selection.

entries.original_title: Robust Sequence Submodular Maximization
entries.original_abstract: Submodularity is an important property of set functions and has been extensively studied in the literature. It models set functions that exhibit a diminishing returns property, where the marginal value of adding an element to a set decreases as the set expands. This notion has been generalized to considering sequence functions, where the order of adding elements plays a crucial role and determines the function value; the generalized notion is called sequence (or string) submodularity. In this paper, we study a new problem of robust sequence submodular maximization with cardinality constraints. The robustness is against the removal of a subset of elements in the selected sequence (e.g., due to malfunctions or adversarial attacks). Compared to robust submodular maximization for set function, new challenges arise when sequence functions are concerned. Specifically, there are multiple definitions of submodularity for sequence functions, which exhibit subtle yet critical differences. Another challenge comes from two directions of monotonicity: forward monotonicity and backward monotonicity, both of which are important to proving performance guarantees. To address these unique challenges, we design two robust greedy algorithms: while one algorithm achieves a constant approximation ratio but is robust only against the removal of a subset of contiguous elements, the other is robust against the removal of an arbitrary subset of the selected elements but requires a stronger assumption and achieves an approximation ratio that depends on the number of the removed elements. Finally, we generalize the analyses to considering sequence functions under weaker assumptions based on approximate versions of sequence submodularity and backward monotonicity
entries.anonymized_problem: Submodular maximization is a well-studied combinatorial optimization paradigm capturing diminishing-returns behavior in set functions. This work extends the problem to the sequential (string) setting, where element order determines function value, and introduces a robustness requirement: the selected sequence must retain good performance even after an adversary removes some subset of its elements, modeling malfunctions or adversarial attacks. Compared to robust set-function submodularity, the sequential setting introduces additional complexity because multiple non-equivalent definitions of sequence submodularity exist, and performance guarantees depend on two distinct monotonicity directions—forward and backward—each playing a critical role in analysis. To address these challenges, two robust greedy algorithms are developed. The first achieves a constant approximation ratio under standard assumptions but guarantees robustness only against removal of contiguous elements. The second handles removal of arbitrary element subsets and achieves an approximation ratio dependent on the number of removed elements, at the cost of a stronger assumption. Both algorithms are further generalized to handle approximate variants of sequence submodularity and backward monotonicity, broadening applicability to settings where exact properties do not hold. The theoretical contributions include formal approximation guarantees for each algorithm under their respective assumptions, providing a principled framework for robust sequential decision-making under adversarial or unreliable conditions.

entries.original_title: Nearly Linear Row Sampling Algorithm for Quantile Regression
entries.original_abstract: We give a row sampling algorithm for the quantile loss function with sample complexity nearly linear in the dimensionality of the data, improving upon the previous best algorithm whose sampling complexity has at least cubic dependence on the dimensionality. Based upon our row sampling algorithm, we give the fastest known algorithm for quantile regression and a graph sparsification algorithm for balanced directed graphs. Our main technical contribution is to show that Lewis weights sampling, which has been used in row sampling algorithms for $\ell_p$ norms, can also be applied in row sampling algorithms for a variety of loss functions. We complement our theoretical results by experiments to demonstrate the practicality of our approach.
entries.anonymized_problem: Row sampling algorithms for quantile regression are studied, focusing on reducing the sample complexity required to obtain a coreset that approximates the quantile (L1-type) loss function. Prior approaches required sample sizes with at least cubic dependence on the data dimensionality, which limits scalability. The approach introduced here achieves sample complexity nearly linear in the dimensionality by extending Lewis weight sampling — a technique previously applied to row sampling for ℓp norms — to a broader class of loss functions including the quantile loss. The key technical contribution is establishing that Lewis weights can be used to control the statistical leverage of rows under these non-standard loss functions, enabling efficient coreset construction. Building on this sampling result, faster algorithms for quantile regression and a graph sparsification algorithm for balanced directed graphs are derived. The theoretical guarantees are complemented by empirical experiments demonstrating that the approach is practical on real data, with the sampling procedure producing compact coresets that faithfully approximate the full quantile regression objective at substantially reduced computational cost.

entries.original_title: Eulerian–Lagrangian direct numerical simulation of preferential accumulation of inertial particles in a compressible turbulent boundary layer
entries.original_abstract: Abstract In this study, direct numerical simulation of the dispersion and motion of inertial particles in a spatially developing compressible turbulent boundary layer at a Mach number of 2 is performed with the Eulerian–Lagrangian point particle method. Two cases are simulated with different particle diameters (Stokes number) but identical inflow particle numbers. Statistical characteristics and preferential accumulation of particles in the very-near-wall and wake regions are systematically investigated through conditional sampling and mechanism analysis. The results reveal that particle streaks are formed in low-speed regions near the wall because of the influence of dominating ejection events. After normalization with the local minimum particle number density, the particle number density profile reveals a self-similar feature at different streamwise positions. Compared with small particles, large particles are more significantly influenced by turbophoresis and demonstrate stronger preferential accumulation; thus, more large particles are clustered in the near-wall regions and the deviation between the mean velocities of the particle and the fluid increases. With the wall effect, both large and small particles are selectively accumulated in high-vorticity regions in the buffer layer in contrast to turbulence without walls. In comparison with incompressible wall-bounded turbulence, a new mechanism for particle preferential accumulation based on local fluid density is discovered. Large particles are located in low-density regions in the inner zones and high-density regions in the outer zones. Nevertheless, small particles remain located in regions with low fluid density, as illustrated by the mechanism analysis of particle dilatation.
entries.anonymized_problem: Direct numerical simulation is employed to study the dispersion and preferential accumulation of inertial particles in a spatially developing compressible turbulent boundary layer at Mach 2, using an Eulerian–Lagrangian point-particle framework. Two particle diameter cases (differing in Stokes number) with identical inflow particle concentrations are simulated. Statistical characteristics and accumulation behavior in the near-wall and wake regions are examined through conditional sampling and mechanistic analysis. Results show that particle streaks form in low-speed near-wall regions due to dominant ejection events, and the particle number density profile, normalized by the local minimum density, exhibits a self-similar character at different streamwise positions. Larger particles experience stronger turbophoresis than smaller particles, leading to greater near-wall clustering and larger velocity differences between particle and fluid phases. In the buffer layer, both particle sizes preferentially accumulate in high-vorticity regions due to wall effects, contrasting with behavior in unbounded turbulence. A compressibility-specific accumulation mechanism is identified, wherein local fluid density variations drive particle distribution: large particles concentrate in low-density regions in the inner layer and high-density regions in the outer layer, while small particles consistently reside in low-density fluid regions. This density-based preferential accumulation mechanism is absent in incompressible wall-bounded turbulence and is attributed to particle dilatation dynamics.

entries.original_title: Spatio-temporal dynamics of flow separation induced by a forward-facing step submerged in a thick turbulent boundary layer
entries.original_abstract: The effects of large-scale motion (LSM) on the spatio-temporal dynamics of separated shear layers induced by a forward-facing step submerged in a thick turbulent boundary layer (TBL) are investigated using a time-resolved particle image velocimetry. The Reynolds number based on the free-stream velocity and step height was 13 200. The oncoming TBL was developed over a cube-roughened surface and the thickness was 6.5 times the step height. The step height was chosen to coincide with the elevation where the dominant frequency of streamwise fluctuating velocity in the TBL occurred. At this elevation, the local turbulence intensity was 14.5 %. Distinct regions of elevated Reynolds stresses were observed upstream and downstream of the leading edge of the step. The unsteady dynamics of the separation bubbles upstream and downstream of the step was investigated using the reverse flow area. Both separation bubbles exhibit low-frequency flapping motion, and the dominant frequency of the downstream separation bubble is identical to the dominant frequency of the streamwise fluctuating velocity in the oncoming TBL at the step height. As the low-velocity region of LSM passes over the step, the downstream separation bubble is enlarged and subsequently undergoes a high-frequency oscillation. Turbulence motions were partitioned into low-, medium- and high-frequency regimes based on spectral analysis of the Reynolds stresses. The contributions from these partitioned turbulence motions are used to elucidate the effects of LSM on the elevated Reynolds stresses in the shear layers upstream and downstream of the step.
entries.anonymized_problem: Flow separation induced by a forward-facing step immersed in a thick turbulent boundary layer (TBL) is examined, with focus on how large-scale motions (LSMs) modulate the spatio-temporal dynamics of the resulting separated shear layers. Experiments were conducted at a Reynolds number of 13,200 based on free-stream velocity and step height, with the oncoming TBL developed over a cube-roughened surface to a thickness 6.5 times the step height. The step height was positioned at the elevation where the dominant frequency of streamwise velocity fluctuations in the TBL occurs, corresponding to a local turbulence intensity of 14.5%. Time-resolved particle image velocimetry was employed to capture the unsteady flow fields. Distinct regions of elevated Reynolds stresses were identified both upstream and downstream of the step's leading edge. The reverse flow area was used to characterize the unsteady behavior of both upstream and downstream separation bubbles, which exhibit low-frequency flapping. The dominant frequency of the downstream separation bubble matches that of streamwise fluctuations in the oncoming TBL at step height. As low-velocity LSM regions pass over the step, the downstream separation bubble enlarges and subsequently undergoes high-frequency oscillation. Spectral decomposition of Reynolds stresses into low-, medium-, and high-frequency regimes reveals the distinct contributions of LSM to elevated Reynolds stresses within the upstream and downstream shear layers.

entries.original_title: Aerodynamic-force production mechanisms in hovering mosquitoes
entries.original_abstract: For many insects in hovering flight, the stroke amplitude is relatively large (above $120^{\circ }$) and the lift is mainly produced by the leading-edge vortex (LEV) attaching to the wing (the delayed-stall mechanism). Mosquitoes have a very small stroke amplitude (${\approx}45^{\circ }$) and the LEV does not have enough time to form before a stroke ends; thus, the delayed-stall mechanism can not be used. In the present study, we show that their lift is produced by different aerodynamic mechanisms from those of insects with a large stroke amplitude: in a downstroke and upstroke, two large lift peaks and a relatively small one are generated. The first large lift peak (at the beginning of the stroke) mainly comes from the added-mass force caused by the large acceleration of the wing. The second large lift peak (in the mid-portion of the stroke) is produced by the ‘fast-pitching-up rotation’ mechanism: the wing fast pitches up while moving forward, generating a large-magnitude, opposite-sign vorticity at the trailing edge of the wing and near the leading edge of the wing; the rapid generation of opposite-sign vorticity at different locations of the wing results in a large time rate of change in the first moment of vorticity, hence a large aerodynamic force. The third lift peak, which is near the end of the stroke and is small, is a result of the fast-pitching-up rotation of a rapidly decelerating wing. Note that although the added-mass force contributes positive lift in the beginning part of the stroke when the wing is in acceleration, it gives negative lift in the next part of the stroke when the wing is in deceleration; i.e. the added-mass force has no effect on the time-average lift, but it greatly changes the time distribution of the lift.
entries.anonymized_problem: Mosquitoes employ an unusually small stroke amplitude (~45°) during hovering flight, which prevents the leading-edge vortex from fully developing before each stroke reversal, rendering the delayed-stall mechanism—dominant in most insects with stroke amplitudes above 120°—unavailable. This study investigates the alternative aerodynamic force-production mechanisms that enable mosquitoes to sustain hovering. The approach involves detailed analysis of the unsteady aerodynamic forces and vorticity dynamics across complete wing strokes. Results identify three distinct lift peaks per half-stroke. The first peak arises from added-mass forces generated by large wing accelerations at stroke initiation. The second, largest peak is attributed to a fast pitching-up rotation mechanism: as the wing pitches up while translating forward, opposite-sign vorticity is rapidly generated at both the trailing and leading edges, producing a large time rate of change in the first moment of vorticity and consequently a large aerodynamic force. A third, smaller peak near stroke end results from fast pitching-up rotation of a rapidly decelerating wing. Although added-mass forces contribute positively during acceleration and negatively during deceleration—canceling out in the time-averaged sense—they substantially redistribute lift within the stroke cycle. These findings clarify how insects with highly constrained stroke kinematics achieve aerodynamic force balance through mechanisms qualitatively distinct from those of typical hovering insects.

entries.original_title: Bubble deformation by a turbulent flow
entries.original_abstract: Abstract We investigate the modes of deformation of an initially spherical bubble immersed in a homogeneous and isotropic turbulent background flow. We perform direct numerical simulations of the two-phase incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, considering a low-density bubble in the high-density turbulent flow at various Weber numbers (the ratio of turbulent and surface tension forces) using the air–water density ratio. We discuss a theoretical framework for the bubble deformation in a turbulent flow using a spherical harmonic decomposition. We propose, for each mode of bubble deformation, a forcing term given by the statistics of velocity and pressure fluctuations, evaluated on a sphere of the same radius. This approach formally relates the bubble deformation and the background turbulent velocity fluctuations, in the limit of small deformations. The growth of the total surface deformation and of each individual mode is computed from the direct numerical simulations using an appropriate Voronoi decomposition of the bubble surface.
