We show that two successive temporal regimes occur: the first regime corresponds to deformations driven only by inertial forces, with the interface deformation growing linearly in time, in agreement with the model predictions, whereas the second regime results from a balance between inertial forces and surface tension. The transition time between the two regimes is given by the period of the first Rayleigh mode of bubble oscillation. We discuss how our approach can be used to relate the bubble lifetime to the turbulence statistics and eventually show that at high Weber numbers, bubble lifetime can be deduced from the statistics of turbulent fluctuations at the bubble scale.
entries.anonymized_problem: Bubble deformation in turbulent flows is studied through direct numerical simulations of the two-phase incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, considering a low-density bubble immersed in a high-density homogeneous isotropic turbulent background at the air–water density ratio across a range of Weber numbers. A theoretical framework based on spherical harmonic decomposition is developed to characterize individual deformation modes. For each mode, a forcing term is derived from the statistics of velocity and pressure fluctuations evaluated on a sphere of equivalent radius, formally connecting bubble deformation to background turbulent velocity fluctuations in the small-deformation limit. Surface deformation growth for each mode is extracted from simulations using a Voronoi decomposition of the bubble surface. Two successive temporal regimes are identified: an initial inertia-dominated regime in which interface deformation grows linearly in time, consistent with theoretical predictions, followed by a regime governed by a balance between inertial forces and surface tension. The transition between regimes is set by the period of the first Rayleigh oscillation mode. At high Weber numbers, bubble lifetime is shown to be determinable from the statistics of turbulent fluctuations at the bubble scale, providing a direct link between turbulence statistics and bubble breakup dynamics.

entries.original_title: The turbulent bubble break-up cascade. Part 1. Theoretical developments
entries.original_abstract: Abstract Breaking waves entrain gas beneath the surface. The wave-breaking process energizes turbulent fluctuations that break bubbles in quick succession to generate a wide range of bubble sizes. Understanding this generation mechanism paves the way towards the development of predictive models for large-scale maritime and climate simulations. Garrett et al. (J. Phys. Oceanogr., vol. 30, 2000, pp. 2163–2171) suggested that super-Hinze-scale turbulent break-up transfers entrained gas from large- to small-bubble sizes in the manner of a cascade. We provide a theoretical basis for this bubble-mass cascade by appealing to how energy is transferred from large to small scales in the energy cascade central to single-phase turbulence theories. A bubble break-up cascade requires that break-up events predominantly transfer bubble mass from a certain bubble size to a slightly smaller size on average. This property is called locality. In this paper, we analytically quantify locality by extending the population balance equation in conservative form to derive the bubble-mass-transfer rate from large to small sizes. Using our proposed measures of locality, we show that scalings relevant to turbulent bubbly flows, including those postulated by Garrett et al. (J. Phys. Oceanogr., vol. 30, 2000, pp. 2163–2171) and observed in breaking-wave experiments and simulations, are consistent with a strongly local transfer rate, where the influence of non-local contributions decays in a power-law fashion. These theoretical predictions are confirmed using numerical simulations in Part 2 (Chan et al., J. Fluid. Mech. vol. 912, 2021, A43), revealing key physical aspects of the bubble break-up cascade phenomenology. Locality supports the universality of turbulent small-bubble break-up, which simplifies the development of cascade-based subgrid-scale models to predict oceanic small-bubble statistics of practical importance.
entries.anonymized_problem: Breaking waves entrain gas beneath the ocean surface, and the resulting turbulence fragments bubbles across a wide range of sizes. Accurately predicting the resulting bubble size distributions is important for large-scale maritime and climate simulations, yet a rigorous theoretical foundation for the cascade-like transfer of bubble mass from large to small sizes has remained incomplete. This work develops an analytical framework for the bubble-mass cascade by drawing an analogy with the energy cascade in single-phase turbulence theory. The central question concerns whether bubble break-up events are predominantly local — transferring bubble mass to slightly smaller sizes on average — a property essential for cascade behavior. The population balance equation in conservative form is extended to derive an expression for the bubble-mass-transfer rate across size scales, and new quantitative measures of locality are introduced. Analysis shows that scaling laws relevant to turbulent bubbly flows, including those inferred from breaking-wave experiments and simulations, are consistent with a strongly local transfer rate in which non-local contributions decay as a power law. These theoretical predictions are subsequently confirmed through numerical simulations reported in a companion study. Locality implies universality of small-bubble break-up dynamics, which in turn supports the development of cascade-based subgrid-scale models for predicting oceanic bubble size statistics.

entries.original_title: Oblique stripe solutions of channel flow
entries.original_abstract: With decreasing Reynolds number, $Re$, turbulence in channel flow becomes spatio-temporally intermittent and self-organises into solitary stripes oblique to the mean flow direction. We report here the existence of localised nonlinear travelling wave solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations possessing this obliqueness property. Such solutions are identified numerically using edge tracking coupled with arclength continuation. All solutions emerge in saddle-node bifurcations at values of $Re$ lower than the non-localised solutions. Relative periodic orbit solutions bifurcating from branches of travelling waves have also been computed. A complete parametric study is performed, including their stability, the investigation of their large-scale flow, and the robustness to changes of the numerical domain.
entries.anonymized_problem: In subcritical channel flow, turbulence at reduced Reynolds numbers organizes into spatially intermittent, oblique stripe patterns aligned at angles to the mean flow direction. This study investigates the existence and properties of localized nonlinear travelling wave solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations that capture this oblique orientation. Solutions are identified numerically through edge tracking combined with arclength continuation in Reynolds number. The computed solutions arise via saddle-node bifurcations at Reynolds numbers below those associated with non-localized counterparts. Relative periodic orbit solutions bifurcating from the travelling wave branches are also computed. A comprehensive parametric study is conducted, encompassing the linear stability of the identified solutions, characterization of the associated large-scale flow structures, and assessment of sensitivity to changes in the computational domain size. The results establish a direct connection between exact coherent structures of the Navier–Stokes equations and the oblique stripe patterns observed in transitional channel flow, providing a dynamical systems framework for understanding spatially localized turbulent–laminar coexistence in this canonical shear flow configuration.

entries.original_title: Velocity distributions, dispersion and stretching in three-dimensional porous media
entries.original_abstract: Using index matching and particle tracking, we measure the three-dimensional velocity field in an isotropic porous medium composed of randomly packed solid spheres. This high-resolution experimental dataset provides new insights into the dynamics of dispersion and stretching in porous media. Dynamic-range velocity measurements indicate that the distribution of the velocity magnitude, $U$, is flat at low velocity (probability density function $(U)\propto U^{0}$). While such a distribution should lead to a persistent anomalous dispersion process for advected non-diffusive point particles, we show that the dispersion of non-diffusive tracers nonetheless becomes Fickian beyond a time set by the smallest effective velocity of the tracers. We derive expressions for the onset time of the Fickian regime and the longitudinal and transverse dispersion coefficients as a function of the velocity field properties. The experimental velocity field is also used to study, by numerical advection, the stretching histories of fluid material lines. The mean and the variance of the line elongations are found to grow exponentially in time and the distribution of elongation is log-normal. These results confirm the chaotic nature of advection within three-dimensional porous media. By providing the laws of dispersion and stretching, the present study opens the way to a complete description of mixing in porous media.
entries.anonymized_problem: Three-dimensional velocity measurements in a porous medium composed of randomly packed solid spheres are reported, obtained via index-matching and particle-tracking techniques. The resulting high-resolution experimental dataset is used to characterize dispersion and stretching dynamics. Velocity magnitude distributions reveal a flat, uniform probability density at low velocities (PDF ∝ U⁰), a form that would ordinarily sustain anomalous dispersion indefinitely for purely advective, non-diffusive tracers. However, analysis demonstrates that dispersion of such tracers nonetheless transitions to a Fickian regime beyond a timescale governed by the minimum effective tracer velocity. Analytical expressions are derived for this onset time and for both longitudinal and transverse dispersion coefficients as functions of the measured velocity field statistics. The experimental velocity field is further employed in numerical advection simulations to track the evolution of fluid material lines. Both the mean and variance of line elongation grow exponentially in time, and the elongation distribution follows a log-normal form—hallmarks of chaotic advection. These findings confirm that advection within three-dimensional porous media is chaotic in nature. By establishing quantitative laws governing dispersion and stretching, the study provides a framework toward a complete characterization of scalar mixing in porous media flows.

entries.original_title: Model-based design of riblets for turbulent drag reduction
entries.original_abstract: Abstract Both experiments and direct numerical simulations have been used to demonstrate that riblets can reduce turbulent drag by as much as $10\,\%$, but their systematic design remains an open challenge. In this paper we develop a model-based framework to quantify the effect of streamwise-aligned spanwise-periodic riblets on kinetic energy and skin-friction drag in turbulent channel flow. We model the effect of riblets as a volume penalization in the Navier–Stokes equations and use the statistical response of the eddy-viscosity-enhanced linearized equations to quantify the effect of background turbulence on the mean velocity and skin-friction drag. For triangular riblets, our simulation-free approach reliably predicts drag-reducing trends as well as mechanisms that lead to performance deterioration for large riblets. We investigate the effect of height and spacing on drag reduction and demonstrate a correlation between energy suppression and drag reduction for appropriately sized riblets. We also analyse the effect of riblets on drag-reduction mechanisms and turbulent flow structures including very large-scale motions. Our results demonstrate the utility of our approach in capturing the effect of riblets on turbulent flows using models that are tractable for analysis and optimization.
entries.anonymized_problem: Turbulent skin-friction drag reduction using surface riblets has been demonstrated experimentally and via direct numerical simulation to reach approximately 10%, yet systematic, optimization-oriented design of riblet geometries remains challenging due to the computational expense of high-fidelity simulations. This work develops a simulation-free, model-based framework to quantify the influence of streamwise-aligned, spanwise-periodic riblets on kinetic energy and skin-friction drag in turbulent channel flow. Riblet geometry is incorporated into the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations through a volume penalization approach, and the statistical response of eddy-viscosity-augmented linearized flow equations is used to characterize how background turbulence modifies the mean velocity profile and skin-friction coefficient. Applied to triangular riblet geometries, the framework reliably predicts drag-reducing trends as well as the performance degradation that occurs when riblet size becomes too large. Parametric studies of riblet height and spacing reveal a clear correlation between turbulent kinetic energy suppression and drag reduction for appropriately sized geometries. The framework also captures riblet-induced changes to turbulent flow structures, including very large-scale motions. Results demonstrate that the linearized, eddy-viscosity-based modeling approach is tractable for analysis and optimization purposes while retaining physical fidelity in predicting riblet performance across a range of geometric parameters.

entries.original_title: Resonance in vortex-induced in-line vibration at low Reynolds numbers
entries.original_abstract: Abstract We present simulations of a circular cylinder undergoing vortex-induced vibration in-line with a free stream in conjunction with a theory for the fluid dynamics. Initially, it is shown that increasing the Reynolds number from 100 to 250 results in a 12-fold increase of the peak response amplitude at a fixed mass ratio of $m^*=5$. Subsequently, $m^*$ is varied from 2 up to 20 at a fixed Reynolds number of 180. The response amplitude as a function of the reduced velocity $U^*$ displays a single excitation region with peak amplitudes of approximately 1% of the cylinder diameter, irrespective of the $m^*$ value. The vibration is always excited by the alternating shedding of single vortices. We develop a new model for the in-line fluid force, which comprises an inviscid inertial force, a quasi-steady drag and a wake drag induced by vortex shedding. Our analysis shows that the wake drag appropriately captures a gradual shift in the timing of vortex shedding in its phase variation as a function of $U^*$ while the magnitude of the wake drag displays a resonant amplification within the excitation region. We use the theory to illustrate why peak amplitudes, which occur when the vibration frequency is equal to the structural frequency in still fluid, do not depend on $m^*$, in agreement with our simulations as well as previous experiments at Reynolds numbers higher than considered here. This new theory provides physical insight which could not be attained heretofore by employing semi-empirical approaches in the literature.
entries.anonymized_problem: Vortex-induced in-line vibration of a circular cylinder at low Reynolds numbers is investigated through direct numerical simulations combined with an analytical fluid-force model. The study first examines how increasing the Reynolds number from 100 to 250 affects peak response amplitude at a fixed mass ratio of m* = 5, finding a 12-fold increase in peak amplitude over this range. Mass ratio is then varied from 2 to 20 at a fixed Reynolds number of 180, revealing a single excitation region in reduced velocity U* space with peak amplitudes of approximately 1% of the cylinder diameter that are insensitive to m*. Vibration is consistently driven by alternating single-vortex shedding. A fluid-force model is developed comprising an inviscid inertial component, a quasi-steady drag, and a wake drag arising from vortex shedding. Analysis shows that the wake drag captures a gradual phase shift in vortex shedding timing across U*, while its magnitude exhibits resonant amplification within the excitation region. The theory explains why peak amplitudes occur when vibration frequency matches the structural natural frequency in still fluid and remain independent of m*, consistent with both the simulations and previously reported experiments at higher Reynolds numbers. This mechanistic framework provides physical insight into in-line VIV that semi-empirical approaches have not previously afforded.

entries.original_title: Deformation of drops by outer eddies in turbulence
entries.original_abstract: Abstract Drop deformation in fluid flows is investigated as an exchange between the kinetic energy of the fluid and the surface energy of the drop. We show analytically that this energetic exchange is controlled only by the stretching (or compression) of the drop surface by the rate-of-strain tensor. This mechanism is analogous to the stretching of the vorticity field in turbulence. By leveraging the non-local nature of turbulence dynamics, we introduce a new decomposition that isolates the energetic exchange arising from local drop-induced surface effects from the non-local action of turbulent fluctuations. We perform direct numerical simulations of single inertial drops in isotropic turbulence and show that an important contribution to the increments of the surface energy arises from the non-local stretching of the fluid–fluid interface by eddies far from the drop surface (outer eddies). We report that this mechanism is dominant and independent of surface dynamics in a range of Weber numbers in which drop breakup occurs. These findings shed new light on drop deformation and breakup in turbulent flows, and opens the possibility for the improvement and simplification of breakup models.
entries.anonymized_problem: Drop deformation and breakup in turbulent flows are examined through an energetic framework that treats the process as an exchange between fluid kinetic energy and drop surface energy. Analytical derivation demonstrates that this energetic exchange is governed solely by the stretching or compression of the drop surface by the rate-of-strain tensor, a mechanism formally analogous to vorticity stretching in turbulence. Exploiting the non-local character of turbulent dynamics, a decomposition is developed that separates contributions to surface energy increments arising from local, drop-induced surface effects from those due to non-local turbulent fluctuations acting away from the interface. Direct numerical simulations of single inertial drops in statistically isotropic turbulence are carried out across a range of Weber numbers spanning the drop breakup regime. Results show that the dominant contribution to surface energy increments originates from non-local stretching of the fluid–fluid interface by eddies located far from the drop surface. This outer-eddy mechanism is found to be independent of local surface dynamics over the Weber number range where breakup occurs. These findings clarify the relative roles of local and non-local flow structures in drop deformation and breakup, and suggest pathways for simplifying and improving physical models of drop breakup in turbulent flows.

entries.original_title: Dynamics of strong swept-shock/turbulent-boundary-layer interactions
entries.original_abstract: The mechanisms of unsteadiness in nominally two-dimensional (2-D) shock/turbulent-boundary-layer interactions (STBLIs) cannot be directly extended to three-dimensional (3-D) STBLIs, because of differences in interaction structure; swept 3-D interactions, including the sharp-fin and swept-compression-ramp configurations, are of particular interest in this work. Complications arise from the observation that the separation length employed to scale low-frequency unsteadiness in 2-D (spanwise homogeneous) interactions is not a global property of 3-D (swept) interactions, due to the quasi-conical symmetry of the latter. Also, flow separation in 3-D interactions is topologically different, in that closure of the primary separation cannot occur without breaking the quasi-conical symmetry of the interaction – consequently, the unsteady properties of the separation are different. To address these points, large-eddy simulations are performed to assess unsteadiness in 3-D interactions, with the aim of understanding key differences relative to analogous 2-D interactions, the former of which have received less attention in the literature. The mechanism underlying the prominent band of low-frequency unsteadiness (two decades below the characteristic boundary-layer frequency) is shown to be significantly muted in swept interactions. An interesting scaling for the band of mid-frequency unsteadiness is uncovered (at least one decade below the characteristic boundary-layer frequency). This is a consequence of the observed connection between coherent fluctuations in the separated shear layer and local mean-flow gradients, indicating a mix between competing 2-D and 3-D free-interaction scaling laws. In contrast, high-frequency fluctuations largely retain the 2-D scaling introduced by the incoming turbulent boundary layer. The spatial structure of the mid-frequency coherence in 3-D STBLIs is isolated, revealing the significant influence of these convective coherent structures on shock rippling/corrugation, as well as a spanwise dependence of coherence size consistent with the 3-D mean-flow similarity scaling. Finally, the dynamic linear response of a representative 3-D interaction is compared to that of a representative 2-D interaction; the absolute instability present in the 2-D interaction is not present in the 3-D interaction. The coincident absence of both the absolute instability and associated band of low-frequency unsteadiness in 3-D STBLIs underscores the significance of this absolute instability in facilitating low-frequency unsteadiness in 2-D interactions.
entries.anonymized_problem: Three-dimensional swept shock/turbulent-boundary-layer interactions (STBLIs) — arising in sharp-fin and swept-compression-ramp configurations — exhibit fundamentally different unsteadiness mechanisms compared to nominally two-dimensional, spanwise-homogeneous interactions, yet these differences remain less thoroughly characterized. This study addresses that gap using large-eddy simulations of strong swept interactions, examining unsteadiness across a broad frequency range and comparing the results against analogous two-dimensional cases. Because swept interactions possess quasi-conical symmetry, the separation length used to scale low-frequency unsteadiness in two-dimensional interactions is not a global property, and primary separation closure requires symmetry breaking, altering the unsteady character of the separated region. Results show that the prominent low-frequency unsteadiness band — occurring roughly two decades below the characteristic boundary-layer frequency — is significantly muted in swept interactions. A distinct mid-frequency band, at least one decade below the boundary-layer frequency, is identified and linked to coherent fluctuations in the separated shear layer coupled to local mean-flow gradients, reflecting a competition between two-dimensional and three-dimensional free-interaction scaling laws. High-frequency fluctuations retain two-dimensional boundary-layer scaling. Coherent mid-frequency structures drive shock rippling and corrugation, with spanwise coherence size consistent with three-dimensional mean-flow similarity. Dynamic linear stability analysis reveals that the absolute instability present in two-dimensional interactions is absent in the three-dimensional case, providing a mechanistic explanation for the suppression of low-frequency unsteadiness in swept configurations.

entries.original_title: The generation mechanism of higher screech tone harmonics in supersonic jets
entries.original_abstract: The generation mechanism of screech harmonics in supersonic exhausts is revealed using shadowgraph imaging and acoustic far-field measurements for a rectangular, high aspect-ratio nozzle. The coherent information associated with screech and its harmonics, i.e. flow structures and acoustic radiation pattern, is extracted from the time-resolved shadowgraph images. We show that, for large lateral distortions of the jet plume, the passage of screech associated flow structures triggers the screech-cyclic formation of shocks, which travel downstream and merge with the original shocks. The interaction of the shock waves with the flow structures associated with screech alters the appearance of the perturbations in the mixing layer, which constitute the higher harmonics of screech. Visualisations of the acoustic radiation pattern expose that the third and higher screech tone harmonics originate from these interaction locations. Further, the occurrence of mode resonance between the screech and its harmonics is demonstrated, where the mode resonance location coincides with the screech tone origin.
entries.anonymized_problem: Screech tone harmonics in supersonic jets represent a class of aeroacoustic phenomena whose generation mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study investigates the physical processes responsible for producing higher harmonics of the screech tone in supersonic exhausts from a rectangular, high aspect-ratio nozzle. The approach combines time-resolved shadowgraph imaging with acoustic far-field measurements; coherent flow structures and acoustic radiation patterns associated with screech and its harmonics are extracted from the shadowgraph data. Results show that large lateral distortions of the jet plume cause screech-associated flow structures to trigger the cyclic formation of new shock waves, which propagate downstream and merge with the pre-existing shock train. The interaction between these shock waves and screech-associated flow structures modifies perturbations in the mixing layer, and these modified perturbations constitute the higher screech harmonics. Visualization of the acoustic radiation pattern confirms that the third and higher harmonics originate at these shock–structure interaction locations. Additionally, mode resonance between the fundamental screech tone and its harmonics is identified, with the resonance location coinciding spatially with the origin of the fundamental screech tone. These findings provide a mechanistic explanation linking shock dynamics, mixing-layer perturbations, and harmonic generation in high-aspect-ratio supersonic jet flows.

entries.original_title: The validity of two-dimensional models of a rotating shallow fluid layer
entries.original_abstract: Abstract We investigate the validity and accuracy of two commonly used two-dimensional models of a rotating, incompressible, shallow fluid layer: the shallow-water (SW) model and the Serre/Green–Naghdi (GN) model. The models differ in just one respect: the SW model imposes the hydrostatic approximation while the GN model does not. Both models assume the horizontal velocity is independent of height throughout the layer. We compare these models with their parent three-dimensional (3-D) model, initialised with a height-independent horizontal velocity, and with a mean height small compared to the domain width. For small to moderate Rossby and Froude numbers, we verify that both models well approximate the vertically averaged 3-D flow. Overall, the GN model is found to be substantially more accurate than the SW model. However, this accuracy is only achieved using an explicit reformulation of the equations in which the vertically integrated non-hydrostatic pressure is found from a novel linear elliptic equation. This reformulation is shown to extend straightforwardly to multi-layer flows having uniform density layers.
entries.anonymized_problem: Two-dimensional depth-averaged models are widely used to approximate rotating shallow fluid dynamics, yet their accuracy relative to full three-dimensional (3D) solutions is not always rigorously established. This study examines the validity and accuracy of two such models for a rotating, incompressible, shallow fluid layer: the shallow-water (SW) model, which imposes the hydrostatic approximation, and the Serre/Green–Naghdi (GN) model, which relaxes this approximation while retaining the assumption that horizontal velocity is independent of depth. Both models are compared against their parent 3D system, initialized with height-independent horizontal velocity and a mean layer depth small relative to the domain width. For small to moderate Rossby and Froude numbers, both models are shown to approximate the vertically averaged 3D flow well, with the GN model demonstrating substantially greater accuracy than the SW model. This improved accuracy, however, is contingent on an explicit reformulation of the GN equations in which the vertically integrated non-hydrostatic pressure is determined by a linear elliptic equation. This reformulation is derived and validated, and is shown to extend naturally to multi-layer configurations with uniform-density layers. The results clarify conditions under which each model is appropriate and provide a computationally tractable framework for incorporating non-hydrostatic effects in rotating shallow-fluid simulations.

entries.original_title: Coupling rheology and segregation in granular flows
entries.original_abstract: Abstract During the last fifteen years there has been a paradigm shift in the continuum modelling of granular materials; most notably with the development of rheological models, such as the $\mu (I)$-rheology (where $\mu$ is the friction and I is the inertial number), but also with significant advances in theories for particle segregation. This paper details theoretical and numerical frameworks (based on OpenFOAM) which unify these currently disconnected endeavours. Coupling the segregation with the flow, and vice versa, is not only vital for a complete theory of granular materials, but is also beneficial for developing numerical methods to handle evolving free surfaces. This general approach is based on the partially regularized incompressible $\mu (I)$-rheology, which is coupled to the gravity-driven segregation theory of Gray & Ancey (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 678, 2011, pp. 353–588). These advection–diffusion–segregation equations describe the evolving concentrations of the constituents, which then couple back to the variable viscosity in the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. A novel feature of this approach is that any number of differently sized phases may be included, which may have disparate frictional properties. Further inclusion of an excess air phase, which segregates away from the granular material, then allows the complex evolution of the free surface to be captured simultaneously. Three primary coupling mechanisms are identified: (i) advection of the particle concentrations by the bulk velocity, (ii) feedback of the particle-size and/or frictional properties on the bulk flow field and (iii) influence of the shear rate, pressure, gravity, particle size and particle-size ratio on the locally evolving segregation and diffusion rates. The numerical method is extensively tested in one-way coupled computations, before the fully coupled model is compared with the discrete element method simulations of Tripathi & Khakhar (Phys. Fluids, vol. 23, 2011, 113302) and used to compute the petal-like segregation pattern that spontaneously develops in a square rotating drum.
entries.anonymized_problem: Granular flows involving mixtures of differently sized particles present a coupled challenge: the bulk rheology governs how the material flows, while particle-size segregation redistributes constituents, which in turn alters the local rheological properties. This work develops unified theoretical and numerical frameworks that simultaneously treat granular rheology and segregation. The rheological foundation is a partially regularized incompressible friction–inertial-number formulation, coupled to a gravity-driven advection–diffusion–segregation theory governing the evolving volume fractions of multiple particle species. Concentration-dependent variable viscosity feeds back into the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, closing the two-way coupling. An excess air phase is incorporated to capture free-surface evolution without additional interface-tracking complexity. Three coupling mechanisms are identified: advection of concentrations by the bulk velocity field, feedback of local particle-size and frictional properties onto bulk flow, and dependence of segregation and diffusion rates on shear rate, pressure, gravity, particle size, and size ratio. The numerical implementation, constructed within an open-source finite-volume framework, is validated through one-way coupled test cases and then applied in fully coupled mode. Results are benchmarked against published discrete element method simulations of bidisperse plane shear flow, and the framework successfully reproduces the spontaneous petal-like segregation pattern observed experimentally in a square rotating drum, demonstrating its ability to capture complex, transient free-surface granular dynamics.

entries.original_title: Hydrodynamic interaction of two deformable torque swimmers
entries.original_abstract: When two swimming cells collide, some ciliates show biological reactions such as avoidance and escape on sensing mechanical agitation through membrane ion channels. However, there is still no clear understanding of the mechanosensing mechanism, despite it being proposed more than 50 years ago. Moreover, it is largely unknown how the deformability of cells affects hydrodynamic interactions between microswimmers. In this study, we investigate hydrodynamic interactions between two deformable microswimmers and quantify the membrane tension during the interaction. A ciliate was modelled as a capsule with a hyperelastic membrane, and thrust generated by the cilia was modelled as torque distributed above the cell body. The model we use is the simplest we could think of that can swim, deform and exert membrane tension, such that hydrodynamic interactions can be analysed non-trivially. The results showed that softer swimmers induced smaller membrane tension during the interaction, and tended to have smaller scattering angles after the interaction. In the case of chasing interactions, swimmers attracted each other, which was not observed in non-deformable velocity squirmer models. Finally, we discuss the biological implications of these results, comparing them to those of our former experiments using Paramecium. This study is useful for understanding the effect of swimmer deformability in hydrodynamic interactions, and provides a theoretical basis for investigating a mechanical picture of the biological reactions of ciliates.
entries.anonymized_problem: Two deformable microswimmers undergoing hydrodynamic interaction are studied to understand how cell deformability influences swimmer-swimmer encounters and the mechanosensing forces experienced during collisions — a question relevant to ciliate avoidance and escape behaviors that have been hypothesized for over 50 years but remain mechanistically unclear. Each swimmer is modeled as a capsule enclosing a hyperelastic membrane, with ciliary thrust represented as a distributed torque applied above the cell body. This minimal model captures swimming, deformation, and membrane tension simultaneously, enabling non-trivial analysis of hydrodynamic interactions. Boundary integral and capsule-dynamics simulations are used to resolve the coupled fluid-structure problem. Results show that softer swimmers generate lower membrane tension during collisions and exhibit smaller scattering angles post-interaction compared to stiffer counterparts. In chasing configurations, deformable swimmers mutually attract, a behavior absent in rigid velocity-squirmer models. These findings suggest that membrane compliance substantially alters both the trajectory outcomes and the mechanical signals available to mechanosensory ion channels. Comparisons with prior experimental observations on Paramecium support the biological relevance of the model and provide a theoretical framework for interpreting mechanical triggers underlying ciliate behavioral responses to hydrodynamic contact.

entries.original_title: Structured to Succeed? Strategy Dynamics in Engineering Systems Design and Their Effect on Collective Performance
entries.original_abstract: Strategy dynamics are hypothesized to be a structural factor of interactive multi-actor design problems that influence collective performance and behaviors of design actors. Using a bi-level model of collective decision processes based on design optimization and strategy selection, we formulate a series of two-actor parameter design tasks that exhibit four strategy dynamics (harmony, coexistence, bistability, and defection) associated with low and high levels of structural fear and greed. In these tasks, design actor pairs work collectively to maximize their individual values while managing the trade-offs between aligning with or deviating from a mutually beneficial collective strategy. Results from a human subject design experiment indicate cognizant actors generally follow normative predictions for some strategy dynamics (harmony and coexistence) but not strictly for others (bistability and defection). Cumulative link model regression analysis shows that a greed factor contributing to strategy dynamics has a stronger effect on collective efficiency and equality of individual outcomes compared to a fear factor. Results of this study provide an initial description of strategy dynamics in engineering design and help to frame future work to mitigate potential unfavorable effects of their underlying strategy dynamics through social constructs or mechanism design.
entries.anonymized_problem: Multi-actor engineering design problems involve structural incentive conditions that may shape collective performance and individual behavior, yet these conditions remain poorly characterized. This work examines how the structural properties of interactive parameter design tasks influence collective decision-making by formulating a bi-level model that couples design optimization with strategy selection. Four distinct incentive regimes—corresponding to variations in structural fear and greed parameters—are instantiated as two-actor design tasks in which participants maximize individual objective values while navigating trade-offs between cooperative and self-interested strategies. A human-subject experiment was conducted to compare observed actor behavior against normative game-theoretic predictions across these four regimes. Results indicate that participants align with normative predictions under two incentive conditions but deviate systematically under the remaining two. Cumulative link model regression analysis reveals that the greed component of the structural incentive conditions exerts a stronger influence on both collective efficiency and equality of individual outcomes than the fear component. These findings provide an empirical characterization of how incentive structure affects collective performance in engineering design contexts and suggest that social mechanisms or mechanism design interventions may be needed to mitigate the adverse effects of unfavorable structural conditions in collaborative design settings.

entries.original_title: Distributed vortex receptivity of a swept-wing boundary layer. Part 2. Receptivity characteristics
entries.original_abstract: Abstract This paper is devoted to an experimental investigation of the distributed receptivity of a laminar swept-wing boundary layer to unsteady freestream vortices with streamwise orientation of the vorticity vector. The experiments were performed on a model of a swept wing with a sweep angle of $25^{\circ }$ at fully controlled disturbance conditions with freestream vortices generated by a special disturbance source. It is found that the unsteady streamwise vortices are able to provide very efficient excitation of cross-flow instability modes without requiring the presence of any surface non-uniformities. The developed experimental approach is shown to allow us to perform a detailed quantitative investigation of the mechanism of distributed excitation of unsteady boundary-layer disturbances due to scattering of freestream vortices on natural base-flow non-uniformity. This mechanism has been studied experimentally in detail. Part 1 of the present investigation (Borodulin et al., J. Fluid Mech., vol. 908, 2021, A14) was devoted to the description of the experimental approach and the base-flow structure, the method of excitation of fully controlled streamwise-elongated freestream vortices, the results of measurements of structure of these vortices and the experimental evidence of high efficiency of the distributed vortex receptivity mechanism under study. Meanwhile, the present paper (Part 2) is devoted to: (a) theoretical background and definition of the distributed receptivity coefficients and (b) obtaining experimental quantitative characteristics of the distributed vortex receptivity including values of the corresponding receptivity coefficients for their three different definitions as functions of the disturbance frequency, spanwise wavenumber and wave propagation angle.
entries.anonymized_problem: Distributed receptivity of a laminar swept-wing boundary layer to unsteady freestream vortices with streamwise vorticity orientation is investigated experimentally. Experiments are conducted on a swept-wing model with a 25° sweep angle under fully controlled disturbance conditions, with freestream vortices generated by a dedicated disturbance source. The study addresses the mechanism by which streamwise-elongated freestream vortices excite cross-flow instability modes through scattering on natural base-flow non-uniformity, without requiring surface roughness or other geometric non-uniformities. This paper provides the theoretical framework for defining distributed receptivity coefficients and presents quantitative experimental characterization of the receptivity process. Three distinct definitions of receptivity coefficients are evaluated as functions of disturbance frequency, spanwise wavenumber, and wave propagation angle. Results demonstrate that unsteady streamwise vortices are capable of efficiently exciting cross-flow instability modes through the distributed receptivity mechanism alone. The experimental approach enables detailed quantitative examination of the excitation mechanism, yielding receptivity coefficient values across a range of disturbance parameters. These findings establish a systematic experimental basis for understanding how freestream turbulence interacts with swept-wing boundary layers to trigger cross-flow instability, with implications for laminar-to-turbulent transition prediction and control in swept-wing configurations.

entries.original_title: Calming the waves, not the storm: measuring the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability in a tangential magnetic field
entries.original_abstract: Abstract We measure the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability in between a layer of a diamagnetic fluid flowing in a channel and a layer of ferrofluid resting on top. When the diamagnetic fluid exceeds a critical flow velocity the interface in between both fluids becomes unstable and waves develop. It has been predicted by Sutyrin & Taktarov (J. Appl. Math. Mech., vol. 39, 1975, pp. 520–524) that a homogeneous magnetic field, oriented horizontally, stabilizes the liquid interface. To test this prediction we apply in a closed flow channel a local periodic perturbation of the interface by magnetic or mechanic means. From the measured growth and decay rates of the interface undulations we determine the critical flow velocity for various driving frequencies and applied magnetic fields. In this way we confirm quantitatively the stabilizing effect of the horizontal field. Moreover we measure the dispersion relation of the interfacial waves.
entries.anonymized_problem: The Kelvin–Helmholtz instability (KHI) at the interface between a flowing diamagnetic fluid and an overlying stationary ferrofluid layer is experimentally investigated to test a classical theoretical prediction regarding magnetic stabilization. When the diamagnetic fluid exceeds a critical velocity, interfacial waves develop; a prior theoretical analysis predicted that a horizontally oriented (tangential) homogeneous magnetic field should stabilize this interface. To evaluate this prediction quantitatively, experiments are conducted in a closed flow channel where periodic perturbations are introduced at the fluid interface via either magnetic or mechanical actuation. Growth and decay rates of the resulting interface undulations are measured as functions of driving frequency and applied magnetic field strength, allowing determination of the critical flow velocity under varying conditions. The dispersion relation of the interfacial waves is also extracted from the measurements. The results confirm quantitatively that a tangential magnetic field raises the critical velocity for onset of the KHI, demonstrating the predicted stabilizing effect. Additionally, the measured dispersion relation characterizes how wave propagation at the ferrofluid–diamagnetic fluid interface depends on wavenumber and applied field, providing experimental validation of the theoretical framework governing magnetically influenced interfacial instabilities in two-fluid systems.

entries.original_title: Spatial organisation of velocity structures for large passive scalar gradients
entries.original_abstract: Velocity structures associated with large streamwise density gradients in an incompressible turbulent boundary layer (with air as the working fluid, $Pr=0.71$) are analysed experimentally using planar image velocimetry and aero-optic measurements. The resulting flow topologies for the velocity fluctuations associated with large negative and positive density gradients are in excellent agreement with results for coolings and heatings in time, respectively (Antonia & Fulachier, J. Fluid Mech., vol. 198, 1989, pp. 429–451). The current results are complimentary to those from Saxton-Fox et al. (AIAA J., vol. 57 (7), 2019, pp. 2828–2839), on the signature of the vertical velocity structures associated with large density gradients. In the present work, these structures are shown to exhibit a sign change, consistent with the scalar gradient, and are localised in the wall-normal direction with an average height of approximately $0.1\unicode[STIX]{x1D6FF}$, almost constant for increasing distance from the wall. The corresponding small-scale streamwise fluctuations also exhibit a consistent sign change, which is found to originate, on average, from upstream leaning structures. The emerging picture for the velocity field is then that of a multiscale phenomenon, where small-scale structures, responsible for large optical aberrations, are superimposed on the back of large-scale bulge-like structures that are known to populate the outer layers. The proposed conceptual model is consistent with early ideas of ‘typical’ eddies (Falco, Phys. Fluids, vol. 20 (10), 1977, pp. S124–S132), the hairpin vortex model and associated shear layers (Adrian et al., J. Fluid Mech., vol. 422, 2000, pp.1–54), as well as with notions of multiscale velocity organisation in shear layers (Klewicki & Hirschi, Phys. Fluids, vol. 16 (11), 2004, pp. 4163–4176; Saxton-Fox et al. 2019), and it provides new insight into the geometry of the small-scale velocity structures.
entries.anonymized_problem: Velocity structures associated with large passive scalar gradients in an incompressible turbulent boundary layer (Pr = 0.71, air as working fluid) are investigated through planar particle image velocimetry combined with aero-optic measurements. The central question concerns how velocity fluctuations spatially organize around regions of large positive and negative streamwise density gradients, and how these structures relate to optical aberrations. Conditional averaging is applied to extract flow topologies corresponding to extreme scalar gradient events. The resulting velocity signatures show a sign change consistent with the scalar gradient polarity and are localized in the wall-normal direction, with an average height of approximately 0.1δ that remains nearly constant with increasing wall distance. Small-scale streamwise velocity fluctuations associated with these events also exhibit a corresponding sign change and are traced, on average, to upstream-leaning structural geometries. The overall picture that emerges is a multiscale velocity organization in which small-scale structures—responsible for large optical path length distortions—are superimposed upon large-scale bulge-like motions populating the outer layer. This conceptual framework is shown to be consistent with established models including the hairpin vortex paradigm and associated internal shear layers, as well as prior notions of multiscale velocity organization, while providing additional geometric detail about the small-scale structures that drive optical wavefront distortion.

entries.original_title: Similarity in Mach stem evolution and termination in unsteady shock-wave reflection
entries.original_abstract: Abstract Shock-wave reflection over concave surfaces poses a difficulty in its analysis due to the unsteady nature of the reflection process and the occurrence of various types of Mach reflections caused by it. In a pseudo-steady flow, the reflection's configuration is self-similar since the shock wave reflects over a surface with constant inclination. The unsteady Mach reflection introduces an additional complexity as it is affected by the changing inclination of the surface, forcing the reflection to continuously adjust itself to the varying boundary condition. In this study, validated simulations of Mach reflection (MR) over cylindrical concave surfaces with different radii were performed for three inviscid perfect gases with moderate incident shock Mach numbers (Ms) ranging from 1.3 to 1.5. The reflection was investigated up to the point of transition from MR to transitioned regular reflection. A similar behaviour of the configuration and evolution of the Mach stem was observed, one that is independent of the surface radius and type of gas. With regards to different gases, the speed of sound a0 is a dominant factor since it dictates the propagation of wall disturbances. A universal condition of the rate of surface change was found, accounting for different radii, different gases and Ms variation. Analysis based on shock dynamics is employed to explain how disturbances caused by surface variations play a significant role in the behaviour of the reflection. This method successfully supports the similarity that was demonstrated and facilitates a more informed perception of the MR process.
entries.anonymized_problem: Shock-wave reflection over concave surfaces presents analytical challenges due to the inherently unsteady nature of the process and the variety of Mach reflection configurations it produces. Unlike pseudo-steady flows, where self-similarity arises from constant surface inclination, unsteady Mach reflection (MR) is complicated by continuously changing boundary conditions as the surface geometry evolves. This study employs validated numerical simulations of MR over cylindrical concave surfaces of varying radii, using three inviscid perfect gases across a range of incident shock Mach numbers (Ms = 1.3–1.5), tracking the reflection through to transition from MR to transitioned regular reflection. The geometry and temporal evolution of the Mach stem are examined systematically to identify universal behavioral patterns. Results demonstrate that the Mach stem configuration and evolution exhibit similarity that is independent of surface radius and gas type. The speed of sound in the undisturbed gas emerges as a dominant parameter, governing the propagation speed of wall-generated disturbances. A universal condition characterizing the rate of surface inclination change is identified, consolidating the effects of varying radius, gas composition, and incident Mach number into a single framework. Analysis based on shock dynamics explains how disturbances originating from surface curvature variations drive the reflection behavior, providing a physically grounded explanation for the observed similarity and improving understanding of the unsteady MR process.

entries.original_title: Optimising the flow through a concertinaed filtration membrane
entries.original_abstract: Abstract Membrane filtration is a vital industrial process, with applications including air purification and blood filtration. In this paper, we study the optimal design for a concertinaed filtration membrane composed of angled porous membranes and dead ends. The geometry of the filter motivates a lubrication scaling for the flow, leading to a system of coupled (modified) Reynolds equations. By analysing this reduced system, we examine how the filter performance depends on the angle, position, thickness and permeance of the membrane, using a combination of numerical and asymptotic approaches, the latter in the limit of a slightly angled membrane. We find that, for a membrane of fixed angle and physical properties, there can exist multiple membrane positions that maximise the flux for an applied pressure difference. More generally, this shows how coupled problems in lubrication flow can exhibit non-trivial bifurcating optima. For the particular application on which we focus, we show that, while the maximal flux achievable depends on the membrane thickness and permeance, the optimal membrane configuration is always in one of two set-ups: centred and diagonal across the full domain; or angled and in the corner of the domain.
entries.anonymized_problem: Membrane filtration is widely used in industrial applications such as air purification and blood filtration, yet the optimal geometric configuration of concertinaed (pleated) filter membranes remains incompletely understood. This study examines the optimal design of a concertinaed filtration membrane composed of angled porous membranes and dead ends, with geometry motivating a lubrication scaling of the governing flow equations. The resulting system of coupled modified Reynolds equations is analyzed to determine how filter performance depends on membrane angle, position, thickness, and permeance, using a combination of numerical methods and asymptotic analysis in the limit of a slightly angled membrane. A key finding is that, for a membrane of fixed angle and physical properties, multiple membrane positions can exist that simultaneously maximize flux under an applied pressure difference, revealing non-trivial bifurcating optima in coupled lubrication flow problems. More broadly, the results demonstrate that while the maximum achievable flux depends on membrane thickness and permeance, the optimal membrane configuration consistently falls into one of two distinct arrangements: centered and oriented diagonally across the full flow domain, or angled and positioned in the corner of the domain. These findings provide geometric design guidelines for improving filtration efficiency in practical concertinaed membrane systems.

entries.original_title: Monopoles in a uniform zonal flow on a quasi-geostrophic $\beta $-plane: effects of the Galilean non-invariance of the rotating shallow-water equations
entries.original_abstract: Abstract Galilean non-invariance of the shallow-water equations describing the motion of a rotating fluid implies that a homogeneous background flow modifies the dynamics of localized vortices even without the $\beta $-effect. In particular, in a divergent quasi-geostrophic model on a $\beta $-plane, which originates from the shallow-water model, the equation of motion in the reference frame attached to a uniform zonal background flow has the same form as in the absence of this flow, but with a modified $\beta $-parameter depending linearly on the flow velocity $\bar{U}$. The evolution of a singular vortex (SV) embedded in such a flow consists of two stages. In the first, quasi-linear stage, the SV motion is induced by the secondary dipole ($\beta $-gyres) generated in the neighbourhood of the SV. During the next, nonlinear stage, the SV merges with the $\beta $-gyre of opposite sign to form a compact vortex pair interacting with far-field Rossby waves radiated previously by the SV, while the other $\beta $-gyre loses connection with the SV and disappears. In the absolute reference frame and with $\beta = 0$, the SV drifts downstream and at an angle to the background flow. The SV always lags behind the background flow, with the strongest resistance during the quasi-linear stage and weakening resistance at the nonlinear stage of SV evolution. In the general case where $\beta \gt 0$, the SV can move both upstream (for small-to-moderate $\bar{U} \gt 0$) and downstream (for $\bar{U} \lt 0$ or sufficiently large $\bar{U} \gt 0$). Under weak-to-moderate westward and all eastward flows the SV cyclone (anticyclone) also moves northward (southward), its meridional drift increasing with $\bar{U}$.
entries.anonymized_problem: Galilean non-invariance of the rotating shallow-water equations implies that a uniform background zonal flow modifies the dynamics of localized vortices beyond the conventional β-effect. This study examines how a homogeneous zonal current alters the evolution of singular vortices (monopoles) within a divergent quasi-geostrophic β-plane framework derived from the shallow-water model. The analysis shows that transforming to the reference frame of the background flow yields governing equations identical in form to the zero-flow case but with an effective β-parameter that varies linearly with background flow velocity. Vortex evolution is characterized by two distinct stages: an initial quasi-linear phase in which motion is driven by secondary dipolar structures (β-gyres) generated near the vortex, followed by a nonlinear phase in which the vortex merges with the same-sign β-gyre to form a compact vortex pair that interacts with previously radiated far-field Rossby waves. In the absolute reference frame with β = 0, the vortex drifts downstream but consistently lags behind the background flow, with resistance strongest during the quasi-linear stage and diminishing in the nonlinear stage. When β > 0, vortex propagation direction depends on flow speed and sign: upstream motion occurs under small-to-moderate eastward flow, while downstream drift prevails for westward or sufficiently strong eastward flow. Meridional drift of cyclones (anticyclones) is poleward (equatorward) and increases with background flow velocity under weak-to-moderate conditions.

entries.original_title: Compressible plane turbulent wakes under pressure gradients evolving in a constant area section
entries.original_abstract: Development of statistically two-dimensional (2-D) turbulent wakes under pressure gradients is a common feature of many industrial and aerodynamic flows. The usual set-up is to generate a wake, and study its development through a passage with a variable area; if the downstream area decreases (increases) a favourable pressure gradient or FPG (adverse pressure gradient or APG) is imposed. In applications such as in turbomachinery, however, the wakes develop in a periodic constant area passage in the stator–rotor gap and with an imposed pressure gradient. To study these flows, here, we develop a canonical set-up for this new kind of wake evolution in FPG and APG of different strengths by placing a 2-D flat plate normal to the flow in a periodic constant area passage and a fixed inflow mass flux. Employing compressible direct numerical simulations, we impose pressure gradients through a ramped body force term to the momentum and total energy equations while the wake is allowed to develop spatially in a region of fixed width. The resultant mean velocity statistics, wake width, energy budgets and entropy generation rates are scrutinised to assess the effect of the pressure gradients, and where possible, the similarities and differences to the conventional case of variable area pressure gradients are discussed. The results show that the effect of a constant area pressure gradient on flow statistics is non-trivial, resulting from significant density changes. The pressure gradients also have an effect on the different energy budgets, which produces a gain for FPG and loss for APG in the mean kinetic energy. Consequently, the entropy generation rate diminishes and augments for the FPG and APG, respectively, compared to the zero pressure gradient. Finally, the effect of different passage heights ($H$) relative to the wake half-width ($\unicode[STIX]{x1D6FF}$) is studied using large eddy simulations. We find that wake width and hence the spreading, depends primarily on the wake–wake interaction for small $H$ and pressure gradients for larger $H$, and this has implications for the design of turbomachinery.
entries.anonymized_problem: Turbulent wakes developing under pressure gradients in constant-area passages are relevant to turbomachinery flows, particularly in stator–rotor gaps, yet prior work has largely focused on variable-area configurations. This study establishes a canonical setup for wake evolution under both favorable (FPG) and adverse (APG) pressure gradients at varying strengths within a periodic constant-area channel. A two-dimensional flat plate is placed normal to the flow in a fixed-width periodic domain with a prescribed inflow mass flux. Pressure gradients are imposed via a ramped body-force term in the momentum and total energy equations, and compressible direct numerical simulations are used to spatially evolve the wake. Mean velocity statistics, wake width, turbulent kinetic energy budgets, and entropy generation rates are analyzed to characterize the pressure-gradient effects, with comparisons drawn to conventional variable-area cases where applicable. Results show that constant-area pressure gradients produce non-trivial changes in flow statistics driven by significant density variations. FPG conditions yield a gain in mean kinetic energy and reduced entropy generation, while APG produces the opposite. Large eddy simulations varying the passage height relative to wake half-width reveal that wake spreading is governed primarily by wake–wake interactions at small passage heights and by pressure gradients at larger heights, with direct implications for turbomachinery passage design.

entries.original_title: A nonlinear impulsive Cauchy–Poisson problem. Part 2. Lagrangian description
entries.original_abstract: Abstract A fully nonlinear Cauchy–Poisson problem is investigated analytically by a small-time expansion. The inviscid incompressible fluid layer has an initially horizontal surface. The fluid is forced into motion by an impulsive surface pressure. The early nonlinear free-surface problem is solved to second order in a small-time expansion by the Lagrangian description of motion. Comparisons are made with two other solution procedures for the same nonlinear problem in the absence of gravity: a third-order small-time expansion and a numerical solution, based on full nonlinearity according to the standard Eulerian description. Good agreement is found between the present second-order Lagrangian solution and the previous third-order Eulerian solution, until both these asymptotic expansions diverge rather abruptly at the same time.
entries.anonymized_problem: A fully nonlinear free-surface problem is investigated analytically using a small-time asymptotic expansion in the Lagrangian reference frame. The configuration consists of an inviscid, incompressible fluid layer with an initially horizontal surface set into motion by an impulsive surface pressure distribution. The Lagrangian description of motion is employed to obtain a second-order small-time solution for the nonlinear free-surface dynamics. Results are compared against two alternative solution approaches applied to the same nonlinear problem in the absence of gravity: a third-order small-time expansion derived in the Eulerian framework and a fully nonlinear numerical simulation based on the standard Eulerian description. Good agreement is demonstrated between the second-order Lagrangian solution and the third-order Eulerian solution, validating the Lagrangian approach despite its lower-order truncation. Both asymptotic expansions exhibit abrupt divergence at approximately the same time instant, indicating a shared limitation of the small-time expansion methodology regardless of the reference frame employed. The study highlights the practical utility of the Lagrangian formulation for capturing early-time nonlinear free-surface behavior and clarifies the temporal domain within which such asymptotic approaches remain reliable.

entries.original_title: Unsteady draining of reservoirs over weirs and through constrictions
entries.original_abstract: The gravitationally driven flow of fluid from a reservoir following the partial collapse of its confining dam, or the partial opening of its confining lock, is modelled using the nonlinear shallow water equations, coupled to outflow conditions, in which the drainage is modelled as flow over a constricted, broad-crested weir. The resulting unsteady motion reveals systematic draining, on which strong and relatively rapid oscillations are imposed. The oscillations propagate between the outflow and the impermeable back wall of the reservoir. This dynamics is investigated utilising three methods: hodograph techniques to yield quasi-analytical solutions, asymptotic analysis at relatively late times after initiation and numerical integration of the governing equations. The hodograph transformation is used to find exact solutions at early times, revealing that from initially quiescent conditions the fluid drains and yet repeatedly generates intervals during which there are regions of constant depth and velocity adjacent to the boundaries. A novel modified multiscale asymptotic analysis designed for late times is employed to determine the limiting rate of draining and wave structure. It is shown that the excess height drains as $t^{-2}$ and, when the obstacle has finite height, the velocity field decays as $t^{-3}$ , and exhibits a wave structure that tends towards a constant and relatively rapid phase speed. In the case of a pure constriction, for which all the fluid ultimately drains out of the reservoir, the motion adjusts to a self-similar state in which the velocity field decays as $t^{-1}$ . Oscillations around this state have an exponentially increasing period. Numerical simulations with a novel implementation of boundary conditions are performed; they confirm the hodograph solution and provide data for the asymptotic results.
entries.anonymized_problem: The gravitationally driven drainage of a fluid reservoir following partial dam collapse or lock opening is studied using the nonlinear shallow water equations coupled to outflow conditions modelling flow over a constricted, broad-crested weir. The resulting unsteady motion exhibits systematic draining superimposed with strong, relatively rapid oscillations that propagate between the outflow boundary and the impermeable back wall. Three complementary approaches are employed: hodograph transformations to obtain quasi-analytical solutions, asymptotic analysis at late times, and numerical integration of the governing equations. The hodograph method yields exact early-time solutions, showing that from initially quiescent conditions the fluid drains while repeatedly generating regions of constant depth and velocity adjacent to the boundaries. A modified multiscale asymptotic framework is developed for late times to determine the limiting drainage rate and wave structure. When an obstacle of finite height is present, excess depth decays as t⁻² and the velocity field decays as t⁻³, tending toward a constant phase speed. For a pure constriction where all fluid ultimately drains, the motion approaches a self-similar state in which velocity decays as t⁻¹ and oscillations exhibit exponentially increasing period. Numerical simulations incorporating a specialized boundary condition implementation confirm the hodograph solutions and provide quantitative support for the asymptotic predictions.

entries.original_title: Membrane flutter induced by radiation of surface gravity waves on a uniform flow
entries.original_abstract: Abstract We consider the stability of an elastic membrane on the bottom of a uniform horizontal flow of an inviscid and incompressible fluid of finite depth with free surface. The membrane is simply supported at the leading and the trailing edges which attach it to the two parts of the horizontal rigid floor. The membrane has an infinite span in the direction perpendicular to the direction of the flow and a finite length in the direction of the flow. For the membrane of infinite length we derive a full dispersion relation that is valid for arbitrary depth of the fluid layer and find conditions for the flutter of the membrane due to emission of surface gravity waves. We describe this radiation-induced instability by means of the perturbation theory of the roots of the dispersion relation and the concept of negative energy waves and discuss its relation to the anomalous Doppler effect.
entries.anonymized_problem: The stability of an elastic membrane mounted on the floor of a finite-depth channel carrying a uniform horizontal flow of an inviscid, incompressible fluid with a free surface is examined. The membrane is simply supported at its leading and trailing edges, has infinite span in the cross-flow direction, and finite length in the streamwise direction. For the limiting case of an infinitely long membrane, a full dispersion relation valid for arbitrary fluid-layer depth is derived analytically. Conditions under which the membrane undergoes flutter driven by the radiation of surface gravity waves are identified. The radiation-induced instability mechanism is analyzed using perturbation theory applied to the roots of the dispersion relation, and interpreted through the framework of negative energy waves. A connection between this instability and the anomalous Doppler effect is established and discussed. The analysis reveals how energy exchange between the elastic structure and the free-surface wave field governs the onset of dynamic instability, providing a physically transparent description of the coupling between membrane vibration and gravity-wave emission in the presence of mean flow.

entries.original_title: Receptivity and stability of hypersonic leading-edge sweep flows around a blunt body
entries.original_abstract: Abstract This study performs global stability/receptivity analyses of hypersonic flows over a swept blunt body with infinite span. For the first time, we obtain the characteristics of the leading attachment-line mode to the variation of sweep angles from $20^{\circ }$ to $70^{\circ }$. The global eigenfunctions exhibit the characteristics of the attachment-line instability at the leading edge. At the same time, cross-flow (at small sweep angles) or second Mack mode (at larger sweep angles) dominates further downstream. We establish an adjoint-based bi-orthogonal eigenfunction system to address the receptivity problem of such flows to any external forces and boundary perturbations. The receptivity analyses indicate that the global modes are the most responsive to external forces and surface perturbations applied in the vicinity of the attachment line, regardless of the sweep angles. It is also proven that the present global extension of the bi-orthogonal eigenfunction system can be successfully applied to complex hypersonic flows.
entries.anonymized_problem: Global stability and receptivity analyses are performed for hypersonic flows over a swept blunt body with infinite span, examining sweep angles ranging from 20° to 70°. The study addresses how leading-edge attachment-line instabilities interact with downstream instability mechanisms and how such flows respond to external perturbations across a range of geometric configurations. A global eigenvalue approach is employed to extract eigenfunctions, which reveal attachment-line instability characteristics at the leading edge, transitioning to cross-flow instability dominance at smaller sweep angles and second Mack mode dominance at larger sweep angles. To address the receptivity problem, an adjoint-based bi-orthogonal eigenfunction system is developed, enabling quantification of the global modes' sensitivity to arbitrary external body forces and boundary perturbations. Receptivity analyses demonstrate that, regardless of sweep angle, the global modes are most responsive to forcing applied in the vicinity of the attachment line, both for volumetric and surface perturbations. The results validate the applicability of the global bi-orthogonal eigenfunction framework to complex hypersonic flow configurations, providing a systematic characterization of how attachment-line mode properties evolve with sweep angle and establishing a rigorous theoretical basis for receptivity assessment in high-speed swept leading-edge flows.

entries.original_title: A Framework for Rationing Ventilators and Critical Care Beds During the COVID-19 Pandemic.
entries.original_abstract: As the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic intensifies, shortages of ventilators have occurred in Italy and are likely imminent in parts of the US. In ordinary clinical circumstances, all patients in need of mechanical ventilation because of potentially-reversible conditions receive it, unless they or their surrogates decline. However, there are mounting concerns in many countries that this will not be possible and that patients who otherwise would likely survive if they received ventilator support will die because no ventilator is available. In this type of public health emergency, the ethical obligation of physicians to prioritize the well-being of individual patients may be overridden by public health policies that prioritize doing the greatest good for the greatest number of patients.1 These circumstances raise a critical question: when demand for ventilators and other intensive treatments far outstrips the supply, what criteria should guide these rationing decisions? Existing recommendations for how to allocate scarce critical care resources during a pandemic or disaster contain ethically problematic provisions, such as categorically excluding large populations of patients from access to scarce intensive care unit (ICU) resources. This
entries.anonymized_problem: During pandemic or disaster conditions, demand for mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit (ICU) beds can far exceed available supply, forcing clinicians and health systems to make allocation decisions that conflict with the standard ethical obligation to prioritize individual patient welfare. Existing guidelines for rationing scarce critical care resources during such emergencies have been identified as containing ethically problematic provisions, including categorical exclusion of broad patient populations from access to ICU-level care. This work addresses the question of what criteria should guide ventilator and critical care bed allocation when demand substantially outstrips supply. A structured ethical and clinical framework is developed to guide rationing decisions, grounded in the principle of maximizing benefit across the largest number of patients while avoiding unjust exclusions. The framework examines how triage criteria can be applied in a manner that is both clinically justified and ethically defensible, attending to concerns about equity and the avoidance of categorical discrimination. Key considerations include the use of short-term survival likelihood, periodic reassessment of patients already receiving ventilator support, and procedural transparency. The analysis highlights tensions between utilitarian public health ethics and individual patient-centered care, and proposes criteria intended to be practically implementable under conditions of severe resource constraint.

entries.original_title: COVID-19 and Italy: what next?
entries.original_abstract: The spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has already taken on pandemic proportions, affecting over 100 countries in a matter of weeks. A global response to prepare health systems worldwide is imperative. Although containment measures in China have reduced new cases by more than 90%, this reduction is not the case elsewhere, and Italy has been particularly affected. There is now grave concern regarding the Italian national health system's capacity to effectively respond to the needs of patients who are infected and require intensive care for SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia. The percentage of patients in intensive care reported daily in Italy between March 1 and March 11, 2020, has consistently been between 9% and 11% of patients who are actively infected. The number of patients infected since Feb 21 in Italy closely follows an exponential trend. If this trend continues for 1 more week, there will be 30 000 infected patients. Intensive care units will then be at maximum capacity; up to 4000 hospital beds will be needed by mid-April, 2020. Our analysis might help political leaders and health authorities to allocate enough resources, including personnel, beds, and intensive care facilities, to manage the situation in the next few days and weeks. If the Italian outbreak follows a similar trend as in Hubei province, China, the number of newly infected patients could start to decrease within 3–4 days, departing from the exponential trend. However, this cannot currently be predicted because of differences between social distancing measures and the capacity to quickly build dedicated facilities in China.
entries.anonymized_problem: This paper addresses the early trajectory of SARS-CoV-2 infections in Italy and the implications for national health system capacity. The approach involves descriptive and trend analysis of daily reported case data from Italy between February 21 and March 11, 2020, with particular focus on the proportion of actively infected patients requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission. The analysis fits an exponential growth model to observed infection counts and projects forward to estimate near-term demand for hospital and ICU beds, comparing the Italian trajectory to the documented course of the outbreak in Hubei province, China, where containment measures reduced new cases by more than 90%. Key findings indicate that ICU admissions in Italy consistently represented 9–11% of active cases during the study window, and that continuation of the exponential trend for one additional week would yield approximately 30,000 infected patients, placing ICUs at maximum capacity and requiring up to 4,000 additional hospital beds by mid-April 2020.
