entries.anonymized_problem: A series of epidemiological and clinical observations examined the intersection of ophthalmology and COVID-19, addressing two related questions: the risk of disease progression in patients with sight-threatening conditions (such as diabetic retinopathy and neovascular age-related macular degeneration) when ophthalmic care is deferred during the pandemic, and whether ocular barriers such as eyeglasses might reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. One observational study conducted early in the pandemic in Hubei province, China, enrolled 276 hospitalized patients with laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 and found that the proportion of regular eyeglass wearers was lower than expected based on population estimates, generating the hypothesis that eyeglasses may reduce eye-touching behavior and thereby limit viral entry. An accompanying commentary highlighted methodological concerns, including potential ascertainment bias and selection bias within the evaluated cohort, and cautioned against inferring causality from a single observational finding. The discussion also considered frameworks for weighing infection-exposure risk against the risk of irreversible vision loss from undertreated retinal disease. Collectively, these observations underscore the need for carefully designed studies to evaluate ocular transmission routes and to guide risk-stratified ophthalmic care delivery during infectious disease outbreaks.

entries.original_title: Increasing Access to FDA Inspection Reports on Irregularities and Misconduct in Clinical Trials.
entries.original_abstract: Transparency related to clinical trial protocols and data has become the expected standard over the past 2 decades, with broad support from patients, the scientific community, and regulatory agencies. Requirements for trial disclosures are codified in US statute and, since 2017, regulation requires timely submission of trial results to ClinicalTrials.gov. However, meaningful clinical trial transparency extends beyond prospective registration and reporting results. The public, for example, must know whether trials were conducted according to international standards for research integrity and must have access to reports investigating departures from good clinical practice guidelines. Transparency around clinical trial conduct is especially relevant for trials supporting approvals for new products, including drugs and devices. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) inspects clinical trial sites that involve FDA-regulated products to ensure the safety of study participants and the quality and integrity of the data. These inspections occasionally reveal objectionable practices, such as failure to obtain informed consent, falsification of data, or violations in adverse event reporting. If research misconduct is identified, the FDA may reject the affected data from the product’s safety and efficacy evaluations and also omit these data from the product labeling. Despite their importance, FDA inspection reports are not proactively disclosed. A common reason is that these reports may contain confidential commercial information. In certain cases, information regarding the FDA’s findings and actions can be found in publicly available review documents and letters to investigators. Still, most reports are extensively redacted to remove information on the investigational product and details of the clinical trial, making it difficult to link the FDA inspections to specific drugs or published trial reports.1 As a result, the frequency with which research irregularities are uncovered is not known. The FDA compiles an annual report with aggregate data on a list of standardized inspection citations, indicating that more than 200 violations related to clinical trial conduct are observed in most years.2 However, the database is not comprehensive, and certain trial irregularities identified during inspections, such as flawed trial procedures that do not necessarily violate federal regulations, are not reported. Two large premarket trials provide examples of the types of deficiencies uncovered in FDA inspections, with the reports made public only after Freedom of Information Act requests (Table; eTable in the Supplement).1 In ARISTOTLE,3 a trial of the anticoagulant apixaban published in 2011, inspection visits revealed concerns with trial conduct, including fraud affecting as many as 24 of 36 sites in China. The FDA engaged in lengthy discussions on how to address the numerous violations, noting that if data from one of the sites were excluded, the statistically significant benefit of apixaban on all-cause mortality would be lost. Ultimately, the approved labeling described the reduction in all-cause mortality associated with apixaban and did not mention data quality problems. Notably, results from this trial have since been incorporated into numerous publications, guidance documents, and meta-analyses. One study of 22 metaanalyses found that reanalyses excluding ARISTOTLE data would yield different findings in 10 (46%).5 In the RECORD4 trial4 of the anticoagulant rivaroxaban published in 2009, FDA site inspections identified deficiencies that affected half of the trial’s 16 clinical sites, and the FDA determined that the extent of the violations warranted exclusion of the entire trial from regulatory assessment. Notwithstanding the FDA’s inspection findings and actions, the RECORD4 publication does not include mention of data integrity issues and has been cited more than 1100 times by other investigators likely unaware of these issues given the lack of proactive disclosure of FDA inspection reports. A more recent example of trial irregularities identified in FDA inspections occurred with Study 201 in support of the 2016 approval of eteplirsen for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. In this case, inspectors noted problems with blinding and technical shortcomings with interpretation of images and data analyses, which rendered the study data unreliable to FDA reviewers.6 While the original inspection report was not released, these key findings contributed to the controversy around the drug’s approval, during which time the FDA commissioner publicly called for retraction or correction of published trial reports, which never occurred.7 As part of its public health mandate, the FDA should consider making clinical trial inspection reports and findings of clinical trial irregularities and misconduct proactively available. Such transparency could be achieved by mandating that inspection reports be posted on the FDA website. The reports also should be included in clinical trial registries, such as ClinicalTrials.gov, which already hosts a number of other study documents, including trial protocols and statistical analysis plans. Trial identifiers assigned by the registry permit consolidation of trial data across sources and are used in publications and throughout FDA review documents. Addition of these identifiers to the inspection reports would enable easy linkage and retrieval to create a comprehensive record of a clinical trial. This type of transparency could produce numerous benefits. First, journal editors could independently assess elements of trial quality in publication decisions. VIEWPOINT
entries.anonymized_problem: Clinical trial transparency has expanded substantially over recent decades, encompassing prospective registration and results reporting, yet transparency around trial conduct—particularly regulatory inspection findings—remains limited. This commentary examines the gap between existing transparency requirements and public access to regulatory inspection findings from clinical trial site audits. The approach draws on examples of inspection reports obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests for two large anticoagulant trials and one neuromuscular disease trial, illustrating how identified deficiencies—including data falsification, informed consent failures, and blinding problems—affected regulatory assessments but remained largely inaccessible to the scientific community. In one anticoagulant trial, fraud was identified at up to 24 of 36 sites in one country, with exclusion of affected data potentially eliminating a statistically significant mortality benefit; reanalyses of 22 meta-analyses incorporating that trial's data found 46% would yield different conclusions if those data were excluded. In a second anticoagulant trial, violations at half of 16 clinical sites prompted regulators to exclude the entire dataset from the regulatory submission, yet the published report—cited more than 1,100 times—contains no mention of these issues. The commentary argues that proactively publishing inspection reports through regulatory agency websites and clinical trial registries, linked via trial identifiers, would enable journal editors, systematic reviewers, and the public to accurately interpret the evidence base and improve research integrity oversight.

entries.original_title: The influence of integration of health-insurance schemes on catastrophic health expenditure in China: a cohort study
entries.original_abstract: Abstract Background Fragmented health-insurance schemes led to inefficiency and inequality in financial protection for universal health-care coverage. The Chinese government proceeded to consolidate the urban and rural health-insurance schemes with a unified fund collection, pooling, and payment system in 2016. Our study aims to establish the effects of the integration policy on incidence and distribution of catastrophic health expenditure (CHE) in China. Methods We obtained nationally representative cohort data for analysis from five China Family Panel Studies from 2010 to 2018, which included 17 858 households from 23 provinces. Families were selected using a probability proportional to size sampling technique with implicit stratification from 25 provinces in mainland China. In this natural experimental design, the five provinces with integrated health-insurance schemes before 2016 were considered to be the treatment group, and the other 18 provinces were considered to be the control group. We used a differences-in-differences method to capture the effects of integration policy on CHE incidence, measured by whether the out-of-pocket health expenditure exceeded 25% of the total household non-food expenditure, controlling for both household characteristics and geographical fixed effects. Further, we used the concentration index to investigate changes in the distribution of CHE. Findings The incidence of CHE for total population decreased from 17·4% (95% CI 16·7–18·0, SE 0·0034) in 2010 to 13·0% (12·4–13·6, 0·0031) in 2018. The incidence of CHE in urban areas decreased from 14·1% (13·3–15·0, 0·0045) in 2010 to 9·6% (8·8–10·3, 0·0038) in 2018, whereas it declined from 20·3% (19·3–21·3, 0·0050) to 16·6% (15·7–17·6, 0·0049) in rural areas. The incidence of CHE in treatment groups reduced from 15·2% (14·0–16·5, 0·0063) in 2010 to 10·1% (9·0–11·2, 0·0057) in 2018, whereas it decreased from 18·1% (17·3–18·9, 0·0040) in 2010 to 14·0% (13·2–14·7, 0·0036) in 2018 in control groups. In addition, consolidation of health-insurance schemes decreased the incidence of CHE by 1·7% (0·68–2·73, p Interpretation The integration of different public health-insurance schemes in China might have increased the financial protection of residents covered by these schemes. However, urban–rural disparity in health insurance and unequal distribution of CHE among poor households have not altered. This study suggests that bulk purchasing and payment reform can be implemented to contain health-care costs and to refrain out-of-pocket payments, particularly for rural and population with low incomes. Funding NHC Key Laboratory of Health Economics and Policy Research, Shandong University (grant NHC-HEPR2019017).
entries.anonymized_problem: This study examines whether consolidating fragmented urban and rural public health-insurance schemes into a unified fund collection, pooling, and payment system reduces catastrophic health expenditure (CHE) and improves equity in financial protection. Using nationally representative longitudinal data from five waves (2010–2018) of a household panel survey covering 17,858 households across 23 provinces, a natural experimental design was employed in which provinces that integrated their insurance schemes before 2016 served as the treatment group and the remaining provinces as controls. A differences-in-differences approach estimated policy effects on CHE incidence—defined as out-of-pocket health spending exceeding 25% of total household non-food expenditure—while controlling for household characteristics and geographical fixed effects. Concentration indices tracked distributional changes. Overall CHE incidence declined from 17.4% in 2010 to 13.0% in 2018. The integration policy was associated with a statistically significant 1.7 percentage-point reduction in CHE incidence (95% CI 0.68–2.73, p<0.05). Despite these gains, urban–rural disparities in insurance coverage persisted, and the disproportionate concentration of CHE among lower-income households did not improve. The findings suggest that while scheme consolidation enhances aggregate financial protection, additional cost-containment measures—such as bulk purchasing and payment reform—are needed to address inequities affecting rural residents and low-income populations.

entries.original_title: Moving to Action on Place-Based Health.
entries.original_abstract: “We Remember” Withers and his colleagues savor their successes but never forget their losses. Operation Safety Net created a memorial wall of bronze plaques beneath a highway overpass in downtown Pittsburgh. It commemorates individuals known to have died since 1989 while homeless in Allegheny County. “We remember” tops each plaque, which also notes the year in which the person died. Most feature the individual’s full name, sometimes with their street name, but some bear only their street name, such as “Sarge” and “Angel.” Some plaques bear no name, just “unknown,” the individual’s identity lost forever on the streets. “We believe you are no longer cold, hungry, lonely or frightened,” reads the large plaque above the smaller individual plaques. “May you watch over us from a warm, caring home above.” Each year on December 21, which is National Homeless Persons Memorial Day and, not coincidentally, the longest night of the year, a candlelight vigil commemorates the individuals behind the newest plaques on the wall. Among the dozen plaques added in 2019 was one for Roberto, the panhandler the Operation Safety Net team had spotted at a downtown intersection that fine fall morning. Just 2 days later, Roberto died. “I presume it was complications from his long alcohol use,” Withers said in an email. “We are all heartbroken, which is an ongoing part of our work. It also highlights that we are in the midst of great suffering, need, and loss.”
entries.anonymized_problem: This piece addresses the challenge of translating awareness of place-based health determinants—particularly homelessness and its associated mortality—into concrete clinical and policy action. The approach is narrative and reflective, centering on the work of a street medicine program serving individuals experiencing homelessness in an urban setting, and using a commemorative memorial to document deaths among this population since 1989. The discussion illustrates the human cost of structural health inequities through case-level detail, including the death of a patient encountered just days before his passing, attributed to complications of chronic alcohol use disorder. The text explores the emotional and ethical dimensions faced by practitioners working at the intersection of medicine and social determinants of health, highlighting grief, systemic insufficiency, and the sustained need for outreach-based care models. Key findings are qualitative and observational: mortality among people experiencing homelessness remains high, often occurs in anonymity, and is closely tied to poverty, substance use, and lack of stable housing. The piece argues that commemorative practices and sustained street-level engagement serve both clinical and advocacy functions, keeping visible a population whose suffering and deaths might otherwise go unrecorded.

entries.original_title: EU migration policies drive health crisis on Greek islands.
entries.original_abstract: Restrictive migration policies that deny migrants and asylum seekers their right to health—a fundamental right enshrined in universal human rights declarations and treaties since 1948—are increasingly prevalent globally. They are the result of the so-called migration crisis that is a politically made humanitarian crisis. States are criminalising people who are in some of the most vulnerable situations, often also denying their right to seek asylum and right to health. Such policies are particularly apparent in situations of indefinite containment, such as on the Greek Islands (Chios, Kos, Leros, Lesvos, and Samos), where people are contained in EU-supported hotspot facilities in overcrowded, unhealthy, and undignified conditions. Despite evidence of the adverse health consequences of migration regimes that force people seeking safety to endure these environments, at the end of 2019, there were more than 42 000 asylum seekers residing in the Greek Islands, even though those hotspot facilities have a maximum capacity of 6178. After arriving in Greece, asylum seekers are subject to geographical restriction, which prevents them from leaving the island unless they receive a positive decision or are deemed “vulnerable”. More than a third of asylum seekers are children, and there are over 1000 unaccompanied minors on Lesvos alone. People are forced to live in tents and under plastic sheeting even in the winter, with insufficient access to water, sanitation, and hygiene, exposing them to respiratory, skin, and gastrointestinal infections as well as environmental risks from hypothermia and fires. Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) working on the Greek islands, such as the International Rescue Committee and Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), have repeatedly warned of the deterioration of health on the islands, especially the mental health distress among asylum seekers that has worsened due to the conditions of containment. The MSF clinic in Lesvos, for example, sees multiple cases of children who have self-harmed or attempted suicide and children younger than 10 years who have acute and complex mental health conditions, including one case of the rare condition resignation syndrome. Alongside the burden of mental health problems, the general conditions compromise health and at least six asylum seekers have died of preventable causes on the Greek islands since August, 2019, including a 9-month-old baby who died due to dehydration. These conditions are not inevitable; they are the result of political choice. The Greek Government and EU continue to insist on the implementation of this approach. People are held in the hotspots for increasingly lengthy periods, ranging from 6 months to 1·5 years. After fleeing war and persecution in countries such as Afghanistan, Syria, or the Democratic Republic of the Congo, many are survivors of violence or torture and have faced adversity in their home countries or during migration routes. The gaps in the provision of health care mean that manageable medical and mental health conditions risk becoming more severe, posing long-term, and even lifethreatening, consequences. In many instances, NGOs and volunteers are left attempting to respond to the basic needs neglected by the state. Additionally, in July, 2019, the Greek Government revoked access to a social security number (known as AMKA) for asylum seekers and undocumented migrants in Greece. Without AMKA, thousands of asylum seekers, unaccompanied children, and undocumented migrants (who did not already have AMKA) do not have free access to health care, including regular treatments and medication, as well as facing difficulties in accessing other social services. The repeal of AMKA, combined with the recently introduced new International Protection Legislation, has resulted in an increased restriction of individual rights and protections for vulnerable people. Protections for vulnerable Published Online January 13, 2020 https://doi.org/10.1016/ S0140-6736(19)33175-7
entries.anonymized_problem: Restrictive migration containment policies and their consequences for the health of asylum seekers are examined through analysis of conditions in EU-supported reception facilities on five Greek islands (Chios, Kos, Leros, Lesvos, and Samos). The study draws on documented evidence from humanitarian organizations, epidemiological observations, and policy analysis to characterize health outcomes under prolonged geographic detention. At the end of 2019, more than 42,000 asylum seekers resided in facilities with a stated maximum capacity of 6,178, resulting in severe overcrowding. Conditions include inadequate shelter, insufficient water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure, exposing residents to respiratory, gastrointestinal, and skin infections, hypothermia, and fire hazards. Mental health burden is described as substantial, including self-harm, suicidal behavior, and complex psychiatric presentations in children under ten years, including at least one case of resignation syndrome. At least six preventable deaths were recorded from August 2019 onward. Administrative revocation of social security registration further restricted formal healthcare access for asylum seekers and undocumented migrants. The analysis concludes that observed health crises are attributable to deliberate policy choices—particularly indefinite geographic containment and reduced legal protections—rather than unavoidable circumstances, and calls for policy revision to uphold the right to health as established under international human rights frameworks.

entries.original_title: Sustainability, Business, and Health.
entries.original_abstract: This Viewpoint discusses examples of how many private sector businesses have aligned their core missions with civil and human rights and sustainability reforms, and emphasizes the importance of engaging the sector in achieving public health goals and accelerating worldwide recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic
entries.anonymized_problem: The relationship between private sector business engagement and public health outcomes presents an important area of inquiry, particularly in the context of pandemic recovery. This analysis examines how private sector organizations can align their core operational missions with civil and human rights principles alongside sustainability reforms, and considers the implications of such alignment for advancing population health goals. Drawing on illustrative examples of businesses that have integrated social and environmental priorities into their central functions, the discussion explores mechanisms by which commercial entities can serve as active contributors to public health infrastructure rather than peripheral actors. The analysis is situated within the broader context of worldwide recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic, where accelerating health improvements may depend on multi-sector collaboration beyond traditional governmental and nonprofit channels. Key findings suggest that strategic engagement of the private sector—when oriented around sustainability and rights-based frameworks—may represent a meaningful lever for achieving public health objectives at scale. The discussion emphasizes the practical and policy relevance of cultivating such partnerships as part of coordinated global health recovery efforts.

entries.original_title: Financial Penalties Imposed on Large Pharmaceutical Firms for Illegal Activities.
entries.original_abstract: Financial Penalties Imposed on Large Pharmaceutical Firms for Illegal Activities Some pharmaceutical companies have received criticism for engaging in illegal activities, such as providing kickbacks and bribes, knowingly shipping adulterated or contaminated drugs to pharmacies, and marketing drugs for unapproved uses. This study examined financial penalties for illegal activities among large pharmaceutical firms in relation to annual revenues.
entries.anonymized_problem: This study examines the relationship between financial penalties for illegal activities and annual revenues among large pharmaceutical firms. The illegal activities under investigation include practices such as providing kickbacks and bribes, knowingly distributing adulterated or contaminated drug products, and marketing pharmaceuticals for uses not approved by regulatory authorities. Using financial penalty data alongside annual revenue figures for large pharmaceutical companies, the analysis assesses the relative magnitude of monetary sanctions imposed for such violations. The findings contextualize penalty amounts against company revenues, providing a measure of whether financial consequences represent a meaningful economic deterrent relative to the scale of business operations. Results suggest that penalties, when expressed as a proportion of annual revenues, may be limited in their deterrent effect, raising questions about the adequacy of financial sanctions as a regulatory enforcement mechanism in the pharmaceutical industry. The study contributes to ongoing discussions about corporate accountability, regulatory oversight, and the design of enforcement frameworks capable of discouraging misconduct among large, high-revenue pharmaceutical enterprises.

entries.original_title: Why WHO needs a feminist economic agenda
entries.original_abstract: Minority ethnic status, class, education, and sexuality determine who is represented in unpaid community health-care worker roles 8 The unpaid and low paid labour of women has contributed to profits for private health-care providers and saved the bottom line of health spending in national budgets: capitalism and patriarchy combine to systematically undervalue social reproductive labour—ie, unpaid care roles as women's work 9 Governments’ ability to fund health-care services is dictated by their revenue and fiscal policy space Yet the IMF and the World Bank continue to prioritise austerity measures and “private sector first” strategies that systematically undermine the ability of governments to provide public services and achieve UHC 14,15 Neither institution has linked its rhetoric on promotion of gender equality to the development of a systematic approach for evaluating the implications of its austerity policies on gender inequality, health delivery, or outcomes 16,17 The key funders of the IMF and the World Bank, and those that hold the greatest number of Executive Board votes, are G7 and G20 members A feminist economic approach to health requires that all people at all levels of health-care decision making reorient their notion of wellbeing to include gender equality for women in all their diversities 19 Feminist knowledge informs what we count as costs and savings: the national income saved from women's low wages or volunteerism as health-care workers;20 the benefit to national budgets and health outcomes when there are gender-based violence health-care prevention programmes;21 and the negative burdens carried by health-care workers exposed to violence, harassment, and exploitation when their work is located in unregulated environments, including homes, non-governmental organisations, and provincial health clinics 22 A WHO economic engagement strategy that does not address the social and political determinants of health delivery, resourcing, and decision making risks perpetuating the falsehood that health is a technical enterprise that can be achieved in a silo
entries.anonymized_problem: The global health financing system systematically undervalues the labour contributions of women, particularly through unpaid and low-paid community health worker roles, with outcomes shaped by intersecting factors including ethnicity, class, education, and sexuality. This analysis examines how capitalist and patriarchal structures combine to depress the recognized value of social reproductive labour, and how international financial institution policy frameworks — specifically austerity measures and private-sector-prioritizing strategies promoted by major multilateral lenders — constrain government fiscal capacity to fund public health services and achieve universal health coverage. The argument is made that neither major multilateral lending institution has systematically linked its gender equality rhetoric to evaluation of how its fiscal conditionality affects gender inequality or health outcomes. A feminist economic framework is proposed as a corrective lens, reorienting definitions of costs and savings to include: the value of women's unpaid or underpaid health labour captured in national budgets; the cost-effectiveness of gender-based violence prevention programmes; and the occupational harms borne by workers in unregulated settings. The analysis concludes that health governance strategies that ignore the social and political determinants of health resourcing and decision-making risk reinforcing the misconception that health delivery is a purely technical, context-independent enterprise.

entries.original_title: Challenge Trials-Could Deliberate Coronavirus Exposure Hasten Vaccine Development?
entries.original_abstract: Josh Morrison, JD, was so moved by a 2007 essay about one woman’s desperate search for a kidney that he decided he wanted to donate one. “Okay, I can save someone’s life,” the self-described nonconformist told himself. It took a few years, but in 2011 he donated a kidney to a stranger who’d been waiting 8 years. Then in 2014, Morrison, a Harvard Law School graduate, left corporate law and cofounded Waitlist Zero, whose mission is to make it easier for patients to ask for a kidney and donors to give one. Living organ donation in the US has dropped because of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, Morrison said. After reading a March 31 article about how young, healthy individuals like himself could accelerate the development of a COVID-19 vaccine, he knew he had found another cause worthy of his passion for doing good. This time, instead of getting donor kidneys to patients more quickly, the 34-yearold Morrison hopes to make a COVID-19 vaccine available at least 1 Day Sooner, which is the name of the organization he cofounded. The group is signing up volunteers willing to enroll in randomized, placebocontrolled trials of candidate COVID-19 vaccines. These wouldn’t be conventional clinical trials, though. After getting either the investigational vaccine or the placebo, volunteers would deliberately be exposed to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) instead of waiting for the virus to find them in the community. “Anything that could get a vaccine sooner and get this over with sounds great to me,” said Morrison, who coauthored a May 14 preprint article, which hasn’t been peer reviewed. It describes scenarios in which human challenge trials, also called controlled human infection models, would be useful in accelerating COVID-19 vaccine development. Human challenge trials have been used to test vaccines against a number of infectious diseases, including malaria and influenza. Participants in such studies remain quarantined in a clinical trials unit while researchers monitor their immune response and whether they develop symptoms. But unlike malaria or inf luenza, COVID-19 has no known cure or, as yet, proven treatment, raising ethical concerns about challenge trials of a vaccine against it. Bioethicist George Annas, JD, MPH, at the Boston University School of Public Health, questions how volunteers in such studies could truly provide informed consent. “Well into this pandemic, we don’t know a lot about this virus,” Annas pointed out in an interview. “This is not the way out of the pandemic. If you want to be serious about science, you have to know how this disease works.”
entries.anonymized_problem: Human challenge trials for COVID-19 vaccine development involve deliberately exposing vaccinated volunteers to SARS-CoV-2 rather than waiting for natural community exposure. This article examines the scientific rationale, practical design considerations, and ethical concerns surrounding controlled human infection models as a potential strategy to accelerate vaccine evaluation during the COVID-19 pandemic. The approach draws on precedent from challenge trials used for other infectious diseases, including malaria and influenza, in which quarantined participants receive either an investigational vaccine or placebo and are subsequently exposed to the pathogen under monitored conditions. Proponents argue that such trials could substantially reduce the time required to obtain efficacy data compared with conventional phase III trials relying on community transmission. However, significant ethical objections have been raised, centering on the absence of a proven treatment or cure for COVID-19 at the time of writing, which complicates the risk–benefit calculus and undermines the standard of acceptable residual risk typically required for challenge study designs. Bioethicists question whether meaningful informed consent is achievable given incomplete understanding of COVID-19 pathophysiology, disease progression, and long-term sequelae. The article weighs these competing considerations without reaching a definitive resolution, reflecting the broader scientific and ethical debate about whether human challenge trials represent a justifiable tool in pandemic vaccine development.

entries.original_title: Cosmology of Sub-MeV Dark Matter Freeze-In.
entries.original_abstract: Dark matter (DM) could be a relic of freeze-in through a light mediator, where the DM is produced by extremely feeble, IR-dominated processes in the thermal standard model plasma. In the simplest viable models with DM lighter than 1 MeV, the DM has a small effective electric charge and is born with a nonthermal phase-space distribution. This DM candidate would cause observable departures from standard cosmological evolution. In this work, we combine data from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), Lyman-α forest, quasar lensing, stellar streams, and Milky Way satellite abundances to set limits on freeze-in DM masses up to ∼20  keV, with the exact constraint depending on whether the DM thermalizes in its own sector. We perform forecasts for the CMB-S4 experiment, the Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array, and the Vera Rubin Observatory, finding that freeze-in DM masses up to ∼80  keV can be explored.
entries.anonymized_problem: Sub-MeV dark matter produced via freeze-in through a light mediator represents a theoretically motivated scenario in which dark matter originates from infrared-dominated, extremely feeble interactions with the standard model plasma. In the simplest viable models, such dark matter carries a small effective electric charge and is produced with a nonthermal phase-space distribution, leading to potentially observable departures from standard cosmological evolution. This work investigates the cosmological signatures of this scenario and derives constraints on the dark matter mass using a combination of cosmic microwave background data, Lyman-α forest observations, quasar lensing, stellar streams, and Milky Way satellite abundances. Upper limits on the freeze-in dark matter mass are placed at approximately 20 keV, with the precise bound depending on whether the dark matter thermalizes within its own sector. Forecasts are additionally performed for upcoming and planned experiments—CMB-S4, the Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array, and the Vera Rubin Observatory—indicating that sensitivity to freeze-in dark matter masses up to approximately 80 keV can be achieved. The analysis demonstrates that current and future cosmological surveys provide meaningful probes of this class of feebly interacting dark matter candidates across a well-defined mass range.

entries.original_title: Origin of Friction in Superlubric Graphite Contacts.
entries.original_abstract: More than thirty years ago, it was theoretically predicted that friction for incommensurate contacts between atomically smooth, infinite, crystalline materials (e.g., graphite, MoS_{2}) is vanishing in the low speed limit, and this corresponding state was called structural superlubricity (SSL). However, experimental validation of this prediction has met challenges, since real contacts always have a finite size, and the overall friction arises not only from the atoms located within the contact area, but also from those at the contact edges which can contribute a finite amount of friction even when the incommensurate area does not. Here, we report, using a novel method, the decoupling of these contributions for the first time. The results obtained from nanoscale to microscale incommensurate contacts of graphite under ambient conditions verify that the average frictional contribution of an inner atom is no more than 10^{-4} that of an atom at the edge. Correspondingly, the total friction force is dominated by friction between the contact edges for contacts up to 10  μm in lateral size. We discuss the physical mechanisms of friction observed in SSL contacts, and provide guidelines for the rational design of large-scale SSL contacts.
entries.anonymized_problem: Structural superlubricity (SSL) refers to the theoretically predicted vanishing of friction at incommensurate contacts between atomically smooth crystalline materials in the low-speed limit. While this prediction dates back over three decades, experimental verification has remained difficult because real contacts are finite in size, meaning friction arises from both interior atoms and edge atoms—the latter capable of contributing finite friction even when the incommensurate bulk region does not. This study addresses the challenge of separating these two contributions by applying a decoupling method to incommensurate graphite contacts ranging from the nanoscale to the microscale under ambient conditions. By systematically analyzing friction as a function of contact geometry and size, the approach isolates the interior and edge contributions independently. The results show that the average frictional contribution of an interior atom is no more than 10⁻⁴ times that of an edge atom, confirming that the total friction force in SSL contacts is dominated by edge friction for contact sizes up to 10 μm in lateral dimension. The physical mechanisms governing friction in SSL contacts are analyzed, and design guidelines are derived for engineering large-scale SSL contacts that minimize total friction by controlling edge geometry and contact dimensions.

entries.original_title: Searching for the Optimal PEEP in Patients Without ARDS: High, Low, or in Between?
entries.original_abstract: infectious diseases control and access to essential medicines. To avoid a backslide with serious ramifications for populations worldwide, the US and other wealthy nations must remain engaged and invested in efforts to strengthen health systems in lowand middle-income countries. Certainly, COVID-19 is a worst-case scenario, one that would strain any health system. But there were quality shortcomings long before COVID-19. Crucially, as the health care community begins to recover after the pandemic, quality must remain a central focus. Now is the time to examine US and global systems through a fresh lens. With the right planning, the COVID-19 recovery efforts could provide the impetus needed to reinvigorate the quality movement and build a system that consistently delivers safe, effective, and affordable care to everyone who needs it. On the threshold of an uncertain future, and one in which the health care system will be forever changed, 3 Viewpoints in this issue of JAMA and related to the 20th anniversary of the IOM reports examine urgent areas of focus for the care quality movement. The Viewpoint by Corrigan and Clancy8 looks holistically at system performance in the context of the pandemic and according to the 6-element quality checklist set forth in the 2001 report. In their Viewpoint, Singh and Carayon9 look beyond the hospital setting, where most quality improvement efforts have focused to date, to the opportunities for ambulatory care and digital health. Acknowledging the interconnectedness of global societies, the Viewpoint by Leatherman and Berwick10 provides an important agenda for accelerating progress in care quality and safety globally in the quest for universal health coverage. The next 20 years of the quality movement will be defined by the priorities established today. As infectious diseases, climate change, health inequity, and information warfare reshape society more quickly than ever imagined, there is an opportunity—and an imperative—to design a system of care that learns, adapts, and holds quality and equity at the center.
