entries.original_title: Well-Posed Formulation of Scalar-Tensor Effective Field Theory.
entries.original_abstract: Effective field theory provides a way of parametrizing strong-field deviations from general relativity that might be observable in the gravitational waves emitted in a black hole merger. To perform numerical simulations of mergers in such theories it is necessary that the equations be written in a form that admits a well-posed initial value formulation. We study gravity coupled to a scalar field including the leading (four-derivative) effective field theory corrections. We introduce a new class of "modified harmonic" gauges and gauge-fixed equations of motion, such that, at weak coupling, the equations are strongly hyperbolic and therefore admit a well-posed initial value formulation.
entries.anonymized_problem: Effective field theory (EFT) provides a framework for parametrizing strong-field deviations from general relativity that could be observable in gravitational waves from black hole mergers. A critical obstacle to performing numerical simulations in such theories is ensuring that the governing equations admit a well-posed initial value formulation. This work examines gravity coupled to a scalar field with leading (four-derivative) EFT corrections and investigates the mathematical well-posedness of the resulting system. A new class of gauge conditions, termed modified harmonic gauges, is introduced along with corresponding gauge-fixed equations of motion. Analysis shows that, in the weak-coupling regime, the resulting equations are strongly hyperbolic, which is the condition required for a well-posed initial value formulation. This result establishes a mathematically consistent framework for future numerical evolutions of black hole mergers in scalar-tensor EFT, providing a pathway to simulating and ultimately constraining strong-field modifications to general relativity through gravitational wave observations.

entries.original_title: Extension of the Generalized Hydrodynamics to the Dimensional Crossover Regime.
entries.original_abstract: In an effort to address integrability breaking in cold gas experiments, we extend the integrable hydrodynamics of the Lieb-Liniger model with two additional components representing the population of atoms in the first and second transverse excited states, thus enabling a description of quasi-1D condensates. Collisions between different components are accounted for through the inclusion of a Boltzmann-type collision integral in the hydrodynamic equation. Contrary to standard generalized hydrodynamics, our extended model captures thermalization of the condensate at a rate consistent with experimental observations from a quantum Newton's cradle setup.
entries.anonymized_problem: Generalized hydrodynamics (GHD) provides an exact framework for integrable systems but fails to capture thermalization observed in quasi-one-dimensional cold-atom experiments, where transverse confinement is finite and integrability is weakly broken. This work addresses that gap by extending the hydrodynamic description of the Lieb-Liniger model to include populations of atoms in the first and second transverse excited states, thereby accounting for the dimensional crossover regime of quasi-1D condensates. Integrability-breaking collisions between atoms in different transverse modes are incorporated via a Boltzmann-type collision integral appended to the hydrodynamic equations of motion. This extended framework retains the structure of GHD for the ground transverse mode while coupling it to excited-mode populations whose dynamics drive thermalization. The resulting model reproduces thermalization rates consistent with experimental measurements from a quantum Newton's cradle setup, a benchmark system for studying relaxation in near-integrable quantum gases. The approach provides a controlled, systematic way to include weak integrability-breaking effects without abandoning the hydrodynamic formalism, bridging the gap between idealized integrable descriptions and the finite-temperature, finite-confinement conditions realized in laboratory experiments.

entries.original_title: Maximum information states for coherent scattering measurements
entries.original_abstract: The use of coherent light for precision measurements has been a key driving force for numerous research directions, ranging from biomedical optics1,2 to semiconductor manufacturing3. Recent work demonstrates that the precision of such measurements can be substantially improved by tailoring the spatial profile of light fields used for estimating an observable system parameter4–10. These advances naturally raise the intriguing question of which states of light can provide the ultimate measurement precision11. Here we introduce a general approach to determine the optimal coherent states of light for estimating any given parameter, regardless of the complexity of the system. Our analysis reveals that the light fields delivering the ultimate measurement precision are eigenstates of a Hermitian operator that quantifies the Fisher information from the system’s scattering matrix12. To illustrate this concept, we experimentally show that these maximum information states can probe the phase or the position of an object that is hidden by a disordered medium with a precision improved by an order of magnitude compared with unoptimized states. Our results enable optimally precise measurements in arbitrarily complex systems, thus establishing a new benchmark for metrology and imaging applications3,13. Wavefront shaping can reduce uncertainties due to measurement noise through disordered media—key to many imaging applications. Optimal precision can be achieved using light fields that are eigenstates of an operator related to the medium’s scattering matrix.
entries.anonymized_problem: Precision measurements using coherent light depend critically on the spatial profile of the illuminating field, yet a general framework for identifying the theoretically optimal illumination states has been lacking. This work addresses the question of which coherent light fields yield the ultimate measurement precision for estimating an arbitrary system parameter, regardless of system complexity. The approach derives optimal states by analyzing the Fisher information content of the system's scattering matrix: the light fields that maximize measurement precision are shown to be eigenstates of a Hermitian operator constructed from the parameter-derivative of the scattering matrix, weighted to extract maximum Fisher information. This theoretical result provides a systematic eigenvalue procedure for computing maximum-information states for any measurable parameter. The framework is validated experimentally by estimating the phase and position of an object concealed behind a disordered scattering medium. Using wavefront-shaped input fields corresponding to the derived eigenstates, measurement precision improves by approximately an order of magnitude relative to unoptimized illumination. The results establish a general upper bound on coherent measurement precision in complex scattering environments and provide a practical algorithm for achieving it, with relevance to biomedical imaging, semiconductor inspection, and other applications where scattering limits measurement fidelity.

entries.original_title: Nonstandard Neutrino Interactions as a Solution to the NOνA and T2K Discrepancy.
entries.original_abstract: The latest data of the two long-baseline accelerator experiments NOνA and T2K, interpreted in the standard three-flavor scenario, display a discrepancy. A mismatch in the determination of the standard CP phase δ_{CP} extracted by the two experiments is evident in the normal neutrino mass ordering. While NOνA prefers values close to δ_{CP}∼0.8π, T2K identifies values of δ_{CP}∼1.4π. Such two estimates are in disagreement at more than 90% C.L. for 2 degrees of freedom. We show that such a tension can be resolved if one hypothesizes the existence of complex neutral-current nonstandard interactions (NSIs) of the flavor changing type involving the e-μ or the e-τ sectors with couplings |ϵ_{eμ}|∼|ϵ_{eτ}|∼0.2. Remarkably, in the presence of such NSIs, both experiments point towards the same common value of the standard CP phase δ_{CP}∼3π/2. Our analysis also highlights an intriguing preference for maximal CP violation in the nonstandard sector with the NSI CP phases having best fit close to ϕ_{eμ}∼ϕ_{eτ}∼3π/2, hence pointing towards imaginary NSI couplings.
entries.anonymized_problem: Two long-baseline accelerator neutrino oscillation experiments have reported mutually inconsistent measurements of the standard CP-violating phase δ_{CP} when their data are interpreted within the conventional three-flavor neutrino framework. In the normal mass ordering, one experiment prefers δ_{CP} ≈ 0.8π while the other favors δ_{CP} ≈ 1.4π, a disagreement exceeding 90% confidence level for two degrees of freedom. This work investigates whether the introduction of complex neutral-current nonstandard neutrino interactions (NSIs) of the flavor-changing type can resolve this tension. A combined analysis is performed considering NSI couplings in the e–μ and e–τ sectors. The results show that with coupling magnitudes |ε_{eμ}| ~ |ε_{eτ}| ~ 0.2, the discrepancy between the two experiments is resolved: both data sets become consistent with a common standard CP phase of δ_{CP} ~ 3π/2. The analysis further reveals a preference for maximal CP violation in the nonstandard sector, with the NSI CP phases having best-fit values near φ_{eμ} ~ φ_{eτ} ~ 3π/2, indicating that purely imaginary NSI couplings are preferred. These findings suggest that physics beyond the standard neutrino interaction framework could simultaneously accommodate both experimental results within a unified oscillation picture.

entries.original_title: Confinement Controls the Bend Instability of Three-Dimensional Active Liquid Crystals.
entries.original_abstract: Spontaneous growth of long-wavelength deformations is a defining feature of active liquid crystals. We investigate the effect of confinement on the instability of 3D active liquid crystals in the isotropic phase composed of extensile microtubule bundles and kinesin molecular motors. When shear aligned, such fluids exhibit finite-wavelength self-amplifying bend deformations. By systematically changing the channel size we elucidate how the instability wavelength and its growth rate depend on the channel dimensions. Experimental findings are qualitatively consistent with a minimal hydrodynamic model, where the fastest growing deformation is set by a balance of active driving and elastic relaxation. Our results demonstrate that confinement determines the structure and dynamics of active fluids on all experimentally accessible length scales.
entries.anonymized_problem: Active liquid crystals exhibit spontaneous long-wavelength deformations driven by internal energy input, but how geometric confinement modifies these instabilities in three dimensions remains incompletely understood. This study investigates the bend instability in three-dimensional active liquid crystals composed of extensile microtubule bundles driven by kinesin molecular motors operating in the isotropic phase. When shear-aligned, these fluids develop finite-wavelength self-amplifying bend deformations. By systematically varying channel dimensions, the dependence of instability wavelength and growth rate on confinement geometry is characterized experimentally. The experimental findings are interpreted using a minimal hydrodynamic model in which the fastest-growing deformation mode is determined by a balance between active driving forces and elastic relaxation. Qualitative agreement between experiment and theory demonstrates that confinement controls both the characteristic length scale and the dynamics of the instability across all experimentally accessible length scales. These results establish that geometric boundaries are a primary determinant of active fluid structure and dynamics, rather than a secondary perturbation, with implications for understanding and engineering confined active matter systems.

entries.original_title: Topological Quantum Compiling with Reinforcement Learning
entries.original_abstract: Quantum compiling, a process that decomposes the quantum algorithm into a series of hardware-compatible commands or elementary gates, is of fundamental importance for quantum computing. We introduce an efficient algorithm based on deep reinforcement learning that compiles an arbitrary single-qubit gate into a sequence of elementary gates from a finite universal set. It generates near-optimal gate sequences with given accuracy and is generally applicable to various scenarios, independent of the hardware-feasible universal set and free from using ancillary qubits. For concreteness, we apply this algorithm to the case of topological compiling of Fibonacci anyons and obtain near-optimal braiding sequences for arbitrary single-qubit unitaries. Our algorithm may carry over to other challenging quantum discrete problems, thus opening up a new avenue for intriguing applications of deep learning in quantum physics.
entries.anonymized_problem: Quantum compiling—decomposing quantum algorithms into sequences of hardware-compatible elementary gates—is a core challenge in quantum computing. This work addresses the problem of efficiently finding near-optimal gate sequences for arbitrary single-qubit unitaries drawn from a finite universal gate set, without requiring ancilla qubits and independent of the specific hardware platform. A deep reinforcement learning approach is developed in which an agent learns to construct gate sequences by sequentially selecting elementary gates, optimizing for both sequence length and approximation accuracy. The method is applied concretely to topological quantum compiling using Fibonacci anyons, where the elementary operations correspond to anyon braidings and exact universality relies on the density of the braid group representation. The algorithm produces near-optimal braiding sequences approximating arbitrary single-qubit unitaries to a specified precision. Benchmarking against known bounds demonstrates that the learned sequences approach optimal length scaling. The framework is general and extends naturally to other discrete optimization problems in quantum information. The results suggest that deep reinforcement learning offers a practical route to solving combinatorially hard compilation problems that arise in topological and other fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

entries.original_title: Quantifying the Robustness of Topological Slow Light.
entries.original_abstract: The backscattering mean free path ξ, the average ballistic propagation length along a waveguide, quantifies the resistance of slow light against unwanted imperfections in the critical dimensions of the nanostructure. This figure of merit determines the crossover between acceptable slow-light transmission affected by minimal scattering losses and a strong backscattering-induced destructive interference when the waveguide length L exceeds ξ. Here, we calculate the backscattering mean free path for a topological photonic waveguide for a specific and determined amount of disorder and, equally relevant, for a fixed value of the group index n_{g} which is the slowdown factor of the group velocity with respect to the speed of light in vacuum. These two figures of merit, ξ and n_{g}, should be taken into account when quantifying the robustness of topological and conventional (nontopological) slow-light transport at the nanoscale. Otherwise, any claim on a better performance of topological guided light over a conventional one is not justified.
entries.anonymized_problem: Slow light in nanoscale waveguides suffers from backscattering due to fabrication disorder, and a key figure of merit for characterizing this sensitivity is the backscattering mean free path ξ — the average ballistic propagation length before disorder-induced scattering becomes significant. When the waveguide length exceeds ξ, destructive interference from backscattering severely degrades transmission. This work addresses the question of whether topological photonic waveguides offer genuine robustness advantages over conventional (nontopological) slow-light waveguides. The backscattering mean free path is calculated for a topological photonic waveguide under controlled conditions: a fixed, specified level of structural disorder and a fixed group index n_g, which quantifies how much the group velocity is reduced relative to the speed of light in vacuum. The analysis demonstrates that both ξ and n_g must be held constant when making fair comparisons between topological and conventional slow-light transport. Comparisons that do not control for these two parameters simultaneously are shown to be methodologically unsound. The findings indicate that claims of superior performance for topologically guided slow light over conventional guided light are not justified unless these figures of merit are properly normalized, providing a rigorous framework for evaluating slow-light robustness at the nanoscale.

entries.original_title: Identification of Symmetry-Protected Topological States on Noisy Quantum Computers.
entries.original_abstract: Identifying topological properties is a major challenge because, by definition, topological states do not have a local order parameter. While a generic solution to this challenge is not available yet, a broad class of topological states, namely, symmetry-protected topological (SPT) states, can be identified by distinctive degeneracies in their entanglement spectrum. Here, we propose and realize two complementary protocols to probe these degeneracies based on, respectively, symmetry-resolved entanglement entropies and measurement-based computational algorithms. The two protocols link quantum information processing to the classification of SPT phases of matter. They invoke the creation of a cluster state and are implemented on an IBM quantum computer. The experimental findings are compared to noisy simulations, allowing us to study the stability of topological states to perturbations and noise.
entries.anonymized_problem: Identifying topological properties in quantum systems is fundamentally difficult because topological states lack a local order parameter. Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) states can, however, be distinguished by characteristic degeneracies in their entanglement spectrum. This work addresses how to probe these degeneracies on near-term, noisy quantum hardware. Two complementary protocols are developed and implemented: one based on symmetry-resolved entanglement entropies and one based on measurement-based computational algorithms. Both protocols connect quantum information processing concepts to the classification of SPT phases of matter and require preparing a cluster state as a key computational resource. The protocols are executed on a superconducting quantum processor, and the experimental results are benchmarked against noisy numerical simulations. This comparison enables a systematic study of how topological signatures in the entanglement spectrum respond to realistic hardware noise and external perturbations. The findings demonstrate that entanglement-spectrum degeneracies characteristic of SPT order can be detected under noisy conditions, providing a viable route for probing topological phases on currently available quantum devices without requiring fault-tolerant computation.

entries.original_title: Many-Body Level Statistics of Single-Particle Quantum Chaos.
entries.original_abstract: We consider a noninteracting many-fermion system populating levels of a unitary random matrix ensemble (equivalent to the q=2 complex Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model)-a generic model of single-particle quantum chaos. We study the corresponding many-particle level statistics by calculating the spectral form factor analytically using algebraic methods of random matrix theory, and match it with an exact numerical simulation. Despite the integrability of the theory, the many-body spectral rigidity is found to have a surprisingly rich landscape. In particular, we find a residual repulsion of distant many-body levels stemming from single-particle chaos, together with islands of level attraction. These results are encoded in an exponential ramp in the spectral form factor, which we show to be a universal feature of nonergodic many-fermion systems embedded in a chaotic medium.
entries.anonymized_problem: A noninteracting many-fermion system is studied in which single-particle levels are drawn from a unitary random matrix ensemble, equivalent to the q=2 complex Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model. This setup serves as a generic model of single-particle quantum chaos in the absence of many-body interactions. The many-body level statistics are analyzed by computing the spectral form factor analytically using algebraic methods from random matrix theory, with results verified against exact numerical simulations. Despite the integrability of the noninteracting theory, the many-body spectral rigidity exhibits a rich structure. Specifically, a residual repulsion between distant many-body energy levels is identified as a consequence of single-particle chaos, coexisting with localized regions of level attraction. These features manifest as an exponential ramp in the spectral form factor—a qualitatively distinct signature from the linear ramp characteristic of ergodic many-body systems. This exponential ramp is argued to be a universal feature of nonergodic many-fermion systems embedded in a chaotic single-particle environment, suggesting that single-particle chaos leaves a nontrivial and structured imprint on many-body spectral correlations even in the absence of interactions.

entries.original_title: Stabilization of Finite-Energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill States.
entries.original_abstract: We introduce a new approach to Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states that treats their finite-energy version in an exact manner. Based on this analysis, we develop new qubit-oscillator circuits that autonomously stabilize a GKP manifold, correcting errors without relying on qubit measurements. Finally, we show numerically that logical information encoded in GKP states is very robust against typical oscillator noise sources when stabilized by these new circuits.
entries.anonymized_problem: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are a promising encoding of logical qubits in harmonic oscillators, but practical implementations require finite-energy versions that differ from the ideal mathematical description, complicating error correction analysis. This work addresses the challenge of stabilizing finite-energy GKP states in an exact, non-perturbative framework rather than treating finite-energy effects as approximate corrections to ideal states. Starting from an exact characterization of finite-energy GKP states, qubit-oscillator circuits are derived that autonomously stabilize the associated code manifold without requiring ancilla qubit measurements—relying instead on engineered dissipation to passively correct errors. The stabilization scheme is analyzed numerically under realistic oscillator noise models, including photon loss and dephasing. Results demonstrate that logical information encoded in finite-energy GKP states and protected by these autonomous circuits is highly robust against typical oscillator noise sources, with the measurement-free nature of the approach offering practical advantages for continuous error correction in quantum hardware. The findings suggest that exact treatment of finite-energy structure is important for designing effective stabilization protocols and that autonomous, dissipation-based methods can provide reliable protection for bosonic code states.

entries.original_title: Minimal Model for Fast Scrambling.
entries.original_abstract: We study quantum information scrambling in spin models with both long-range all-to-all and short-range interactions. We argue that a simple global, spatially homogeneous interaction together with local chaotic dynamics is sufficient to give rise to fast scrambling, which describes the spread of quantum information over the entire system in a time that is logarithmic in the system size. This is illustrated in two tractable models: (1) a random circuit with Haar random local unitaries and a global interaction and (2) a classical model of globally coupled nonlinear oscillators. We use exact numerics to provide further evidence by studying the time evolution of an out-of-time-order correlator and entanglement entropy in spin chains of intermediate sizes. Our results pave the way towards experimental investigations of fast scrambling and aspects of quantum gravity with quantum simulators.
entries.anonymized_problem: Quantum information scrambling — the process by which local information spreads and becomes inaccessible to local measurements — is investigated in spin models combining long-range all-to-all interactions with short-range interactions. The central question is whether a spatially homogeneous global interaction, when combined with local chaotic dynamics, is sufficient to produce fast scrambling, defined as the spread of quantum information across an entire system in time logarithmic in system size. Two tractable models are analyzed: a random circuit composed of Haar-random local unitaries supplemented by a global interaction, and a classical model of globally coupled nonlinear oscillators. Exact numerical simulations track the time evolution of out-of-time-order correlators and entanglement entropy in spin chains of intermediate sizes, providing quantitative evidence for the logarithmic scrambling timescale. The results establish that the combination of a simple global coupling and locally chaotic dynamics is sufficient to achieve fast scrambling, without requiring more complex nonlocal interaction structures. These findings identify experimentally accessible settings — relevant to quantum simulators — in which fast scrambling and connections to quantum gravity phenomenology could be probed directly.

entries.original_title: Properties of ^{187}Ta Revealed through Isomeric Decay.
entries.original_abstract: Mass-separated ^{187}Ta_{114} in a high-spin isomeric state has been produced for the first time by multinucleon transfer reactions, employing an argon gas-stopping cell and laser ionization. Internal γ rays revealed a T_{1/2}=7.3±0.9  s isomer at 1778±1  keV, which decays through a rotational band with perturbations associated with the approach to a prolate-oblate shape transition. Model calculations show less influence from triaxiality compared to heavier elements in the same mass region. The isomer-decay reduced E2 hindrance factor f_{ν}=27±1 supports the interpretation that axial symmetry is approximately conserved.
entries.anonymized_problem: The neutron-rich nucleus ¹⁸⁷Ta₁₁₄ was studied via the decay of a high-spin isomeric state, produced for the first time using multinucleon transfer reactions combined with an argon gas-stopping cell and laser ionization for mass separation. Internal γ-ray spectroscopy identified an isomer at an excitation energy of 1778 ± 1 keV with a half-life of T₁/₂ = 7.3 ± 0.9 s. The isomer decays through a rotational band exhibiting perturbations attributed to proximity to a prolate-oblate shape transition. Model calculations indicate that triaxial deformation plays a less significant role in this nucleus compared to heavier isotopes in the same mass region. The reduced E2 hindrance factor for isomer decay, f_ν = 27 ± 1, supports the interpretation that axial symmetry is approximately conserved in ¹⁸⁷Ta. These results provide new spectroscopic constraints on nuclear deformation and shape evolution in the tantalum isotopic chain near the neutron-rich boundary of experimentally accessible nuclei.

entries.original_title: Probing Surface-Bound Atoms with Quantum Nanophotonics.
entries.original_abstract: Quantum control of atoms at ultrashort distances from surfaces would open a new paradigm in quantum optics and offer a novel tool for the investigation of near-surface physics. Here, we investigate the motional states of atoms that are bound weakly to the surface of a hot optical nanofiber. We theoretically demonstrate that with optimized mechanical properties of the nanofiber these states are quantized despite phonon-induced decoherence. We further show that it is possible to influence their properties with additional nanofiber-guided light fields and suggest heterodyne fluorescence spectroscopy to probe the spectrum of the quantized atomic motion. Extending the optical control of atoms to smaller atom-surface separations could create opportunities for quantum communication and instigate the convergence of surface physics, quantum optics, and the physics of cold atoms.
entries.anonymized_problem: Achieving quantum control of atoms at nanometer-scale distances from solid surfaces represents an open challenge at the intersection of quantum optics, cold-atom physics, and surface science. This work theoretically investigates the motional quantum states of atoms weakly bound to the surface of a thermally excited optical nanofiber. Analysis demonstrates that, despite phonon-induced decoherence from the hot fiber, the motional states of surface-bound atoms can remain quantized when the nanofiber's mechanical properties are appropriately optimized. The study further shows that nanofiber-guided light fields can be used to manipulate the properties of these bound states. Heterodyne fluorescence spectroscopy is proposed as a diagnostic technique to probe the spectrum of the quantized atomic motion. The theoretical framework identifies parameter regimes in which coherent quantum behavior persists near the surface, suggesting that extending optical control to sub-nanometer atom-surface separations could enable applications in quantum communication and provide a new platform for studying near-surface interactions such as Casimir-Polder forces. The results point toward a convergence of surface physics, quantum optics, and cold-atom physics facilitated by nanophotonic waveguide geometries.

entries.original_title: Complex Density of Continuum States in Resonant Quantum Tunneling.
entries.original_abstract: We introduce a complex-extended continuum level density and apply it to one-dimensional scattering problems involving tunneling through finite-range potentials. We show that the real part of the density is proportional to a real "time shift" of the transmitted particle, while the imaginary part reflects the imaginary time of an instantonlike tunneling trajectory. We confirm these assumptions for several potentials using the complex scaling method. In particular, we show that stationary points of the potentials give rise to specific singularities of both real and imaginary densities which represent close analogues of excited-state quantum phase transitions in bound systems.
entries.anonymized_problem: A complex-extended formulation of the continuum level density is developed and applied to one-dimensional quantum scattering problems involving tunneling through finite-range potentials. The central question concerns how to capture both real and imaginary temporal aspects of the tunneling process within a unified density-of-states framework. The real part of this complex density is shown to be proportional to a real time shift experienced by the transmitted particle, while the imaginary part encodes the imaginary time associated with an instanton-like tunneling trajectory through the classically forbidden region. These interpretations are verified for several model potentials using the complex scaling method, which analytically continues the Hamiltonian into the complex plane to expose resonance structure. A key finding is that stationary points of the potential generate specific singularities in both the real and imaginary components of the density, and these singularities are identified as close analogues of excited-state quantum phase transitions known to occur in bound systems. The results establish a direct connection between tunneling dynamics, complex-time semiclassical paths, and critical phenomena in the continuum, providing a unified perspective on resonant transmission through finite barriers.

entries.original_title: Bidirectional dynamic scaling in an isolated Bose gas far from equilibrium
entries.original_abstract: Understanding and classifying non-equilibrium many-body phenomena, analogously to the classification of equilibrium states of matter into universality classes1,2, is an outstanding problem in physics. From stellar matter to financial markets, any many-body system can be out of equilibrium in a myriad of ways, and many are difficult to experiment on. It is therefore a major goal to establish universal principles that apply to different phenomena and physical systems. For equilibrium states, the universality seen in the self-similar spatial scaling of systems close to phase transitions lies at the heart of their classification. Recent theoretical work3–14 and experimental evidence15,16 suggest that isolated many-body systems far from equilibrium generically exhibit dynamic (spatiotemporal) self-similar scaling, akin to turbulent cascades17 and the Family–Vicsek scaling in classical surface growth18,19. Here we observe bidirectional dynamic scaling in an isolated quench-cooled atomic Bose gas; as the gas thermalizes and undergoes Bose–Einstein condensation, it shows self-similar net flows of particles towards the infrared (smaller momenta) and energy towards the ultraviolet (smaller length scales). For both infrared and ultraviolet dynamics we find that the scaling exponents are independent of the strength of the interparticle interactions that drive the thermalization. Momentum-space transport behaviour studied in a quench-cooled isolated atomic Bose gas shows a self-similar scaling character, implying the existence of a far-from-equilibrium universality class.
entries.anonymized_problem: Non-equilibrium many-body dynamics lack a systematic classification analogous to equilibrium universality classes, which are characterized by self-similar spatial scaling near phase transitions. Recent theoretical frameworks and preliminary experiments suggest that isolated many-body systems far from equilibrium can exhibit dynamic spatiotemporal self-similar scaling, reminiscent of turbulent cascades and classical surface-growth scaling laws. This work investigates whether such dynamic scaling occurs bidirectionally in a quenched isolated atomic Bose gas undergoing thermalization and Bose–Einstein condensation. An atomic Bose gas was quench-cooled and its momentum-space dynamics monitored as it evolved toward equilibrium. The system exhibits simultaneous self-similar scaling in two directions: a net particle flow toward the infrared (lower momenta) and a net energy flow toward the ultraviolet (smaller length scales). Crucially, the extracted scaling exponents governing both the infrared and ultraviolet dynamics are found to be independent of the strength of interparticle interactions driving thermalization, despite interactions setting the timescale for the process. This interaction-independence of the exponents implies that the observed dynamic scaling behavior constitutes a far-from-equilibrium universality class, extending the concept of universality beyond equilibrium critical phenomena to isolated quantum systems relaxing after a strong perturbation.

entries.original_title: Anisotropy-Induced Soliton Excitation in Magnetized Strong-Rung Spin Ladders.
entries.original_abstract: We report low temperature electron spin resonance experimental and theoretical studies of an archetype S=1/2 strong-rung spin ladder material (C_{5}H_{12}N)_{2}CuBr_{4}. Unexpected dynamics is detected deep in the Tomonaga-Luttinger spin liquid regime. Close to the point where the system is half-magnetized (and believed to be equivalent to a gapless easy plane chain in zero field) we observed orientation-dependent spin gap and anomalous g-factor values. Field theoretical analysis demonstrates that the observed low-energy excitation modes in magnetized (C_{5}H_{12}N)_{2}CuBr_{4} are solitonic excitations caused by Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction presence.
entries.anonymized_problem: Low-temperature electron spin resonance (ESR) measurements and field-theoretical analysis are used to investigate the spin dynamics of a S=1/2 strong-rung spin ladder compound, (C₅H₁₂N)₂CuBr₄, in an applied magnetic field. The study addresses unexpected dynamical behavior observed deep within the Tomonaga-Luttinger spin liquid (TLSL) regime, specifically near the half-magnetization point where the system is theoretically equivalent to a gapless easy-plane chain in zero field. ESR experiments reveal orientation-dependent spin gap features and anomalous g-factor values that are inconsistent with a purely gapless description. Field-theoretical analysis is applied to interpret these observations, demonstrating that the detected low-energy excitation modes are solitonic in character and arise from the presence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction. The anisotropy introduced by DM coupling induces a finite spin gap and modifies the effective g-factor in an orientation-dependent manner, generating soliton excitations within what would otherwise be a gapless TLSL phase. These results establish that weak spin-orbit-driven anisotropy can fundamentally alter the low-energy excitation spectrum of magnetized spin ladder systems, producing solitonic modes that are directly detectable by ESR spectroscopy.

entries.original_title: Dissecting Strong-Field Excitation Dynamics with Atomic-Momentum Spectroscopy.
entries.original_abstract: Observation of internal quantum dynamics relies on correlations between the system being observed and the measurement apparatus. We propose using the c.m. degrees of freedom of atoms and molecules as a "built-in" monitoring device for observing their internal dynamics in nonperturbative laser fields. We illustrate the idea on the simplest model system-the hydrogen atom in an intense, tightly focused infrared laser beam. To this end, we develop a numerically tractable, quantum-mechanical treatment of correlations between internal and c.m. dynamics. We show that the transverse momentum records the time excited states experience the field, allowing femtosecond reconstruction of the strong-field excitation process. The ground state becomes weak-field seeking, an unambiguous and long sought-for signature of the Kramers-Henneberger regime.
entries.anonymized_problem: The internal quantum dynamics of atoms and molecules in strong laser fields are difficult to observe directly, as detection typically requires correlating the system with an external measurement apparatus. This work explores the use of center-of-mass (c.m.) degrees of freedom as an intrinsic monitoring device for probing internal dynamics under nonperturbative laser fields. The approach is demonstrated on a hydrogen atom subjected to an intense, tightly focused infrared laser beam. A numerically tractable quantum-mechanical framework is developed to treat correlations between internal electronic states and c.m. motion. Analysis shows that the transverse momentum of the atom encodes the duration for which excited states interact with the field, enabling femtosecond-scale reconstruction of the strong-field excitation process. A key finding is that the ground state exhibits weak-field-seeking behavior under these conditions, providing a clear and long-anticipated signature of the Kramers-Henneberger regime—a high-frequency, high-intensity limiting case in which the electron dynamics are described in the frame of a quiver motion. These results establish atomic momentum spectroscopy as a viable diagnostic for resolving strong-field excitation pathways with high temporal resolution.

entries.original_title: Automatic Fine-Tuning in the Two-Flavor Schwinger Model.
entries.original_abstract: I discuss the two-flavor Schwinger model both without and with fermion masses. I argue that the phenomenon of "conformal coalescence," in unparticle physics in which linear combinations of short-distance operators can disappear from the long-distance theory, makes it easy to understand some puzzling features of the model with small fermion masses. In particular, I argue that for an average fermion mass m_{f} and a mass difference δm, so long as both are small compared to the dynamical gauge boson mass m=esqrt[2/π], isospin-breaking effects in the low-energy theory are exponentially suppressed by powers of exp[-(m/m_{f})^{2/3}] even if δm≈m_{f}. In the low-energy theory, this looks like exponential fine-tuning, but it is done automatically by conformal coalescence.
entries.anonymized_problem: The two-flavor Schwinger model — quantum electrodynamics in 1+1 dimensions with two fermion flavors — is examined both in the massless limit and with small fermion masses. A key puzzle in this model concerns the apparent fine-tuning required to suppress isospin-breaking effects at low energies even when the fermion mass difference is comparable to the average fermion mass. To address this, the analysis draws on the concept of "conformal coalescence" from unparticle physics, wherein specific linear combinations of short-distance operators decouple from the long-distance effective theory due to renormalization group flow near a conformal fixed point. By identifying how operator mixing near the ultraviolet fixed point causes certain isospin-breaking combinations to acquire large anomalous dimensions, it is argued that isospin-breaking effects in the infrared theory are exponentially suppressed by factors of the form exp[-(m/m_f)^{2/3}], where m is the dynamical gauge boson mass and m_f is the average fermion mass. This suppression holds even when the mass splitting δm is of order m_f. The result explains why the low-energy spectrum appears finely tuned without any explicit parameter adjustment: the suppression arises automatically from the conformal structure of the ultraviolet theory rather than from any imposed cancellation.

entries.original_title: State Aggregations in Markov Chains and Block Models of Networks.
entries.original_abstract: We consider state-aggregation schemes for Markov chains from an information-theoretic perspective. Specifically, we consider aggregating the states of a Markov chain such that the mutual information of the aggregated states separated by T time steps is maximized. We show that for T=1 this recovers the maximum-likelihood estimator of the degree-corrected stochastic block model as a particular case, which enables us to explain certain features of the likelihood landscape of this generative network model from a dynamical lens. We further highlight how we can uncover coherent, long-range dynamical modules for which considering a timescale T≫1 is essential. We demonstrate our results using synthetic flows and real-world ocean currents, where we are able to recover the fundamental features of the surface currents of the oceans.
entries.anonymized_problem: This work examines state-aggregation schemes for Markov chains using an information-theoretic framework. The central question is how to group states of a Markov chain such that the mutual information between aggregated states separated by T time steps is maximized. It is shown analytically that for T = 1, this criterion recovers the maximum-likelihood estimator of the degree-corrected stochastic block model as a special case, providing a dynamical interpretation of the likelihood landscape of this generative network model and clarifying certain features of its optimization geometry. The framework is then extended to T ≫ 1, where maximizing lagged mutual information identifies coherent, long-range dynamical modules that persist across multiple timescales—structures that short-timescale analyses would miss. The approach is validated on synthetic flow systems and applied to real-world ocean current data, where aggregations at appropriate timescales recover the fundamental large-scale circulation features of global ocean surface currents. The results establish a unified perspective connecting community detection in networks with dynamical coarse-graining of stochastic processes, showing that the choice of timescale T controls which structural or dynamical features of the system are emphasized in the resulting partition.

entries.original_title: Emergence of Constructor-Based Irreversibility in Quantum Systems: Theory and Experiment.
entries.original_abstract: How irreversibility arises in a universe with time-reversal symmetric laws is a central problem in physics. In this Letter, we discuss a radically different take on the emergence of irreversibility, adopting the recently proposed constructor theory framework. Irreversibility is expressed as the requirement that a task is possible, while its inverse is not. We prove the compatibility of such irreversibility with quantum theory's time-reversal symmetric laws, using a dynamical model based on the universal quantum homogenizer. We also test the physical realizability of this model by means of an experimental demonstration with high-quality single-photon qubits.
entries.anonymized_problem: The emergence of irreversibility in a universe governed by time-reversal symmetric laws is a longstanding open problem in physics. This work examines irreversibility through the lens of constructor theory, a framework in which physical tasks are characterized by whether they can be performed reliably and repeatedly. Within this framework, irreversibility is defined as the condition in which a given task is possible while its inverse task is not. A theoretical proof is presented establishing that this form of irreversibility is compatible with the time-reversal symmetric structure of quantum mechanics. The proof relies on a dynamical model built around the universal quantum homogenizer, a process that drives a quantum system toward a fixed state through repeated interactions. To assess the physical realizability of this model, an experimental demonstration is carried out using high-quality single-photon qubits. The results confirm that constructor-based irreversibility can be instantiated within quantum mechanics without violating its fundamental symmetries, providing a concrete physical mechanism through which irreversible behavior emerges from reversible underlying dynamics.

entries.original_title: Precision Measurement of the Beam-Normal Single-Spin Asymmetry in Forward-Angle Elastic Electron-Proton Scattering.
entries.original_abstract: A beam-normal single-spin asymmetry generated in the scattering of transversely polarized electrons from unpolarized nucleons is an observable related to the imaginary part of the two-photon exchange process. We report a 2% precision measurement of the beam-normal single-spin asymmetry in elastic electron-proton scattering with a mean scattering angle of θ_{lab}=7.9° and a mean energy of 1.149 GeV. The asymmetry result is B_{n}=-5.194±0.067(stat)±0.082 (syst) ppm. This is the most precise measurement of this quantity available to date and therefore provides a stringent test of two-photon exchange models at far-forward scattering angles (θ_{lab}→0) where they should be most reliable.
entries.anonymized_problem: The beam-normal single-spin asymmetry (B_n) in elastic electron-proton scattering is an observable sensitive to the imaginary part of the two-photon exchange (TPE) amplitude, a process relevant to understanding radiative corrections in electron-nucleon scattering. This work presents a precision measurement of B_n at forward scattering angles, using transversely polarized electrons incident on unpolarized protons at a mean laboratory scattering angle of θ_lab = 7.9° and a mean beam energy of 1.149 GeV. The measured asymmetry is B_n = −5.194 ± 0.067(stat) ± 0.082(syst) ppm, representing a 2% total precision. This precision enables a stringent test of theoretical TPE models in the far-forward kinematic regime (θ_lab → 0°), where such models are expected to be most reliable because hadronic intermediate states are most constrained. The result provides an important benchmark for evaluating the accuracy of TPE calculations, which are necessary for interpreting parity-violating electron scattering experiments and resolving discrepancies in proton electromagnetic form factor extractions. The measurement constrains the hadronic structure entering the two-photon amplitude and offers a high-precision data point against which competing theoretical approaches to TPE can be quantitatively compared.

entries.original_title: Electronic Nematicity in URu_{2}Si_{2} Revisited.
entries.original_abstract: The nature of the hidden-order (HO) state in URu_{2}Si_{2} remains one of the major unsolved issues in heavy-fermion physics. Recently, torque magnetometry, x-ray diffraction, and elastoresistivity data have suggested that the HO phase transition at T_{HO}≈ 17.5  K is driven by electronic nematic effects. Here, we search for thermodynamic signatures of this purported structural instability using anisotropic thermal expansion, Young's modulus, elastoresistivity, and specific-heat measurements. In contrast to the published results, we find no evidence of a rotational symmetry breaking in any of our data. Interestingly, our elastoresistivity measurements, which are in full agreement with published results, exhibit a Curie-Weiss divergence, which we however attribute to a volume and not to a symmetry-breaking effect. Finally, clear evidence for thermal fluctuations is observed in our heat-capacity data, from which we estimate the HO correlation length.
entries.anonymized_problem: The nature of the hidden-order (HO) phase transition in URu₂Si₂ at T_HO ≈ 17.5 K remains a central unresolved problem in heavy-fermion physics. Prior torque magnetometry, x-ray diffraction, and elastoresistivity measurements have been interpreted as evidence that this transition is driven by electronic nematic order, implying rotational symmetry breaking. To critically examine this interpretation, thermodynamic and transport measurements were performed, including anisotropic thermal expansion, Young's modulus, elastoresistivity, and specific-heat measurements. No signatures of rotational symmetry breaking were found in any of the thermodynamic probes. Elastoresistivity data, consistent with previously published results, display a Curie-Weiss divergence; however, this divergence is attributed here to a volume (non-symmetry-breaking) effect rather than a nematic instability. Additionally, specific-heat data near T_HO reveal clear evidence of thermal fluctuations, from which an estimate of the hidden-order correlation length is extracted. These findings challenge the electronic nematicity interpretation of the hidden-order transition and suggest that the Curie-Weiss behavior in elastoresistivity does not constitute unambiguous evidence for rotational symmetry breaking in URu₂Si₂.

entries.original_title: Measuring Gaussian Rigidity Using Curved Substrates.
entries.original_abstract: The Gaussian (saddle splay) rigidity of fluid membranes controls their equilibrium topology but is notoriously difficult to measure. In lipid mixtures, typical of living cells, linear interfaces separate liquid ordered (LO) from liquid disordered (LD) bilayer phases at subcritical temperatures. Here, we consider such membranes supported by curved substrates that thereby control the membrane curvatures. We show how spectral analysis of the fluctuations of the LO-LD interface provides a novel way of measuring the difference in Gaussian rigidity between the two phases. We provide a number of conditions for such interface fluctuations to be both experimentally measurable and sufficiently sensitive to the value of the Gaussian rigidity, while remaining in the perturbative regime of our analysis.
entries.anonymized_problem: The Gaussian (saddle-splay) rigidity of fluid membranes governs their equilibrium topology but remains experimentally inaccessible through conventional approaches. This work examines lipid-bilayer membranes composed of mixtures representative of biological cell membranes, in which linear interfaces separate liquid-ordered and liquid-disordered phases at subcritical temperatures. By supporting such membranes on curved substrates that impose controlled mean and Gaussian curvatures, a theoretical framework is developed showing that spectral analysis of thermal fluctuations of the liquid-ordered/liquid-disordered domain boundary provides a route to measuring the difference in Gaussian rigidity between the two coexisting phases. The analysis proceeds perturbatively, treating the substrate curvature as a small parameter, and yields explicit expressions relating the fluctuation spectrum of the interface to the Gaussian rigidity contrast. A set of practical conditions is derived under which the interface fluctuations are simultaneously detectable experimentally, sensitive to the Gaussian rigidity difference, and consistent with the perturbative approximation. The results offer a physically transparent and experimentally actionable strategy for extracting a material parameter that conventional flat-membrane fluctuation experiments cannot resolve.

entries.original_title: Complex Geometric Structure of a Simple Solid-Liquid Interface: GaN(0001)-Ga.
entries.original_abstract: The equilibrium atomic interface structure between Ga and GaN(0001) is shown to contain substrate surface vacancies followed by substrate-induced layering and preferential lateral ordering in the liquid. The uncovered presence of point defects, in the form of vacancies at both sides of the solid-liquid interface, is an important structural feature which governs the local physical properties. Our x-ray diffraction study reveals that the layering is very stable and persists up to a temperature of 1123 K and a nitrogen pressure of 32 bar. The Ga layer spacing agrees remarkably well with the Friedel oscillation period for this system.
entries.anonymized_problem: The atomic-scale structure of the equilibrium solid-liquid interface between gallium liquid and the GaN(0001) substrate surface is investigated to understand how interfacial ordering and defects govern local physical properties. X-ray diffraction is employed to probe the interface structure across a range of thermodynamic conditions. The study reveals that the interface contains substrate surface vacancies on both sides of the solid-liquid boundary, representing a significant structural feature with implications for local physical behavior. Beyond these point defects, the liquid gallium exhibits substrate-induced layering accompanied by preferential lateral ordering. This layered structure is found to be remarkably stable, persisting up to temperatures of 1123 K and nitrogen pressures of 32 bar. The measured gallium interlayer spacing shows strong agreement with the Friedel oscillation period predicted for this system, providing a quantitative connection between interfacial ordering and electronic screening in the liquid metal. These findings demonstrate that even an apparently simple solid-liquid interface can exhibit complex structural features—including point defects, induced layering, and lateral ordering—that are important for understanding crystal growth and surface phenomena in technologically relevant nitride systems.

entries.original_title: Superfluid Flow of Polaron Polaritons above Landau's Critical Velocity.
entries.original_abstract: We develop a theory for the interaction of light with superfluid optical media, describing the motion of quantum impurities that are created and dragged through the liquid by propagating photons. It is well known that a mobile impurity suffers dissipation due to phonon emission as soon as it moves faster than the speed of sound in the superfluid-Landau's critical velocity. Surprisingly we find that in the present hybrid light-matter setting, polaritonic impurities can be protected against environmental decoherence and be allowed to propagate well above the Landau velocity without jeopardizing the superfluid response of the medium.
entries.anonymized_problem: A theoretical framework is developed to describe the interaction of light with superfluid optical media, specifically addressing the dynamics of quantum impurities created and transported through a superfluid by propagating photons. In conventional superfluid physics, a mobile impurity undergoes dissipation via phonon emission once its velocity exceeds the speed of sound in the medium — Landau's critical velocity — which typically disrupts superfluid behavior. The central question is whether this dissipation threshold can be circumvented in hybrid light-matter systems. Using a theoretical treatment of polaritonic impurities (quasiparticles formed from the coupling of photons with mobile impurities in a superfluid), it is found that the photonic component of these hybrid quasiparticles provides effective protection against environmental decoherence. This protection allows the polaritonic impurities to propagate at velocities significantly exceeding the Landau critical velocity without compromising the superfluid response of the surrounding medium. The result reveals a qualitative departure from standard polaron physics in purely matter-based systems, suggesting that the light-matter hybridization fundamentally modifies the dissipation mechanisms that ordinarily enforce the Landau velocity constraint.

entries.original_title: Tunable Three-Body Loss in a Nonlinear Rydberg Medium.
entries.original_abstract: Long-range Rydberg interactions, in combination with electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT), give rise to strongly interacting photons where the strength, sign, and form of the interactions are widely tunable and controllable. Such control can be applied to both coherent and dissipative interactions, which provides the potential for generating novel few-photon states. Recently it has been shown that Rydberg-EIT is a rare system in which three-body interactions can be as strong or stronger than two-body interactions. In this work, we study three-body scattering loss for Rydberg-EIT in a wide regime of single and two-photon detunings. Our numerical simulations of the full three-body wave function and analytical estimates based on Fermi's golden rule strongly suggest that the observed features in the outgoing photonic correlations are caused by the resonant enhancement of the three-body losses.
entries.anonymized_problem: Strongly interacting photon systems realized through Rydberg atom electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) offer widely tunable two- and three-body interactions, including both coherent and dissipative channels. A particularly notable feature of this platform is that three-body interactions can be comparable to or exceed two-body interactions in strength—an unusual regime in quantum optical systems. This work investigates three-body scattering loss in a Rydberg-EIT medium across a broad parameter space of single-photon and two-photon detunings. The approach combines full numerical simulations of the three-body photonic wave function with analytical estimates derived from Fermi's golden rule. The results strongly indicate that characteristic features observed in outgoing photonic correlation functions arise from resonant enhancement of three-body loss processes. By systematically mapping the dependence of these loss features on detuning parameters, the study clarifies the mechanism by which three-body dissipative interactions shape few-photon output statistics. These findings advance understanding of how multi-body loss channels can be controlled in nonlinear quantum optical media, with implications for engineering specific few-photon quantum states through selective enhancement or suppression of multi-body scattering pathways.
